#  torch.cumprod  ¶

torch.  cumprod  (  _ input  _ , _ dim  _ , _ *  _ , _ dtype  =  None  _ , _
out  =  None  _ )  →  [ Tensor  ](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor")
¶

    

Returns the cumulative product of elements of ` input  ` in the dimension `
dim  ` .

For example, if ` input  ` is a vector of size N, the result will also be a
vector of size N, with elements.

y  i  =  x  1  ×  x  2  ×  x  3  ×  ⋯  ×  x  i  y_i = x_1 \times x_2\times
x_3\times \dots \times x_i  y  i  ​  =  x  1  ​  ×  x  2  ​  ×  x  3  ​  ×  ⋯
×  x  i  ​

Parameters

    

  * **input** ( [ _Tensor_ ](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor") ) – the input tensor. 

  * **dim** ( [ _int_ ](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int "\(in Python v3.12\)") ) – the dimension to do the operation over 

Keyword Arguments

    

  * **dtype** ( [ ` torch.dtype  ` ](../tensor_attributes.html#torch.dtype "torch.dtype") , optional) – the desired data type of returned tensor. If specified, the input tensor is casted to [ ` dtype  ` ](../tensor_attributes.html#torch.dtype "torch.dtype") before the operation is performed. This is useful for preventing data type overflows. Default: None. 

  * **out** ( [ _Tensor_ ](../tensors.html#torch.Tensor "torch.Tensor") _,_ _optional_ ) – the output tensor. 

Example:

    
    
    >>> a = torch.randn(10)
    >>> a
    tensor([ 0.6001,  0.2069, -0.1919,  0.9792,  0.6727,  1.0062,  0.4126,
            -0.2129, -0.4206,  0.1968])
    >>> torch.cumprod(a, dim=0)
    tensor([ 0.6001,  0.1241, -0.0238, -0.0233, -0.0157, -0.0158, -0.0065,
             0.0014, -0.0006, -0.0001])
    
    >>> a[5] = 0.0
    >>> torch.cumprod(a, dim=0)
    tensor([ 0.6001,  0.1241, -0.0238, -0.0233, -0.0157, -0.0000, -0.0000,
             0.0000, -0.0000, -0.0000])

Usage notes  ¶
  * A privilege can be granted to a role multiple times by different grantors. A REVOKE _ <privilege> _ statement only revokes grants for which the active role, or a lower role in a hierarchy, is the grantor. Any additional grants of a specified privilege by other grantors are ignored. 
Also note that a REVOKE _ <privilege> _ statement is successful even if no
privileges are revoked. A REVOKE _ <privilege> _ statement only returns an
error if a specified privilege has dependent grants and the CASCADE clause is
omitted in the statement.
  * Multiple privileges can be specified for the same object type in a single GRANT statement (with each privilege separated by commas), or the special ` ALL  [  PRIVILEGES  ]  ` keyword can be used to grant all applicable privileges to the specified object type. Note, however, that only privileges held and grantable by the role executing the GRANT command are actually granted to the target role. A warning message is returned for any privileges that could not be granted. 
You cannot specify this keyword for tags.
  * For schemas and objects in schemas, an option is provided to grant privileges on all objects of the same type within the container (i.e. database or schema). This is a convenience option; internally, the command is expanded into a series of individual GRANT commands on each object. Only objects that currently exist within the container are affected. 
However, note that, in the Snowflake model, bulk granting of privileges is not
a recommended practice. Instead, Snowflake recommends creating a shared role
and using the role to create objects that are automatically accessible to all
users who have been granted the role.
  * For stages: 
    * USAGE only applies to external stages. 
    * READ | WRITE only applies to internal stages. In addition, to grant the WRITE privilege on an internal stage, the READ privilege must first be granted on the stage. 
For more details about external and internal stages, see [ CREATE STAGE

  * ` Gallery `
  * ` UiPurchaseCard ` that is responsible for “add to cart” functionality 
  * ` ProductProperties ` that allows to select a different product configuration 
  * ` ProductAccordion ` with full product description and customer reviews 
  * ` RecommendedProducts `

They all have one thing in common - they can remain completely static until
the user interacts with them (eg. by clicking ). In some (many) cases, this
could never happen - for example, a user could never click on the slider
below, yet we download and execute it’s code.

If our components do not need to be hydrated eagerly, wouldn’t it be better to
perform this process lazily? This way, we will make the hydration almost
instantaneous and execute only the needed code.

While Nuxt doesn’t work this way out of the box, lazy hydration can be
achieved very easily with a third-party library called [ nuxt-lazy-hydrate
](https://github.com/Baroshem/nuxt-lazy-hydrate) (which is a Nuxt wrapper for
a [ Vue 3 Lazy Hydration Plugin ](https://github.com/freddy38510/vue3-lazy-
hydration) that can be used for any server-side-rendered Vue.js application).
It’s dead simple to use.

First, install the module in your Nuxt application:

    
    
    npm install nuxt-lazy-hydrate
    
    
    // nuxt.config.js
    {
      modules: [
            "nuxt-lazy-hydrate"
        ],
    }

Once it’s installed, wrap the desired piece of the UI and specify when it
should be hydrated using one of the available directives:

  * ` when-idle ` runs when the main thread work is done and the browser goes idle. It’s important to be aware that it is using ` window.requestIdleCallback ` under the hood which is [ not supported ](https://caniuse.com/requestidlecallback) in Safari. 

    
    
    <NuxtLazyHydrate when-idle>
        <ProductSlider>
    </NuxtLazyHydrate>

  * ` on-interaction ` as the name suggests runs only after interacts with a component in a certain way, eg. via ` click ` or ` focus ` . 

    
    
    <NuxtLazyHydrate :on-interaction="['click', 'touchstart']">
      <ProductSlider>
    </NuxtLazyHydrate>

  * ` when-triggered ` allows you to bind a custom function that returns a boolean reactive value 

    
    
    <template>
        <NuxtLazyHydrate when-triggered="triggerHydration">
          <ProductSlider>
          </NuxtLazyHydrate>
    </template>
    
    <script setup>
        triggerHydration () {
          // custom logic for hydration trigger
        }
    </script>

  * ` when-visible ` hydrates the component when it appears in the viewport 

    
    
    <NuxtLazyHydrate when-visible>
      <ProductSlider>
    </NuxtLazyHydrate>

  * If you don’t use any properties on the hydration wrapper, the child component will never get hydrated 

    
    
    <NuxtLazyHydrate>
      <ProductSlider>
    </NuxtLazyHydrate>

Now that you know what options are available, get back to the Product Page
code snippet above and think about which components you would wrap with `
NuxtLazyHydrate ` component and what hydration conditions you would use. Once
you do it, you can [ check how we did it
](https://github.com/vuestorefront/storefront-
nuxt3-boilerplate/blob/develop/apps/web/pages/product/%5Bslug%5D.vue) but
don’t get discouraged if it does not match your ideas. There is usually more
than one good approach and as long as the component hydration is not blocking
the main thread it’s a correct one.

##  How does lazy hydration work?

So, how does this plugin work, and what savings does it bring? As we learned a
few paragraphs earlier, JavaScript code must be downloaded and executed to
make a component dynamic. This is precisely what we are saving by leveraging
the lazy hydration technique. At its core, it’s nothing else than the [ lazy
loading of a component ](https://vueschool.io/articles/vuejs-tutorials/lazy-
loading-and-code-splitting-in-vue-js/) . The only difference between regular
lazy loading and lazy hydration is that we also use it to hydrate a piece of

##  Class and Module Fixtures  Â¶

Class and module level fixtures are implemented in  ` TestSuite  ` . When the
test suite encounters a test from a new class then ` tearDownClass()  ` from
the previous class (if there is one) is called, followed by ` setUpClass()  `
from the new class.

Similarly if a test is from a different module from the previous test then `
tearDownModule  ` from the previous module is run, followed by ` setUpModule
` from the new module.

After all the tests have run the final ` tearDownClass  ` and ` tearDownModule
` are run.

Note that shared fixtures do not play well with [potential] features like test
parallelization and they break test isolation. They should be used with care.

The default ordering of tests created by the unittest test loaders is to group
all tests from the same modules and classes together. This will lead to `
setUpClass  ` / ` setUpModule  ` (etc) being called exactly once per class and
module. If you randomize the order, so that tests from different modules and
classes are adjacent to each other, then these shared fixture functions may be
called multiple times in a single test run.

Shared fixtures are not intended to work with suites with non-standard
ordering. A ` BaseTestSuite  ` still exists for frameworks that donât want
to support shared fixtures.

If there are any exceptions raised during one of the shared fixture functions
the test is reported as an error. Because there is no corresponding test
instance an ` _ErrorHolder  ` object (that has the same interface as a  `
TestCase  ` ) is created to represent the error. If you are just using the
standard unittest test runner then this detail doesnât matter, but if you
are a framework author it may be relevant.

###  setUpClass and tearDownClass  Â¶

These must be implemented as class methods:

    
    
    import unittest
    
    class Test(unittest.TestCase):
        @classmethod
        def setUpClass(cls):
            cls._connection = createExpensiveConnectionObject()
    
        @classmethod
        def tearDownClass(cls):
            cls._connection.destroy()
    

If you want the ` setUpClass  ` and ` tearDownClass  ` on base classes called
then you must call up to them yourself. The implementations in  ` TestCase  `
are empty.

If an exception is raised during a ` setUpClass  ` then the tests in the class
are not run and the ` tearDownClass  ` is not run. Skipped classes will not
have ` setUpClass  ` or ` tearDownClass  ` run. If the exception is a  `
SkipTest  ` exception then the class will be reported as having been skipped
instead of as an error.

###  setUpModule and tearDownModule  Â¶

These should be implemented as functions:

    
    
    def setUpModule():
        createConnection()
    
    def tearDownModule():
        closeConnection()
    

If an exception is raised in a ` setUpModule  ` then none of the tests in the
module will be run and the ` tearDownModule  ` will not be run. If the
exception is a  ` SkipTest  ` exception then the module will be reported as
having been skipped instead of as an error.

To add cleanup code that must be run even in the case of an exception, use `
addModuleCleanup  ` :

unittest.  addModuleCleanup  (  _ function  _ , _ /  _ , _ *  args  _ , _ **
kwargs  _ )  Â¶

    

Add a function to be called after ` tearDownModule()  ` to cleanup resources
used during the test class. Functions will be called in reverse order to the
order they are added (  LIFO  ). They are called with any arguments and
keyword arguments passed into  ` addModuleCleanup()  ` when they are added.

If ` setUpModule()  ` fails, meaning that ` tearDownModule()  ` is not called,
then any cleanup functions added will still be called.

i.e. at index ` 0 ` , which can be also seen from the function’s metadata
presented just above.

Similarly, ` LOAD_FAST 1 ` pushes a reference to ` y ` onto the stack,
resulting in the following state after the first two bytecode instructions
have been executed:

    
    
        +---+  <-- TOS (Top Of Stack)
        | y |
        +---+
        | x |
     ---+---+---
    

The next instruction, [ BINARY_ADD
](https://docs.python.org/3.7/library/dis.html#opcode-BINARY_ADD) , takes no
arguments. It simply takes the top two elements from the stack, performs an
addition on them, and pushes the result of the operation back onto the stack.

At the end, [ RETURN_VALUE
](https://docs.python.org/3.7/library/dis.html#opcode-RETURN_VALUE) takes
whatever the remaining element on the stack is, and returns that element to
the caller of the ` add() ` function.

#####  Going even deeper (enter the C level)

The bytecode instructions themselves are also just an abstraction, and
something needs to make sense of them. That “something” is the Python
interpreter. In CPython, its reference implementation, this is a program
written in C that loops through the bytecode given to it, and interprets the
instructions in it one by one.

The heart of this machinery is implemented in [ Python/ceval.c
](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.7.0b1/Python/ceval.c) file. It
runs an infinite loop that contains a [ giant switch statement
](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.7.0b1/Python/ceval.c#L1056) with
each case (target) handling on of the possible bytecode operations.

This is how [ the code
](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.7.0b1/Python/ceval.c#L1264-L1288)
for the instruction BINARY_ADD looks like:

    
    
    TARGET(BINARY_ADD) {
        PyObject *right = POP();
        PyObject *left = TOP();
        PyObject *sum;
    
        /* the computation of the "sum" omitted */
    
        SET_TOP(sum);
        if (sum == NULL)
            goto error;
        DISPATCH();
    }
    

` POP() ` , ` TOP() ` , and ` SET_TOP() ` are convenience C macros that
perform primitive interpreter stack operations such as popping the top value
from the stack, or replacing the current TOS (Top Of Stack) value with a
different one.

The code above is actually pretty straightforward. It pops the right-hand
operand from the top of the stack, which is a reference to ` y ` in our case,
and stores it under the name ` right ` . It then also stores a reference to
the left-hand side operand, i.e. ` x ` , that became the new TOS.

After performing the calculation, it sets the ` sum ` , i.e. a reference to
the result, as the new TOS, performs a quick error check, and dispatches the
control to the next bytecode instruction in the line.

The column ` foo  ` is updated where the column ` bar  ` is greater than 5.
This violates the CoW principles though, because it would have to modify the
view ` df["foo"]  ` and ` df  ` in one step. Hence, chained assignment will
consistently never work and raise a ` ChainedAssignmentError  ` warning with
CoW enabled:

    
    
    In [46]: df = pd.DataFrame({"foo": [1, 2, 3], "bar": [4, 5, 6]})

##  Read-only NumPy arrays  #

Accessing the underlying NumPy array of a DataFrame will return a read-only
array if the array shares data with the initial DataFrame:

The array is a copy if the initial DataFrame consists of more than one array:

    
    
    In [49]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [1.5, 2.5]})
    
    In [50]: df.to_numpy()
    Out[50]: 
    array([[1. , 1.5],
           [2. , 2.5]])
    

The array shares data with the DataFrame if the DataFrame consists of only one
NumPy array:

    
    
    In [51]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
    
    In [52]: df.to_numpy()
    Out[52]: 
    array([[1, 3],
           [2, 4]])
    

This array is read-only, which means that it canât be modified inplace:

    
    
    In [53]: arr = df.to_numpy()
    
    In [54]: arr[0, 0] = 100
    ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
    ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
    Cell In[54], line 1
    ----> 1 arr[0, 0] = 100
    
    ValueError: assignment destination is read-only
    

The same holds true for a Series, since a Series always consists of a single
array.

There are two potential solution to this:

  * Trigger a copy manually if you want to avoid updating DataFrames that share memory with your array. 

  * Make the array writeable. This is a more performant solution but circumvents Copy-on-Write rules, so it should be used with caution. 

    
    
    In [55]: arr = df.to_numpy()
    
    In [56]: arr.flags.writeable = True
    
    In [57]: arr[0, 0] = 100
    
    In [58]: arr
    Out[58]: 
    array([[100,   3],
           [  2,   4]])
    

##  Patterns to avoid  #

No defensive copy will be performed if two objects share the same data while
you are modifying one object inplace.

    
    
    In [59]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
    
    In [60]: df2 = df.reset_index(drop=True)
    
    In [61]: df2.iloc[0, 0] = 100
    

This creates two objects that share data and thus the setitem operation will
trigger a copy. This is not necessary if the initial object ` df  ` isnât
needed anymore. Simply reassigning to the same variable will invalidate the
reference that is held by the object.

    
    
    In [62]: df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3], "b": [4, 5, 6]})
    
    In [63]: df = df.reset_index(drop=True)
    
    In [64]: df.iloc[0, 0] = 100
    

No copy is necessary in this example. Creating multiple references keeps
unnecessary references alive and thus will hurt performance with Copy-on-
Write.

##  Copy-on-Write optimizations  #

A new lazy copy mechanism that defers the copy until the object in question is
modified and only if this object shares data with another object. This
mechanism was added to methods that donât require a copy of the underlying
data. Popular examples are [ ` DataFrame.drop()  `
](../reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.drop.html#pandas.DataFrame.drop
"pandas.DataFrame.drop") for ` axis=1  ` and [ ` DataFrame.rename()  `
](../reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.rename.html#pandas.DataFrame.rename
"pandas.DataFrame.rename") .

These methods return views when Copy-on-Write is enabled, which provides a
significant performance improvement compared to the regular execution.

# How to Configure DHCP Reservations on Your Home Router  

If you’ve ever experienced devices on your network getting random IP addresses, you know it can cause headaches—especially when you rely on consistent IPs for things like file sharing, remote access, or smart home integrations. One way to solve this is by setting **DHCP reservations** on your home router. This ensures specified devices always get the same IP address from the router’s DHCP server.  

In this guide, we’ll walk through the process step by step, from accessing your router’s admin panel to assigning fixed IPs, and provide tips for troubleshooting common issues.  

---

## Step 1: Access Your Router’s Admin Panel  

1. **Connect to your network**  
   Make sure your computer or mobile device is connected to your home network—either via Wi-Fi or Ethernet.  

2. **Find your router’s IP address**  
   - On Windows: Open Command Prompt and type `ipconfig`. Look for the *Default Gateway* entry.  
   - On macOS: Go to *System Preferences → Network*, select your active connection, and click *Advanced → TCP/IP*.  
   - On mobile devices: Check your Wi-Fi network’s settings.  

3. **Log in to the router**  
   Open a web browser, enter the router’s IP address into the address bar, and press Enter. You’ll be prompted for a username and password. If you haven’t changed these, check the sticker on the router or the manufacturer’s documentation.  

---

## Step 2: Locate the DHCP Settings  

Once inside the admin panel, look for sections labeled **LAN Setup**, **Network Settings**, or **Advanced Settings**. The exact wording varies by manufacturer, but the DHCP configuration page is usually under *LAN* or *Local Network*.  

You should see a table listing connected devices, their assigned IP addresses, and their MAC addresses.  

---

## Step 3: Identify the Devices You Want to Reserve  

A **MAC address** is a unique identifier assigned to each network card. You’ll need this to set a reservation.  

- **Find the MAC address**:  
  - On Windows: Open Command Prompt, type `ipconfig /all`, and look for *Physical Address*.  
  - On macOS: Go to *System Preferences → Network*, select your active connection, click *Advanced*, and check the *Hardware* tab.  
  - On mobile devices: Check your Wi-Fi settings; often the MAC address is listed as *Wi-Fi Address*.  

Make a note of the MAC address and the current IP address for each device you want to reserve.  

---

## Step 4: Create DHCP Reservations  

On the DHCP configuration page, look for an option like **Address Reservation**, **Static Lease**, or **DHCP Binding**.  

1. **Add new reservation**  
   There will typically be a form where you enter:  
   - **Device Name** (for your reference)  
   - **MAC Address**  
   - **Desired IP Address**  

2. **Choose an IP address**  
   It’s best to pick an IP within your router’s DHCP range but outside the range used for automatic assignment. For example, if your DHCP pool is `192.168.1.100` to `192.168.1.200`, you might reserve `192.168.1.50` for a specific device.  

3. **Save and apply changes**  
   After adding the reservation, save the settings. Some routers require a reboot to apply changes.  

---

## Step 5: Verify the Reservation  

Restart the device or disconnect/reconnect it to the network. It should now receive the reserved IP address every time it connects. You can verify this by checking the device’s network properties or viewing the router’s DHCP table.  

---

## Troubleshooting DHCP Reservations  

Even with reservations set, some issues can arise. Here are common problems and solutions:  

- **Device still gets a different IP**  
  - Ensure the MAC address was entered correctly (no typos, correct format).  
  - Check if the device is using a static IP configuration in its own settings, which can override DHCP.  

- **IP address conflict**  
  - Avoid assigning the same IP to multiple devices.  
  - Make sure the reserved IP isn’t part of another static IP configuration elsewhere on the network.  

- **Router not applying changes**  
  - Some routers require a reboot after changes.  
  - Try clearing the router’s DHCP lease table.  

- **Device not appearing in DHCP list**  
  - Connect the device to the network and refresh the router’s admin page.  
  - If it still doesn’t appear, verify the device’s network settings or update its drivers/firmware.  

---

## Why DHCP Reservations Are Useful  

Consistent IP addresses can make network management much easier. They’re essential if you:  
- Host a local server or NAS device.  
- Use port forwarding for gaming or remote access.  
- Have smart home devices that rely on fixed IPs.  
- Need predictable network behavior for troubleshooting.  

By taking the time to set up DHCP reservations, you’ll save yourself from the frustration of devices “jumping” to new addresses and avoid many connectivity problems down the line.  

---

With these steps, you can ensure your most important devices always get the same IP address from your router, keeping your network stable and predictable.

Return the dataframe interchange object implementing the interchange protocol.

Parameters  :

    

**nan_as_null** bool, default False

    

nan_as_null  is DEPRECATED and has no effect. Please avoid using it; it will
be removed in a future release.

**allow_copy** bool, default True

    

Whether to allow memory copying when exporting. If set to False it would cause
non-zero-copy exports to fail.

Returns  :

    

DataFrame interchange object

    

The object which consuming library can use to ingress the dataframe.

Notes

Details on the interchange protocol: [ https://data-apis.org/dataframe-
protocol/latest/index.html ](https://data-apis.org/dataframe-
protocol/latest/index.html)

Examples

    
    
    >>> df_not_necessarily_pandas = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
    >>> interchange_object = df_not_necessarily_pandas.__dataframe__()
    >>> interchange_object.column_names()
    Index(['A', 'B'], dtype='object')
    >>> df_pandas = (pd.api.interchange.from_dataframe
    ...              (interchange_object.select_columns_by_name(['A'])))
    >>> df_pandas
         A
    0    1
    1    2
    

These methods ( ` column_names  ` , ` select_columns_by_name  ` ) should work
for any dataframe library which implements the interchange protocol.

# Converting Unix Epoch Timestamps to Readable Local Time in Python for Real-Time Logging

In real-time system monitoring, clarity and precision in displaying time are essential. Logs that are easy to interpret allow operators and developers to quickly understand events, correlate activities, and diagnose issues. One common challenge in this context involves converting raw time data—often stored as Unix epoch timestamps—into a human-readable format that includes both date and time. This article explores how Python’s `datetime` module can be leveraged to perform this conversion efficiently, while ensuring the output is suitable for continuous logging in live environments.

---

## Understanding Unix Epoch Time

Unix epoch time represents the number of seconds that have elapsed since 00:00:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) on January 1, 1970, excluding leap seconds. Because it is a simple integer or floating-point value, epoch time is an ideal format for computation and storage. However, it is not immediately interpretable by humans. In system monitoring logs, raw epoch values can make it difficult to discern the actual time of events without conversion.

For example, a timestamp like `1706870400` is just a number to the human eye, but to the system it represents a precise moment in time. The goal is to transform this number into something like `2024-02-02 15:30:00`, which is informative at a glance.

---

## Python’s `datetime` Module

Python’s built-in `datetime` module provides a straightforward way to convert epoch timestamps into formatted strings. The core concept involves creating a `datetime` object from the epoch value and then formatting it for display. The process typically follows three steps:

1. **Import the module**  
   ```python
   import datetime
   ```

2. **Generate a datetime object from the epoch value**  
   ```python
   dt_object = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(epoch_value)
   ```

   Here, `fromtimestamp()` interprets the epoch value in the system’s local time zone by default. This is often desirable for logs that need to reflect the local time of the monitored system.

3. **Format the output string**  
   ```python
   formatted_time = dt_object.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
   ```

   The `strftime()` method allows full control over the output format. `%Y` yields the four-digit year, `%m` the two-digit month, `%d` the day, `%H` the hour (24-hour clock), `%M` the minute, and `%S` the second.

---

## Integrating Conversion into Real-Time Monitoring

In a live monitoring scenario, data often arrives as a stream of events, each with its own timestamp. By integrating the conversion process into the logging pipeline, each event can be recorded with a human-readable date and time.

For example, consider a loop that reads system metrics and logs them:

```python
import datetime
import time

def log_metric(epoch_time, metric_value):
    dt_object = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(epoch_time)
    formatted_time = dt_object.strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
    print(f"{formatted_time} | Metric: {metric_value}")

# Simulate incoming metrics every second
while True:
    current_epoch = time.time()
    sample_metric = 42  # placeholder value
    log_metric(current_epoch, sample_metric)
    time.sleep(1)
```

This approach ensures that every log entry is timestamped in a format that is immediately understandable, aiding rapid interpretation when reviewing logs.

---

## Local vs. UTC Time

While local time is often used for operational convenience, some monitoring systems prefer UTC to avoid confusion when logs are aggregated across multiple time zones. The `datetime` module supports this as well through `datetime.datetime.utcfromtimestamp(epoch_value)`. This creates a `datetime` object in UTC, which can then be formatted in the same way.

For global systems, storing logs in UTC and converting to local time only for display purposes can help maintain consistency, especially when analyzing historical data.

---

## Formatting for Various Use Cases

Different monitoring contexts may require variations in the timestamp format. For example:

- **Full precision with milliseconds:**  
  `%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f`
- **Date only for daily reports:**  
  `%Y-%m-%d`
- **Time only for intra-day trend charts:**  
  `%H:%M:%S`

By adjusting the format string in `strftime()`, developers can tailor the output to the needs of specific logging or reporting tools.

---

## Conclusion

Converting Unix epoch timestamps into human-readable local time using Python’s `datetime` module is a practical skill for anyone working in system monitoring or log analysis. The ability to display both date and time in a clear format enhances situational awareness, supports quick decision-making, and simplifies correlation of events. Whether logs are kept in local time for operational use or in UTC for global coordination, Python’s flexible formatting capabilities make it easy to produce timestamps that serve their intended purpose in real-time monitoring systems.

# Optimizing Data Processing in Python with Memory-Mapped Files and Efficient I/O

When working with large datasets in Python, performance bottlenecks often arise from reading and processing data stored on disk. Loading an entire dataset into memory may be impractical or impossible, especially when dealing with gigabytes or terabytes of information. This article explores strategies to overcome these challenges by using **memory-mapped files** and carefully designed I/O operations, enabling you to process data efficiently without exhausting system resources.

---

## Understanding Memory-Mapped Files

A memory-mapped file allows a file on disk to be accessed as if it were an array in memory. Rather than reading the entire file into RAM, the operating system loads only the portions of the file that are needed at any given time. This can significantly reduce memory usage and improve performance by leveraging the OS’s virtual memory management.

In Python, the `mmap` module provides a convenient interface for creating and working with memory-mapped files. The general workflow involves:
1. Opening the file in binary mode.
2. Creating an `mmap` object from the file descriptor.
3. Reading or slicing data directly from the mapped object.

Here’s a simple example:

```python
import mmap

with open('large_dataset.bin', 'rb') as f:
    mm = mmap.mmap(f.fileno(), 0, access=mmap.ACCESS_READ)
    # Read first 100 bytes without loading the entire file
    chunk = mm[:100]
    mm.close()
```

Because `mmap` works like a bytearray, you can process slices incrementally, which is ideal for streaming large binary datasets.

---

## Efficient I/O for Text Data

Memory-mapping is most straightforward with binary data, but large text files can also benefit from efficient I/O patterns.

For example, when reading a massive CSV file, instead of using `read()` to load it entirely, you can:
- Use buffered reading with `io.BufferedReader`.
- Process the file line-by-line with a generator pattern.
- Combine this with `csv.reader` to parse only the needed rows.

```python
import csv
import io

with open('large_dataset.csv', 'r', newline='') as f:
    buf = io.BufferedReader(f)
    reader = csv.reader(buf)
    for row in reader:
        process_row(row)  # custom function
```

This approach minimizes memory overhead and allows you to start processing data immediately without waiting for the entire file to load.

---

## Comparing File Formats for Performance

File format choice can have a dramatic impact on read performance. Common formats include:
- **CSV**: Human-readable but relatively slow to parse; large files can be inefficient.
- **Binary (e.g., NumPy `.npy`)**: Fast to load and parse; ideal for numeric arrays.
- **Parquet**: Columnar storage optimized for analytical queries; supports compression and partial reads.
- **HDF5**: Hierarchical data format with support for large, complex datasets and selective reading.

Benchmarking these formats for your specific workload is essential. For example, reading a subset of columns from a Parquet file is often orders of magnitude faster than doing the same from a CSV, because Parquet can skip irrelevant data blocks entirely.

---

## Combining Memory Mapping with Format Choices

When the dataset is stored in a binary format, memory mapping can be combined with structured unpacking. For example, NumPy’s `memmap` allows you to treat the mapped file as a NumPy array, enabling vectorized operations without fully loading the data:

```python
import numpy as np

data = np.memmap('large_array.dat', dtype='float64', mode='r', shape=(1000000,))
mean_value = data.mean()  # Efficiently computed without full RAM load
```

This is particularly powerful for scientific computing and machine learning pipelines where datasets are too large for system memory.

---

## Practical Considerations

- **Alignment and Access Patterns**: Sequential reads are generally faster than random access; design your data layout accordingly.
- **Concurrency**: Memory-mapped files can be shared between processes, making them suitable for parallel processing.
- **Resource Cleanup**: Always close `mmap` objects and file descriptors to avoid resource leaks.
- **Platform Differences**: Behavior and performance may vary between operating systems; test on your deployment environment.

---

## Conclusion

By leveraging memory-mapped files and efficient I/O strategies, Python developers can process large datasets with minimal memory footprint and improved speed. Choosing the right file format, adopting incremental reading patterns, and combining these with memory mapping capabilities can transform the way data pipelines handle massive inputs. These techniques not only reduce hardware requirements but also allow faster iteration and analysis, making them invaluable tools for performance-conscious data processing workflows.

# Managing Database Connection Strings in Node.js with Environment Variables and Docker Compose

When building and deploying Node.js applications, one of the critical aspects of configuration is the database connection string. This string contains details such as the database host, port, username, password, and database name. Hardcoding these values into application code or configuration files can lead to security risks, cumbersome updates, and inconsistent environments. A more secure and flexible approach is to use environment variables to store and reference these credentials—especially when working with Docker Compose.

## Why Environment Variables Matter

Environment variables provide a way to decouple sensitive configuration from application code. This has several benefits:

- **Security**: Credentials are not committed to source control, reducing the risk of accidental exposure.
- **Flexibility**: Different environments (development, staging, production) can use different values without modifying the application code.
- **Automation**: CI/CD pipelines can inject the correct variables during deployment without manual intervention.

In the context of database connection strings, this means you can manage credentials centrally and avoid embedding them in your Node.js source files or Compose manifests.

## Structuring Your Node.js Application

A standard Node.js application might use a package such as `dotenv` to load variables from a `.env` file during local development:

```javascript
require('dotenv').config();

const { Pool } = require('pg');

const pool = new Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL
});

module.exports = pool;
```

Here, `DATABASE_URL` is an environment variable containing the full connection string, e.g.:

```
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:password@db:5432/mydatabase
```

In production, particularly when using Docker Compose, you typically don’t load `.env` from within the application; instead, you pass environment variables directly into the container at runtime.

## Integrating Environment Variables with Docker Compose

Docker Compose allows you to define environment variables in several ways:

1. **Inline in the `docker-compose.yml`**:
   ```yaml
   services:
     app:
       build: .
       environment:
         - DATABASE_URL=${DATABASE_URL}
   ```

2. **Via an external `.env` file**:
   ```yaml
   services:
     app:
       build: .
       env_file:
         - .env
   ```

With the second approach, you keep your sensitive credentials in a `.env` file that is excluded from version control, and Compose will inject them into your container environment at runtime.

For example:

```
DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:securepass@db:5432/prod_db
```

This keeps your Compose file clean and makes updates as simple as editing the `.env` file.

## Security Considerations

While `.env` files are convenient, they must be handled carefully:

- **Never commit `.env` to public repositories**.
- **Restrict file permissions** so that only authorized users and processes can read them.
- **Use secrets management tools** for production deployments, such as Docker secrets, AWS Secrets Manager, or HashiCorp Vault, to store and inject credentials securely.

In CI/CD environments, credentials should be stored in the pipeline’s secure variable store rather than in plaintext files. The pipeline can then export these variables before running `docker-compose up` or `docker stack deploy`.

## Automating Updates Through CI/CD

One of the advantages of externalizing connection strings is the ease of automation. When you need to rotate database passwords or switch to a new database host, you can update the environment variable in your CI/CD configuration or secrets manager, and redeploy the application without touching the codebase.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:

```yaml
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2
      - name: Set up environment
        run: echo "DATABASE_URL=${{ secrets.DATABASE_URL }}" >> .env
      - name: Deploy with Docker Compose
        run: docker-compose up -d --build
```

This approach ensures that sensitive data is injected securely at build or deploy time, and can be updated independently of your application code.

## Conclusion

Using environment variables to configure database connection strings in Node.js applications deployed with Docker Compose offers a secure, maintainable, and automation-friendly workflow. By separating sensitive credentials from your code and Compose manifests, you reduce the risk of exposure, simplify environment management, and enable seamless updates through CI/CD pipelines. Whether for local development or production deployment, this method helps keep your application configurations clean, adaptable, and secure.

insensitive dictionary with item, attribute, and call access to variables. If

#  Tag:  Sentinel

##  [ Distinguishing between None and missing values in dictionaries with a
sentinel ](https://blog.peterlamut.com/2020/04/01/distinguishing-between-none-
and-missing-values-in-dictionaries-with-a-sentinel/)

Whoa, it’s been quite a while since my last blog post. This is, of course, not
my fault (it _never_ is 😛), let’s instead blame the architect of this world
that only gave us 24 hours in a single day. That’s not nearly enough to do all
the things one wants! Anyhow, now that I optimistically deluded myself that
the excuse I just gave is convincing, I would like to share a tip when dealing
with maybe-missing dictionary data.

This situation is quite common when receiving JSON data from an external APIs,
which is normally handed to you, the programmer, parsed in a dictionary.
Reading values from such dictionaries requires some caution to avoid
unnecessary errors:

    
    
    data = dict(foo=1, bar=2)
    baz_value = data['baz']  # KeyError
    

The obvious, but somewhat naive, way of dealing with this is to first check if
` baz ` exists in the first place:

    
    
    baz_value = data['baz'] if 'baz' in data else None
    

It works, but it’s verbose, and there is already a ` dict.get(key[, default])
` method that does exactly that – return the value stored under ` key ` , if
such key exists, otherwise return the ` default ` value (which defaults to `
None ` ). It is thus a common practice to just use ` get() ` instead:

    
    
    baz_value = data.get('baz')
    

However, sometimes there are cases when one actually needs to distinguish
between the _missing_ values and the values explicitly set to ` None ` . If `
get() ` returns ` None ` , it is not clear _why_ it returned it without an
additional check. It is also not recommended to use a different default value
that can “never” possibly represent an actual value in the dictionary, as that
assumption can change and break our code.

    
    
    baz_value = data.get('baz', 'NO VALUE')
    
    if baz_value == 'NO VALUE':
        # handle the "missing" case
    else:
        # handle the "normal" case
    

If ` baz ` somehow happens to end up with the value ` 'NO VALUE' ` in ` data `
, the code above will not work as intended. One solution is to again use an
explicit membership test, and only read the value if the latter succeeds:

    
    
    if 'baz' not in data:
        # handle the "missing" case
    else:
        baz_value = data['baz']
        # handle the "normal" case
    

The downside is that we need to do two dictionary lookups, one for the
membership test, and another to actually retrieve the ` baz ` value.

Fortunately, there is an elegant fix to this – [ sentinels
](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentinel_value) . A value picked for a
sentinel must be something that is always uniquely distinguishable from the
data. One option is to generate a unique string (with, say, [ uuid.uuid4()
](https://docs.python.org/3.8/library/uuid.html#uuid.uuid4) ), which is
“unique enough” for practical purposes, another is to instantiate a new object
and test for _identity_ :

    
    
    MISSING = object()  # a sentinel
    baz_value = data.get('baz', MISSING)
    
    if baz_value is MISSING:
        # handle the "missing" case
    elif baz_value is None:
        # handle the "normal" case when None
    else:
        # handle all other "normal" cases
    

The explicit check for ` None ` is optional and you might not even need it,
but it is nevertheless included in the above

##  Examples

###  Different ways to create a Float32Array

js

    
    
    // From a length
    const float32 = new Float32Array(2);
    float32[0] = 42;
    console.log(float32[0]); // 42
    console.log(float32.length); // 2
    console.log(float32.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT); // 4
    
    // From an array
    const x = new Float32Array([21, 31]);
    console.log(x[1]); // 31
    
    // From another TypedArray
    const y = new Float32Array(x);
    console.log(y[0]); // 21
    
    // From an ArrayBuffer
    const buffer = new ArrayBuffer(32);
    const z = new Float32Array(buffer, 4, 4);
    console.log(z.byteOffset); // 4
    
    // From an iterable
    const iterable = (function* () {
      yield* [1, 2, 3];
    })();
    const float32FromIterable = new Float32Array(iterable);
    console.log(float32FromIterable);
    // Float32Array [1, 2, 3]

##  Decorator Evaluation

There is a well defined order to how decorators applied to various
declarations inside of a class are applied:

  1. _Parameter Decorators_ , followed by _Method_ , _Accessor_ , or _Property Decorators_ are applied for each instance member. 
  2. _Parameter Decorators_ , followed by _Method_ , _Accessor_ , or _Property Decorators_ are applied for each static member. 
  3. _Parameter Decorators_ are applied for the constructor. 
  4. _Class Decorators_ are applied for the class.

` torch.distributed.rpc. ` ` shutdown ` (  _graceful=True_ )  [ [source]
](_modules/torch/distributed/rpc/api.html#shutdown) ¶

    

Perform a shutdown of the RPC agent, and then destroy the RPC agent. This
stops the local agent from accepting outstanding requests, and shuts down the
RPC framework by terminating all RPC threads. If ` graceful=True  ` , this
will block until all local and remote RPC processes reach this method and wait
for all outstanding work to complete. Otherwise, if ` graceful=False  ` , this
is a local shutdown, and it does not wait for other RPC processes to reach
this method.

Warning

For [ ` Future  ` ](futures.html#torch.futures.Future "torch.futures.Future")
objects returned by  ` rpc_async()  ` , ` future.wait()  ` should not be
called after ` shutdown()  ` .

Parameters

    

**graceful** ( [ _bool_
](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool "\(in Python v3.8\)")
) – Whether to do a graceful shutdown or not. If True, this will 1) wait until
there is no pending system messages for ` UserRRefs  ` and delete them; 2)
block until all local and remote RPC processes have reached this method and
wait for all outstanding work to complete.

Example::

    

Make sure that ` MASTER_ADDR  ` and ` MASTER_PORT  ` are set properly on both
workers. Refer to [ ` init_process_group()  `
](distributed.html#torch.distributed.init_process_group
"torch.distributed.init_process_group") API for more details. For example,

    
    
    >>> export MASTER_ADDR=localhost
    >>> export MASTER_PORT=5678
    

Then run the following code in two different processes:

    
    
    >>> # On worker 0:
    >>> import torch
    >>> import torch.distributed.rpc as rpc
    >>> rpc.init_rpc("worker0", rank=0, world_size=2)
    >>> # do some work
    >>> result = rpc.rpc_sync("worker1", torch.add, args=(torch.ones(1), 1))
    >>> # ready to shutdown
    >>> rpc.shutdown()
    
    
    
    >>> # On worker 1:
    >>> import torch.distributed.rpc as rpc
    >>> rpc.init_rpc("worker1", rank=1, world_size=2)
    >>> # wait for worker 0 to finish work, and then shutdown.
    >>> rpc.shutdown()

#  SAMPLE (U-SQL)

  * Article 
  * 02/10/2021 
  * 5 contributors 

Feedback

##  In this article

##  Summary

U-SQL supports samplers natively. The ` SAMPLE ` clause enables convenient
access from within a ` SELECT ` expression. All samplers execute in one pass
on data and in parallel on portions of the input; they do not require
partitioning, shuffle etc. Samplers have been implemented in a single pass
over data and have very small memory footprint; log( SIZE(input), SIZE(output)
).

##  Syntax

    
    
    Sample_Expression_Simple :=                                                                              
         [Query_Expression](../../../query-statements-and-expressions) 'SAMPLE' ( 'ANY' '(' row_count ')' | 'UNIFORM' '(' row_fraction ')' ).
    

##  Remarks

  * **` ANY ` **   
_Any_ ` row_count ` rows from the input rowset. ` ANY ` does not return a
randomly chosen subset of rows; do not use where randomness is needed.

  * **` row_count ` **   
A positive integer.

  * **` UNIFORM ` **   
Rows are picked uniformly at random with probability equal to ` row_fraction `
. The size of the output is governed by a binomial distribution. In
expectation, the size of output is ` row_fraction ` * SIZE(input rowset).

  * **` row_fraction ` **   
A double between 0 and 1 that indicates the probability with which a row in
the input rowset will be passed.

Tip

Ensure your sample probability, ` row_fraction ` , is adequate for the size of
your dataset to minimize the possibility of an empty result set being
returned.

###  Examples

  * The examples can be executed in Visual Studio with the [ Azure Data Lake Tools plug-in ](https://www.microsoft.com/download/details.aspx?id=49504) . 
  * The scripts can be executed [ locally ](/en-us/azure/data-lake-analytics/data-lake-analytics-data-lake-tools-get-started#run-u-sql-locally) . An Azure subscription and Azure Data Lake Analytics account is not needed when executed locally. 
  * The examples below are based on the dataset defined below. Ensure your execution includes the rowset variable, ` @data ` . 

**Dataset**

    
    
    @data = 
        SELECT * FROM 
            ( VALUES
            ("02143",   30,     100,  "Smith"),
            ("98052",   25,     50,   "Andersen"),
            ("02139",   30,     75,   "Todd"),
            ("02139",   25,     60,   "Roberts"),
            ("61801",   23,     80,   "Sanders")
            ) AS T(ZipCode, Age, Salary, LastName);
    

* * *

**ANY**  
Samples the ` @data ` rowset by selecting the specified number of rows (2) in
a completely arbitrary way.

    
    
    @result = 
        SELECT * FROM @data SAMPLE ANY (2);
    
    OUTPUT @result
    TO "/ReferenceGuide/QSE/Sample/any.txt"
    USING Outputters.Tsv();

Samples the ` @data ` rowset using a random uniform sampling with the provided
probability (10%).

    
    
    @result =
        SELECT * FROM @data SAMPLE UNIFORM (0.1);

#  Static Files  ¶

You can serve static files automatically from a directory using ` StaticFiles
` .

##  Use ` StaticFiles ` ¶

  * Import ` StaticFiles ` . 
  * "Mount" a ` StaticFiles() ` instance in a specific path. 

    
    
    from fastapi import FastAPI
    from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles
    
    app = FastAPI()
    
    app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory="static"), name="static")
    

Technical Details

You could also use ` from starlette.staticfiles import StaticFiles ` .

**FastAPI** provides the same ` starlette.staticfiles ` as `
fastapi.staticfiles ` just as a convenience for you, the developer. But it
actually comes directly from Starlette.

###  What is "Mounting"  ¶

"Mounting" means adding a complete "independent" application in a specific
path, that then takes care of handling all the sub-paths.

This is different from using an ` APIRouter ` as a mounted application is
completely independent. The OpenAPI and docs from your main application won't
include anything from the mounted application, etc.

You can read more about this in the [ Advanced User Guide ](../../advanced/) .

##  Details  ¶

The first ` "/static" ` refers to the sub-path this "sub-application" will be
"mounted" on. So, any path that starts with ` "/static" ` will be handled by
it.

The ` directory="static" ` refers to the name of the directory that contains
your static files.

The ` name="static" ` gives it a name that can be used internally by
**FastAPI** .

All these parameters can be different than " ` static ` ", adjust them with
the needs and specific details of your own application.

##  More info  ¶

For more details and options check [ Starlette's docs about Static Files
](https://www.starlette.io/staticfiles/) .

##  Try it

##  Syntax

js

    
    
    push()
    push(element1)
    push(element1, element2)
    push(element1, element2, /* â¦, */ elementN)
    

###  Parameters

` element1 ` , â¦, ` elementN `

    

The element(s) to add to the end of the array.

###  Return value

The new [ ` length ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/length) property of the
object upon which the method was called.

##  Description

The ` push() ` method appends values to an array.

[ ` Array.prototype.unshift() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/unshift) has similar
behavior to ` push() ` , but applied to the start of an array.

The ` push() ` method is a [ mutating method ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#copying_methods_and_mutating_methods)
. It changes the length and the content of ` this ` . In case you want the
value of ` this ` to be the same, but return a new array with elements
appended to the end, you can use [ ` arr.concat([element0, element1, /* ...
,*/ elementN]) ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/concat) instead. Notice
that the elements are wrapped in an extra array â otherwise, if the element
is an array itself, it would be spread instead of pushed as a single element
due to the behavior of ` concat() ` .

The ` push() ` method is [ generic ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#generic_array_methods) .
It only expects the ` this ` value to have a ` length ` property and integer-
keyed properties. Although strings are also array-like, this method is not
suitable to be applied on them, as strings are immutable.

##  Examples

###  Adding elements to an array

The following code creates the ` sports ` array containing two elements, then
appends two elements to it. The ` total ` variable contains the new length of
the array.

js

    
    
    const sports = ["soccer", "baseball"];
    const total = sports.push("football", "swimming");
    
    console.log(sports); // ['soccer', 'baseball', 'football', 'swimming']
    console.log(total); // 4
    

###  Merging two arrays

This example uses [ spread syntax ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Spread_syntax) to push all elements
from a second array into the first one.

js

    
    
    const vegetables = ["parsnip", "potato"];
    const moreVegs = ["celery", "beetroot"];
    
    // Merge the second array into the first one
    vegetables.push(...moreVegs);
    
    console.log(vegetables); // ['parsnip', 'potato', 'celery', 'beetroot']
    

Merging two arrays can also be done with the [ ` concat() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array/concat) method.

###  Calling push() on non-array objects

The ` push() ` method reads the ` length ` property of ` this ` . It then sets
each index of ` this ` starting at ` length ` with the arguments passed to `
push() ` . Finally, it sets the ` length ` to the previous length plus the
number of pushed elements.

js

    
    
    const arrayLike = {
      length: 3,
      unrelated: "foo",
      2: 4,
    };
    Array.prototype.push.call(arrayLike, 1, 2);
    console.log(arrayLike);
    // { '2': 4, '3': 1, '4': 2, length: 5, unrelated: 'foo' }
    
    const plainObj = {};
    // There's no length property, so the length is 0
    Array.prototype.push.call(plainObj, 1, 2);
    console.log(plainObj);
    // { '0': 1, '1': 2, length: 2 }
    

###  Using an object in an array-like fashion

As mentioned above, ` push ` is intentionally generic, and we can use that to
our advantage. ` Array.prototype.push ` can work on an object just fine, as
this example shows.

Note that we don't create an array to store a collection of objects. Instead,
we store the collection on the object itself and use ` call ` on `
Array.prototype.push ` to trick

# When VS Code Ignores Your Python Linting Configuration: Common Causes and Solutions

For many Python developers, linting tools such as **Pylint** and **Flake8** are indispensable for maintaining code quality and consistency. Configuring these tools can be straightforward in theory, but sometimes Visual Studio Code seems to ignore your `.pylintrc`, `setup.cfg`, or `.flake8` configuration files entirely. This can be frustrating, especially when you’ve invested time fine-tuning rules for your project.  

In this post, we’ll explore common reasons why VS Code may fail to recognize linting configurations, and outline practical steps to ensure your linting setup works smoothly.

---

## Understanding How VS Code Integrates Linting Tools

VS Code leverages extensions to provide linting functionality for Python. The **Python extension** by Microsoft supports Pylint and Flake8, but it requires the correct interpreter, environment, and extension settings to locate and apply your configuration.

When you run linting from within VS Code, the editor calls the linter executable from the Python environment selected in the workspace. If that environment doesn’t have the linter installed, or if the PATH used by VS Code differs from your terminal, configuration files may be ignored.

---

## Common Causes of Configuration Misreads

### 1. Configuration File Location
Pylint and Flake8 both search for configuration files in specific locations. If your configuration file is not in the project root or is named incorrectly, the linter may revert to default settings. For example:

- **Pylint** looks for `.pylintrc`, `pylintrc`, `setup.cfg`, or `pyproject.toml` in the current working directory or parent directories.
- **Flake8** checks for `.flake8`, `setup.cfg`, or `tox.ini`.

If VS Code’s working directory differs from where the file resides, the linter won’t pick up your rules.

### 2. Multiple Python Interpreters
Many developers work with multiple Python environments—virtualenvs, Conda environments, or system Python. If VS Code is pointed at an interpreter that doesn’t have the linter installed, it may silently fail or run a different version without your configuration.

### 3. PATH Discrepancies
The PATH environment variable determines where executables are found. VS Code may inherit a different PATH from your shell, especially on macOS and Linux when launched from the application icon rather than the terminal. This can lead to VS Code using a globally installed linter that ignores your local config.

### 4. Workspace vs. User Settings
VS Code settings can be applied at the user level or workspace level. If the linter path or arguments are set differently in user settings, they may override workspace configurations and cause unexpected behavior.

---

## Steps to Ensure VS Code Reads Your Configurations

1. **Verify Configuration Placement**  
   Place your `.pylintrc` or `.flake8` file in the root of your workspace folder. Confirm that the filename matches what the linter expects.

2. **Select the Correct Interpreter**  
   Use the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P` or `Cmd+Shift+P`) and select **Python: Select Interpreter** to ensure you are using the environment that has your linter installed.

3. **Check Extension Settings**  
   In `settings.json`, ensure that:
   ```json
   "python.linting.pylintEnabled": true,
   "python.linting.flake8Enabled": false,
   "python.linting.pylintPath": "pylint"
   ```
   Adjust according to the linter you’re using, and confirm paths are correct.

4. **Run Linting in the Integrated Terminal**  
   Execute `pylint your_file.py` or `flake8 your_file.py` in VS Code’s integrated terminal. If it doesn’t apply your rules, the problem is with the linter’s configuration recognition, not the editor.

5. **Align PATH Variables**  
   If running from the terminal works but VS Code ignores configs, launch VS Code from the terminal (`code .`) so it inherits the shell’s PATH. Alternatively, adjust VS Code’s environment variables in your system settings.

---

## Conclusion

When VS Code fails to recognize linting configurations for Python, the root cause is often a mismatch between the editor’s runtime environment and your intended setup. By confirming configuration file placement, interpreter selection, and PATH alignment, you can restore proper linting behavior. Once resolved, your customized rules from Pylint or Flake8 should integrate seamlessly into your workflow, helping ensure clean, consistent code across your projects.

Extension of the Distribution class, which applies a sequence of Transforms to
a base distribution. Let f be the composition of transforms applied:

    
    
    X ~ BaseDistribution
    Y = f(X) ~ TransformedDistribution(BaseDistribution, f)
    log p(Y) = log p(X) + log |det (dX/dY)|
    

Note that the ` .event_shape  ` of a  ` TransformedDistribution  ` is the
maximum shape of its base distribution and its transforms, since transforms
can introduce correlations among events.

An example for the usage of  ` TransformedDistribution  ` would be:

    
    
    # Building a Logistic Distribution
    # X ~ Uniform(0, 1)
    # f = a + b * logit(X)
    # Y ~ f(X) ~ Logistic(a, b)
    base_distribution = Uniform(0, 1)
    transforms = [SigmoidTransform().inv, AffineTransform(loc=a, scale=b)]
    logistic = TransformedDistribution(base_distribution, transforms)

##  Set / reset index  #

Occasionally you will load or create a data set into a DataFrame and want to
add an index after youâve already done so. There are a couple of different
ways.

###  Set an index  #

DataFrame has a [ ` set_index()  `
](../reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.set_index.html#pandas.DataFrame.set_index
"pandas.DataFrame.set_index") method which takes a column name (for a regular
` Index  ` ) or a list of column names (for a ` MultiIndex  ` ). To create a
new, re-indexed DataFrame:

    
    
    In [361]: data = pd.DataFrame({'a': ['bar', 'bar', 'foo', 'foo'],
       .....:                      'b': ['one', 'two', 'one', 'two'],
       .....:                      'c': ['z', 'y', 'x', 'w'],
       .....:                      'd': [1., 2., 3, 4]})
       .....: 
    
    In [362]: data
    Out[362]: 
         a    b  c    d
    0  bar  one  z  1.0
    1  bar  two  y  2.0
    2  foo  one  x  3.0
    3  foo  two  w  4.0
    
    In [363]: indexed1 = data.set_index('c')
    
    In [364]: indexed1
    Out[364]: 
         a    b    d
    c               
    z  bar  one  1.0
    y  bar  two  2.0
    x  foo  one  3.0
    w  foo  two  4.0
    
    In [365]: indexed2 = data.set_index(['a', 'b'])
    
    In [366]: indexed2
    Out[366]: 
             c    d
    a   b          
    bar one  z  1.0
        two  y  2.0
    foo one  x  3.0
        two  w  4.0
    

The ` append  ` keyword option allow you to keep the existing index and append
the given columns to a MultiIndex:

    
    
    In [367]: frame = data.set_index('c', drop=False)
    
    In [368]: frame = frame.set_index(['a', 'b'], append=True)
    
    In [369]: frame
    Out[369]: 
               c    d
    c a   b          
    z bar one  z  1.0
    y bar two  y  2.0
    x foo one  x  3.0
    w foo two  w  4.0
    

Other options in ` set_index  ` allow you not drop the index columns.

    
    
    In [370]: data.set_index('c', drop=False)
    Out[370]: 
         a    b  c    d
    c                  
    z  bar  one  z  1.0
    y  bar  two  y  2.0

# Turning Embedded Numbers into Factors in R: A Guide for Categorical Analysis

When working with data in R, it is common to encounter numeric values embedded within strings—perhaps in codes, identifiers, or mixed-format labels. While these numbers might appear to be quantitative at first glance, in many analytical contexts they function as categorical markers. Converting such embedded numbers into factors can unlock powerful tools for statistical modeling, grouping, and visualization. This post explores practical strategies for parsing these values and transforming them into factors for categorical analysis.

## Understanding the Role of Factors in R

Factors in R are a data type designed to handle categorical variables. They store both the underlying integer codes and a set of associated labels. This dual structure enables R’s statistical functions to recognize and treat the data as categorical rather than continuous. For example, in an ANOVA or a regression with categorical predictors, factors ensure that each unique category is treated as a distinct level with its own effect.

When numeric values are embedded within strings—such as `"group1"`, `"group2"`, `"group3"`—they often indicate categories rather than quantities. Treating them as numbers risks misleading analyses, since the numeric order might not represent a meaningful scale. Converting them into factors preserves their categorical nature.

## Extracting Embedded Numbers

The first step is to isolate the numeric segments from the strings. The `stringr` package, part of the tidyverse, provides robust tools for this task. Regular expressions can match the numeric portions while ignoring surrounding text. For instance, a pattern like `\\d+` will match sequences of digits, and more complex expressions can target digits following a specific letter or prefix.

Once extracted, the numeric values can be stored as a vector. At this point, it is useful to inspect them: are they sequential codes, identifiers, or arbitrary labels? This informs how you should define the factor levels.

## Converting to Factors

After extraction, you can convert the numeric vector into a factor using the `factor()` function. The simplest approach is:

```r
numeric_codes <- c(10, 17, 22)
factor_codes <- factor(numeric_codes)
```

By default, R will order the factor levels according to the unique values’ increasing order. If you prefer to preserve the original order of appearance in the data, you can set `levels` explicitly:

```r
factor_codes <- factor(numeric_codes, levels = unique(numeric_codes))
```

This ensures that any subsequent grouping or plotting respects the original sequence.

## Using Factors in Statistical Modeling

Once you have factor variables, you can incorporate them into a variety of modeling functions. In regression models, factors are expanded into dummy variables (contrast-coded), allowing the model to estimate separate effects for each category. In ANOVA, factors define the groups whose means are compared.

For example:

```r
model <- lm(outcome ~ factor_codes, data = df)
summary(model)
```

Here, `factor_codes` is treated as a categorical predictor, and the model will produce coefficients for each level relative to a baseline.

## Visualizing Grouped Data Distributions

Factors are equally valuable in visualization. In `ggplot2`, mapping a factor to a fill or color aesthetic automatically groups the data and applies discrete scales:

```r
ggplot(df, aes(x = factor_codes, y = outcome, fill = factor_codes)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

This produces separate boxplots for each category, allowing you to compare distributions across groups. Similarly, bar plots, violin plots, and faceted charts all benefit from well-defined factor variables.

## Practical Considerations

- **Labeling**: You can assign descriptive labels to factor levels, replacing raw numeric codes with meaningful names. This improves interpretability in both tables and plots.
- **Ordering**: For ordinal categories, you can specify ordered factors (`ordered = TRUE`), which tells R to respect a natural sequence in comparisons and visualizations.
- **Data Integrity**: Ensure that the extraction process correctly captures all intended numeric segments and does not inadvertently merge or split codes.

## Conclusion

Converting embedded numbers within strings into factors in R is a crucial step when those numbers represent categorical information. By extracting the numeric portions, defining factor levels thoughtfully, and leveraging R’s modeling and visualization capabilities, you can conduct more accurate and interpretable analyses. Whether you are preparing data for statistical models or creating grouped visualizations, understanding how to handle these embedded numbers as factors will enhance both the rigor and clarity of your work.

# Optimizing Heap Management in C++ Applications: Techniques for Performance and Stability

In modern C++ development, efficient heap management is critical to ensuring application performance, scalability, and stability. Poor control over dynamic memory allocation can lead to fragmentation, excessive overhead, and even application crashes. This article examines a range of optimization techniques that focus on manual memory allocation and deallocation, and discusses how custom allocators can be leveraged to improve performance in high-demand scenarios.

## Understanding Heap Allocation in C++

The heap is a pool of memory used for dynamic allocation—objects are created at runtime using operators such as `new` or functions like `malloc()`. Unlike stack memory, which is automatically managed and has predictable lifetime, heap memory persists until explicitly deallocated. This flexibility comes at a cost: allocation and deallocation operations are relatively expensive, and improper management can lead to memory leaks or fragmentation.

In performance-sensitive applications, particularly those requiring high throughput or handling large datasets, the default allocation mechanisms may not be sufficient. Understanding how the heap is managed by the runtime library and operating system is the first step toward optimization.

## Manual Memory Management Strategies

While modern C++ encourages the use of smart pointers (`std::unique_ptr`, `std::shared_ptr`) for automatic memory management, manual allocation and deallocation still have their place in scenarios where developers need precise control.

1. **Minimize Allocations**  
   Repeatedly allocating and deallocating small objects can lead to fragmentation and performance degradation. Group related objects together in larger blocks to reduce the number of heap operations.

2. **Reuse Memory**  
   Implement object pooling for frequently used types. By recycling memory blocks, you avoid repeated allocation overhead and reduce pressure on the heap.

3. **Avoid Unnecessary Copies**  
   Use references and move semantics to prevent duplicate allocations when passing or returning large objects.

4. **Explicit Deallocation**  
   Ensure that every allocation has a corresponding deallocation. In complex systems, this often means carefully tracking ownership and lifetimes.

## Leveraging Custom Allocators

C++ offers allocator interfaces that allow developers to override default memory allocation behavior for containers such as `std::vector` or `std::map`. Custom allocators can be designed to work with preallocated memory pools, specialized alignment requirements, or optimized strategies for specific workloads.

### Benefits of Custom Allocators
- **Reduced Fragmentation:** By managing memory in fixed-size blocks or pools, custom allocators can prevent the uneven gaps that lead to fragmentation.
- **Improved Performance:** Tailoring allocation strategies to the usage patterns of your application can significantly reduce allocation time.
- **Predictable Behavior:** In real-time systems, custom allocators help ensure deterministic allocation and deallocation times.

### Designing a Custom Allocator
A basic custom allocator needs to implement methods for `allocate()` and `deallocate()` that work with your chosen memory pool. You can also incorporate debugging features, such as tracking allocations or detecting misuse, to aid in maintenance.

For example, a pool allocator might reserve a large block of memory at startup and then hand out fixed-size chunks as needed, avoiding calls to the system allocator during runtime.

## Monitoring and Profiling Heap Usage

Optimization is not purely about theory—it requires measurement. Tools such as Valgrind’s `massif`, Visual Studio’s Diagnostic Tools, or custom logging can help identify allocation hotspots and memory leaks. By profiling heap usage, you can make data-driven decisions about where manual management or custom allocators will have the most impact.

Key metrics to monitor include:
- Allocation frequency and size distribution
- Peak heap usage
- Fragmentation levels
- Lifetime patterns of allocated objects

## Conclusion

Heap management is a critical aspect of efficient C++ application design. While default allocation mechanisms are suitable for many scenarios, manual strategies and custom allocators provide powerful tools for optimizing performance in demanding environments. By reducing unnecessary allocations, reusing memory, and tailoring allocation strategies to application needs, developers can achieve faster execution, lower memory overhead, and improved stability. The key lies in understanding your application’s memory usage patterns and applying targeted optimizations that balance control with maintainability.

##  Converting to .NET Assembly

When [ converting script to .NET Assembly ](/eng/docs/library_from_script) ,
map ` mkdir ` command to ` [ Session.CreateDirectory
](/eng/docs/library_session_createdirectory) ` method.

Parameters mapping: Command parameter ` directory ` maps to method parameter `
path ` . You have to [ convert relative path to absolute path
](/eng/docs/library_from_script#paths) .

For example, following script snippet:

    
    
    [cd](https://winscp.net/eng/docs/scriptcommand_cd) /home/martinp
    [mkdir](https://winscp.net/eng/docs/scriptcommand_mkdir) private

    $session.CreateDirectory("/home/martinp/private")

The following function retrieves status information for the “echo_service”
service. The function specifies a 5-second timeout:
    SELECT SYSTEM$GET_SERVICE_STATUS('echo_service', 5);
Copy
Example outputs:
  * **Running one service instance that has one container.** The function returns the container information as shown: 
        [
     {
        "status":"READY",
        "message":"Running",
        "containerName":"echo",
        "instanceId":"0",
        "serviceName":"ECHO_SERVICE",
        "image":"<account>.registry.snowflakecomputing.com/tutorial_db/data_schema/tutorial_repository/my_echo_service_image:tutorial",
        "restartCount":0,
        "startTime":"2023-01-01T00:00:00Z"
     }
    ]
Copy
` instanceId  ` is the service instance ID. If you have two instances of this
service running, the array includes two objects in the output, providing
container status for two separate service instances (the ` instanceId  ` will
be 0 and 1).
  * **Running one service instance that has three containers (as defined in the service specification).** The function returns an array with three objects (one for each container): 
        [
      {
      "status":"READY",
      "message":"Running",
      "containerName":"echo-1",
      "instanceId":"0",
      "serviceName":"ECHO_SERVICE",

      {
      "status":"READY",
      "message":"Running",

      "instanceId":"0",
      "serviceName":"ECHO_SERVICE",

      "restartCount":0,
      "startTime":"2023-01-01T00:00:00Z"

orientation at a time. When widgets are initially queried for their minimum
sizes it is generally done in two initial passes in the ` GtkSizeRequestMode `
chosen by the toplevel.

For example, when queried in the normal ` GTK_SIZE_REQUEST_HEIGHT_FOR_WIDTH `
mode: First, the default minimum and natural width for each widget in the
interface will be computed using gtk_widget_get_preferred_width(). Because the
preferred widths for each container depend on the preferred widths of their
children, this information propagates up the hierarchy, and finally a minimum
and natural width is determined for the entire toplevel. Next, the toplevel
will use the minimum width to query for the minimum height contextual to that
width using gtk_widget_get_preferred_height_for_width(), which will also be a
highly recursive operation. The minimum height for the minimum width is
normally used to set the minimum size constraint on the toplevel (unless `
gtk_window_set_geometry_hints() ` is explicitly used instead).

After the toplevel window has initially requested its size in both dimensions
it can go on to allocate itself a reasonable size (or a size previously
specified with gtk_window_set_default_size()). During the recursive allocation
process it’s important to note that request cycles will be recursively
executed while container widgets allocate their children. Each container
widget, once allocated a size, will go on to first share the space in one
orientation among its children and then request each child’s height for its
target allocated width or its width for allocated height, depending. In this
way a ` GtkWidget ` will typically be requested its size a number of times
before actually being allocated a size. The size a widget is finally allocated
can of course differ from the size it has requested. For this reason, `
GtkWidget ` caches a small number of results to avoid re-querying for the same
sizes in one allocation cycle.

See [GtkContainer’s geometry management section][container-geometry-
management] to learn more about how height-for-width allocations are performed
by container widgets.

If a widget does move content around to intelligently use up the allocated
size then it must support the request in both ` GtkSizeRequestModes ` even if
the widget in question only trades sizes in a single orientation.

For instance, a ` GtkLabel ` that does height-for-width word wrapping will not
expect to have ` GtkWidgetClass ` .get_preferred_height() called because that
call is specific to a width-for-height request. In this case the label must
return the height required for its own minimum possible width. By following
this rule any widget that handles height-for-width or width-for-height
requests will always be allocated at least enough space to fit its own
content.
