Digest) instead. For ` id-* ` digest algorithms, use [ ` Want-Repr-Digest `
](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Want-Repr-Digest) .

The **` Want-Digest ` ** request or response HTTP header requests the other
side to provide a [ digest ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Digest) using the [ ` Digest
` ](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Digest) header.

The header contains identifiers for one or more digest algorithms that the
sender wishes the server to use to create the digest. The request may use [
quality values ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Quality_values) to indicate its
preference/order for particular digest algorithms.

If ` Want-Digest ` does not include any digest algorithms that the server
supports, the server may respond with:

  * a digest calculated using a different digest algorithm, or 
  * a [ ` 400 Bad Request ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status/400) error, and include another ` Want-Digest ` header with that response, listing the algorithms that it does support. 

See also the [ ` Digest ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Digest) header.

Header type  |  [ Request header ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Request_header) , [ Response header ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Response_header)  
---|---  
[ Forbidden header name ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Forbidden_header_name) |  no   
  
##  Syntax

http

    
    
    Want-Digest: <digest-algorithm>
    
    // Multiple algorithms, weighted with the quality value syntax:
    Want-Digest: <digest-algorithm><q-value>,<digest-algorithm><q-value>
    

##  Directives

<digest-algorithm>

    

Digest algorithms are defined in [ Digest Headers
](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpbis-digest-headers/) .

  * Permitted digest algorithms values include: ` unixsum ` , ` unixcksum ` , ` crc32c ` , ` sha-256 ` and ` sha-512 ` , ` id-sha-256 ` , ` id-sha-512 `
  * Deprecated algorithms values include: ` md5 ` , ` sha ` , ` adler32 ` . 

<q-value>

    

The [ quality value ](/en-US/docs/Glossary/Quality_values) to apply to that
option.

##  Examples

http

    
    
    Want-Digest: sha-256
    Want-Digest: SHA-512;q=0.3, sha-256;q=1, md5;q=0
    

###  Basic operation

The sender provides a list of digests which it is prepared to accept, and the
server uses one of them:

Request:

http

    
    
    GET /item
    Want-Digest: sha-256;q=0.3, sha;q=1
    

Response:

http

    
    
    HTTP/1.1 200 Ok
    Digest: sha-256=X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=
    

###  Unsupported digests

The server does not support any of the requested digest algorithms, so uses a
different algorithm:

Request:

http

    
    
    GET /item
    Want-Digest: sha;q=1
    

Response:

http

    
    
    HTTP/1.1 200 Ok
    Digest: sha-256=X48E9qOokqqrvdts8nOJRJN3OWDUoyWxBf7kbu9DBPE=
    

The server does not support any of the requested digest algorithms. In this
case it responds with a 400 error and includes another ` Want-Digest ` header,
listing the algorithms that it does support:

Request:

http

    
    
    GET /item
    Want-Digest: sha;q=1
    

Response:

http

    
    
    HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
    Want-Digest: sha-256, sha-512

#  pandas.DataFrame.notnull  #

DataFrame.  notnull  (  )  [ [source]  ](https://github.com/pandas-
dev/pandas/blob/v2.2.2/pandas/core/frame.py#L6505-L6510) #

    

DataFrame.notnull is an alias for DataFrame.notna.

Detect existing (non-missing) values.

Return a boolean same-sized object indicating if the values are not NA. Non-
missing values get mapped to True. Characters such as empty strings ` ''  ` or
` numpy.inf  ` are not considered NA values (unless you set `
pandas.options.mode.use_inf_as_na  =  True  ` ). NA values, such as None or `
numpy.NaN  ` , get mapped to False values.

Returns  :

    

DataFrame

    

Mask of bool values for each element in DataFrame that indicates whether an
element is not an NA value.

See also

` DataFrame.notnull  `

    

Alias of notna.

[ ` DataFrame.isna  ` ](pandas.DataFrame.isna.html#pandas.DataFrame.isna
"pandas.DataFrame.isna")

    

Boolean inverse of notna.

[ ` DataFrame.dropna  ` ](pandas.DataFrame.dropna.html#pandas.DataFrame.dropna
"pandas.DataFrame.dropna")

    

Omit axes labels with missing values.

[ ` notna  ` ](pandas.notna.html#pandas.notna "pandas.notna")

    

Top-level notna.

Examples

Show which entries in a DataFrame are not NA.

    
    
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame(dict(age=[5, 6, np.nan],
    ...                        born=[pd.NaT, pd.Timestamp('1939-05-27'),
    ...                              pd.Timestamp('1940-04-25')],
    ...                        name=['Alfred', 'Batman', ''],
    ...                        toy=[None, 'Batmobile', 'Joker']))
    >>> df
       age       born    name        toy
    0  5.0        NaT  Alfred       None
    1  6.0 1939-05-27  Batman  Batmobile
    2  NaN 1940-04-25              Joker
    
    
    
    >>> df.notna()
         age   born  name    toy
    0   True  False  True  False
    1   True   True  True   True
    2  False   True  True   True
    

Show which entries in a Series are not NA.

    
    
    >>> ser = pd.Series([5, 6, np.nan])
    >>> ser
    0    5.0
    1    6.0
    2    NaN
    dtype: float64
    
    
    
    >>> ser.notna()
    0     True
    1     True
    2    False
    dtype: bool

# Efficient Text Splitting in Pandas for NLP Workflows

In large-scale natural language processing (NLP) pipelines, one of the earliest and most critical steps is splitting text into smaller, meaningful units. Whether the goal is sentiment analysis, topic modeling, or named entity recognition, effective tokenization and organization of text data can greatly influence downstream model performance. In this post, we’ll explore practical strategies for splitting text data in Python using the pandas library, with an emphasis on creating new DataFrame columns to store processed tokens for later analysis.

---

## Understanding the Role of Text Splitting

Text splitting, or tokenization, is the process of breaking down a string into smaller parts—words, phrases, or sentences—based on rules or learned patterns. In sentiment analysis, for example, splitting a sentence into words allows us to inspect the sentiment-bearing terms individually. By structuring the split tokens into separate DataFrame columns, we can enable more complex feature engineering, such as counting positive words, detecting negations, or applying part-of-speech tagging.

When working with large datasets, efficiency and clarity of operations become paramount. Pandas provides convenient methods for applying tokenization functions to entire columns without resorting to explicit Python loops, which can be slow.

---

## Setting Up the Data

Let’s imagine a dataset where each row contains a sentence and an associated metadata label:

```python
import pandas as pd

data = {
    'sentence': [
        'I love this product!',
        'The service was terrible.',
        'Absolutely fantastic experience.',
        'Not worth the price.'
    ],
    'label': ['positive', 'negative', 'positive', 'negative']
}

df = pd.DataFrame(data)
```

Here, the `sentence` column will be our target for splitting. Our aim is to tokenize each sentence and store the tokens in a new column for later sentiment feature extraction.

---

## Applying Tokenization with Pandas

Python’s built-in string methods, combined with pandas’ vectorized operations, make it straightforward to split text. For simple whitespace tokenization:

```python
df['tokens'] = df['sentence'].str.split()
```

This creates a `tokens` column where each entry is a list of words from the corresponding sentence. While basic, this approach is often sufficient for initial exploration.

For more advanced splitting—such as removing punctuation or splitting on multiple delimiters—we can use regular expressions:

```python
import re

df['tokens'] = df['sentence'].str.lower().str.findall(r'\b\w+\b')
```

This extracts only alphanumeric word sequences, ensuring that punctuation marks are excluded from the tokens.

---

## Custom Tokenization Functions

In many NLP tasks, tokenization requires domain-specific rules. For example, handling contractions, emoticons, or special symbols may necessitate a custom function. Pandas’ `.apply()` method allows us to apply such functions to each row:

```python
def custom_tokenizer(text):
    # Example: split on spaces and remove exclamation points
    tokens = text.replace('!', '').split(' ')
    return tokens

df['custom_tokens'] = df['sentence'].apply(custom_tokenizer)
```

This approach offers flexibility, though it is generally slower than vectorized string methods for very large datasets. For large-scale production pipelines, using libraries like spaCy or NLTK in combination with pandas can provide optimized tokenization routines.

---

## Organizing Tokens for Downstream Tasks

Once tokens are stored in a DataFrame column, they can be used for a variety of sentiment analysis features:

- **Word frequency counts** per sentiment class
- **Presence/absence flags** for sentiment lexicon terms
- **Sequence models** that process tokens directly

For example, to count the number of words in each sentence:

```python
df['token_count'] = df['tokens'].str.len()
```

Or to detect if a sentence contains a specific sentiment term:

```python
df['contains_love'] = df['tokens'].apply(lambda toks: 'love' in toks)
```

These derived columns can be fed into machine learning models as features alongside other metadata.

---

## Scaling for Large Datasets

When processing millions of rows, efficiency matters. Here are some tips:

1. **Use vectorized string methods** (`.str.split`, `.str.findall`) whenever possible.
2. **Minimize Python-level loops**; prefer `.apply()` only for complex logic not achievable with built-in methods.
3. **Consider chunked processing**: read and tokenize data in chunks to avoid memory overload.
4. **Leverage specialized NLP libraries** for complex tokenization that can still integrate smoothly with pandas DataFrames.

---

## Conclusion

Splitting text effectively in pandas is a foundational skill for NLP practitioners. By combining vectorized operations, regular expressions, and custom tokenization functions, you can prepare your text data efficiently for sentiment analysis and other tasks. Structuring tokens in new DataFrame columns not only makes the data easier to inspect but also streamlines the feature engineering process for downstream models. With these strategies, you can handle large-scale text datasets with clarity and speed, setting the stage for accurate and insightful analysis.

# Automating RSS Feed Scraping and Daily Digest Emails with Python’s `schedule` Library

Keeping up with multiple news sources can be difficult, especially if you want to aggregate headlines into a single, easy-to-read digest. Fortunately, Python’s `schedule` package makes it straightforward to run periodic jobs—such as fetching data from RSS feeds—without manually starting scripts each time. In this post, we’ll walk through setting up a small system to scrape headlines from various RSS feeds, store them in a database, and send out a daily digest email.

---

## Why Use `schedule` for Data Collection?

The `schedule` library offers a clean, human-friendly syntax for running functions at fixed intervals or specific times. This is perfect for tasks like:

- Fetching RSS feeds every hour
- Sending summary emails once a day
- Cleaning up old records weekly

Instead of relying on external cron jobs or complex threading logic, `schedule` allows you to keep scheduling logic inside your Python script, making it easier to manage and deploy.

---

## Step 1: Installing Dependencies

Before we start, install the required packages:

```bash
pip install schedule requests feedparser sqlite3 smtplib
```

Here’s what each does:

- **schedule**: Handles recurring job execution.
- **requests**: Fetches RSS feed URLs.
- **feedparser**: Parses RSS and Atom feeds.
- **sqlite3**: Stores headlines locally in a simple database.
- **smtplib**: Sends digest emails via SMTP.

---

## Step 2: Setting Up the Database

We’ll use SQLite for simplicity. Create a small helper to initialize the database:

```python
import sqlite3

def init_db():
    conn = sqlite3.connect('news.db')
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute('''
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS headlines (
            id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
            source TEXT,
            title TEXT,
            url TEXT,
            pub_date TEXT
        )
    ''')
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()
```

This table will store headlines along with their source, publication date, and URL.

---

## Step 3: Fetching and Parsing RSS Feeds

Next, we define a function to retrieve headlines from a given feed URL:

```python
import feedparser
from datetime import datetime

def fetch_feed(source_name, feed_url):
    feed = feedparser.parse(feed_url)
    conn = sqlite3.connect('news.db')
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    for entry in feed.entries:
        cursor.execute('''
            INSERT INTO headlines (source, title, url, pub_date)
            VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
        ''', (source_name, entry.title, entry.link, entry.published))
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()
    print(f"[{datetime.now()}] Fetched {len(feed.entries)} headlines from {source_name}")
```

---

## Step 4: Scheduling Multiple Feeds

We can now set up recurring jobs for each source:

```python
import schedule
import time

def scrape_all_sources():
    fetch_feed("BBC News", "http://feeds.bbci.co.uk/news/rss.xml")
    fetch_feed("Reuters", "http://feeds.reuters.com/reuters/topNews")
    fetch_feed("NY Times", "https://rss.nytimes.com/services/xml/rss/nyt/HomePage.xml")

init_db()

# Schedule scraping every hour
schedule.every().hour.do(scrape_all_sources)
```

This ensures our database is updated regularly with fresh headlines.

---

## Step 5: Sending a Daily Digest Email

Once we have stored headlines, we can send a summary email once per day:

```python
import smtplib
from email.mime.text import MIMEText

def send_digest():
    conn = sqlite3.connect('news.db')
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute('SELECT source, title, url FROM headlines ORDER BY pub_date DESC LIMIT 20')
    rows = cursor.fetchall()
    conn.close()
    
    content = "\n".join([f"{src}: {title} ({url})" for src, title, url in rows])
    msg = MIMEText(content)
    msg['Subject'] = 'Daily News Digest'
    msg['From'] = 'you@example.com'
    msg['To'] = 'recipient@example.com'

    with smtplib.SMTP('smtp.example.com', 587) as server:
        server.starttls()
        server.login('you@example.com', 'password')
        server.send_message(msg)
    print(f"[{datetime.now()}] Digest email sent.")

# Schedule digest at 8:00 AM daily
schedule.every().day.at("08:00").do(send_digest)
```

---

## Step 6: Running the Scheduler

Finally, keep the script running to execute scheduled tasks:

```python
while True:
    schedule.run_pending()
    time.sleep(1)
```

---

## Conclusion

By combining the `schedule` library with `requests`, `feedparser`, and a lightweight database, we can automate the process of collecting headlines from multiple RSS feeds and delivering them via email. This approach is flexible enough to accommodate additional sources, more complex filtering, or alternative delivery methods (such as SMS or Slack notifications). With minimal code, you can have a fully functioning news aggregation and digest system running around the clock.

# Report on Strategies for Efficient Aggregation of Meteorological Data Across Multiple Weather Stations

## Abstract  
The effective analysis of meteorological data requires the transformation of raw time-series measurements into aggregated summaries that are meaningful for climatological interpretation. This report examines strategies for aggregating temperature and rainfall data collected from multiple weather stations distributed across different regions. Emphasis is placed on methodologies for deriving daily and monthly averages, ensuring temporal alignment across stations, and managing heterogeneous data intervals. The discussion also addresses the use of specialized climate analysis software to automate and standardize aggregation processes.

---

## 1. Introduction  
Meteorological monitoring networks often comprise numerous stations recording environmental parameters such as temperature, precipitation, humidity, and wind speed at varying intervals. To support climate studies, agricultural planning, and hydrological forecasting, these high-frequency measurements must be aggregated into daily, monthly, or seasonal summaries. However, differences in recording schedules, missing data, and regional variability pose challenges for efficient and accurate aggregation.

This report explores structured approaches to temporal aggregation, focusing on temperature and rainfall data, and leveraging specialized analytical platforms designed for climate data processing.

---

## 2. Data Sources and Collection Intervals  
Weather stations may record observations at sub-hourly, hourly, or daily intervals. For temperature, sensors often log instantaneous readings or rolling averages, whereas rainfall gauges typically record accumulated precipitation over a given period. When multiple stations contribute data, discrepancies in sampling intervals can complicate aggregation.  

For example, Station A may report temperature every 15 minutes, while Station B reports hourly values. Rainfall data may also be irregular, with some gauges reporting only when measurable precipitation occurs. Addressing these inconsistencies is a prerequisite for accurate aggregation.

---

## 3. Temporal Aggregation Methodologies  

### 3.1 Daily Averages and Totals  
Daily aggregation for temperature generally involves computing the arithmetic mean of all valid measurements within a 24-hour period, adjusted for time zone and local observation practices. Rainfall is typically summed over the same period to yield total daily precipitation.  

Key considerations include:  
- **Time alignment**: Ensuring that all stations’ data are synchronized to a common daily boundary (e.g., midnight local time).  
- **Handling missing intervals**: Applying interpolation or gap-filling methods when data are absent, while flagging estimated values for quality control.  

### 3.2 Monthly Aggregates  
Monthly summaries are computed from daily aggregates rather than raw measurements to reduce computational load and maintain consistency. For temperature, monthly means are derived from the average of daily means, while monthly rainfall totals are obtained by summing daily totals.  

This hierarchical aggregation—minute/hour → day → month—ensures that irregular reporting frequencies do not bias the monthly statistics.

---

## 4. Cross-Station Aggregation  
When multiple stations operate within a region, spatial aggregation is often required to produce regional climate indicators. This involves:  
- Normalizing data to account for station-specific biases or calibration differences.  
- Weighting observations based on station representativeness (e.g., elevation, proximity to population centers).  
- Combining daily or monthly summaries across stations using arithmetic means or spatial interpolation techniques.

---

## 5. Software Tools and Automation  
Specialized climate analysis software, such as those developed by national meteorological agencies or research institutions, offer built-in functions for resampling, aggregation, and quality control. These platforms can:  
- Automatically detect and fill missing timestamps.  
- Resample data to fixed intervals (hourly, daily, monthly) while preserving station identifiers.  
- Generate summary reports and visualizations for end-users.  

Automation reduces manual processing errors, enhances reproducibility, and facilitates the integration of new data as it becomes available.

---

## 6. Quality Assurance and Validation  
Aggregated datasets must undergo rigorous quality checks to ensure reliability. Validation steps include:  
- Comparing aggregated values against independent reference datasets.  
- Identifying outliers and anomalies that may indicate sensor malfunctions.  
- Documenting all processing steps, including interpolation and aggregation methods, for transparency.

---

## 7. Conclusion  
Efficient aggregation of meteorological data from multiple stations is essential for accurate climate analysis. By standardizing temporal alignment, employing hierarchical aggregation methods, and leveraging specialized software, it is possible to produce robust daily and monthly summaries of temperature and rainfall. These aggregated datasets form the foundation for downstream applications in climate modeling, agricultural planning, and environmental monitoring.

---

**Keywords**: meteorological data, temporal aggregation, daily averages, monthly totals, climate analysis software, weather stations, rainfall, temperature.

The ` engine_kwargs  ` argument is a dictionary of keyword arguments that will
be passed into the [ numba.jit decorator ](https://numba.pydata.org/numba-
doc/latest/reference/jit-compilation.html#numba.jit) . These keyword arguments
will be applied to _both_ the passed function (if a standard Python function)
and the apply for loop over each window.

This page contains a high-level overview of some of the core concepts of
ESLint.

##  What is ESLint?

ESLint is a configurable JavaScript linter. It helps you find and fix problems
in your JavaScript code. Problems can be anything from potential runtime bugs,
to not following best practices, to styling issues.

##  Rules

Rules are the core building block of ESLint. A rule validates if your code
meets a certain expectation, and what to do if it does not meet that
expectation. Rules can also contain additional configuration options specific
to that rule.

For example, the [ ` semi ` ](../../rules/semi) rule lets you specify whether
or not JavaScript statements should end with a semicolon ( ` ; ` ). You can
set the rule to either always require semicolons or require that a statement
never ends with a semicolon.

ESLint contains hundreds of built-in rules that you can use. You can also
create custom rules or use rules that others have created with  plugins  .

For more information, refer to [ Rules ](../../rules/) .

###  Rule Fixes

Rules may optionally provide fixes for violations that they find. Fixes safely
correct the violation without changing application logic.

Fixes may be applied automatically with the [ ` --fix ` command line option
](../command-line-interface#--fix) and via editor extensions.

Rules that may provide fixes are marked with 🔧 in [ Rules ](../../rules/) .

###  Rule Suggestions

Rules may optionally provide suggestions in addition to or instead of
providing fixes. Suggestions differ from fixes in two ways:

  1. Suggestions may change application logic and so cannot be automatically applied. 
  2. Suggestions cannot be applied through the ESLint CLI and are only available through editor integrations. 

Rules that may provide suggestions are marked with 💡 in [ Rules
](../../rules/) .

##  Configuration Files

An ESLint configuration file is a place where you put the configuration for
ESLint in your project. You can include built-in rules, how you want them
enforced, plugins with custom rules, shareable configurations, which files you
want rules to apply to, and more.

For more information, refer to [ Configuration Files
](../configure/configuration-files) .

##  Shareable Configurations

Shareable configurations are ESLint configurations that are shared via npm.

Often shareable configurations are used to enforce style guides using ESLint’s
built-in rules. For example the sharable configuration [ eslint-config-airbnb-
base ](https://www.npmjs.com/package/eslint-config-airbnb-base) implements the
popular Airbnb JavaScript style guide.

For more information, refer to [ Using a shareable configuration package
](../configure/configuration-files#using-a-shareable-configuration-package) .

##  Plugins

An ESLint plugin is an npm module that can contain a set of ESLint rules,
configurations, processors, and environments. Often plugins include custom
rules. Plugins can be used to enforce a style guide and support JavaScript
extensions (like TypeScript), libraries (like React), and frameworks
(Angular).

# Leveraging JSON Configuration Files in Django for Dynamic Environment Management

In modern web applications, the ability to adapt configuration parameters without redeploying the entire project is a significant advantage. For Django developers, this flexibility can be achieved by integrating JSON-based configuration files into the application's settings structure. This approach enables rapid adjustments to environment-specific variables, feature flags, and service endpoints, while keeping the deployment pipeline lean.

## Why JSON for Configuration?

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) offers a lightweight, human-readable format that is widely supported across programming languages. Its hierarchical structure makes it ideal for storing complex configurations, such as nested dictionaries or lists, without sacrificing clarity. In Django projects, JSON files can complement or even replace certain environment variables, providing a centralized, editable source for runtime settings.

## Structuring Your Configuration Files

A typical JSON configuration file for Django might be organized by environment—development, staging, production—each containing relevant keys and values. For example:

```json
{
    "development": {
        "DEBUG": true,
        "DATABASES": {
            "default": {
                "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
                "NAME": "dev_db",
                "USER": "dev_user",
                "PASSWORD": "dev_pass",
                "HOST": "localhost",
                "PORT": 5432
            }
        },
        "FEATURE_FLAGS": {
            "enable_new_ui": false
        }
    },
    "production": {
        "DEBUG": false,
        "DATABASES": {
            "default": {
                "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.postgresql",
                "NAME": "prod_db",
                "USER": "prod_user",
                "PASSWORD": "secure_pass",
                "HOST": "db.example.com",
                "PORT": 5432
            }
        },
        "FEATURE_FLAGS": {
            "enable_new_ui": true
        }
    }
}
```

This structure allows developers to switch between environments by selecting the appropriate top-level key, without altering the core Django `settings.py` file.

## Parsing JSON in Django Settings

To integrate JSON configuration into Django settings, the JSON file can be read and parsed at runtime using Python’s built-in `json` module. A common pattern is to store the configuration file in a secure, known location (such as `/etc/myapp/config.json` or a project-level `config` folder), then load it during initialization:

```python
import os
import json

BASE_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
config_path = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, 'config', 'settings.json')

with open(config_path) as config_file:
    configs = json.load(config_file)

env = os.getenv('DJANGO_ENV', 'development')
current_config = configs.get(env, {})

# Apply JSON configuration to Django settings
DEBUG = current_config.get('DEBUG', False)
DATABASES = current_config.get('DATABASES', {})
FEATURE_FLAGS = current_config.get('FEATURE_FLAGS', {})
```

This method allows environment-specific settings to be adjusted simply by editing the JSON file and restarting the application, avoiding a full code redeployment.

## Benefits of Dynamic Configuration

1. **Reduced Deployment Overhead** – Changes to database credentials, API endpoints, or feature toggles can be made without touching the codebase.
2. **Centralized Management** – All environment settings are stored in one file, simplifying auditing and updates.
3. **Improved Security Practices** – Sensitive values can be managed through secure storage and file permissions, keeping them out of version control.
4. **Rapid Feature Rollout** – Feature flags in JSON enable toggling features on or off in production instantly.

## Considerations and Best Practices

- **Validation**: Implement checks when loading JSON to ensure required keys are present and values are of the correct type. This prevents runtime errors due to malformed configurations.
- **Security**: Store configuration files outside of the public repository, and ensure proper file permissions.
- **Versioning**: Keep backups or version history of configuration files to revert changes if needed.
- **Environment Awareness**: Use environment variables to select which configuration section to load, ensuring that deployments in different environments pick the correct settings.

## Conclusion

Integrating JSON-based configuration files into Django settings can transform the way applications are managed across environments. By adopting this approach, developers gain the ability to modify critical parameters on the fly, streamline deployment processes, and maintain cleaner codebases. With careful structuring and validation, JSON configurations become a powerful tool for dynamic environment management in Django projects.

###  Passing Arguments to Formatters

While formatter functions do not receive arguments in addition to the results
object and the context, it is possible to pass additional data into custom
formatters using the methods described below.

####  Using Environment Variables

Custom formatters have access to environment variables and so can change their
behavior based on environment variable data.

Here’s an example that uses a ` FORMATTER_SKIP_WARNINGS ` environment variable
to determine whether to show warnings in the results:

    
    
    module.exports = function(results) {
        var skipWarnings = process.env.FORMATTER_SKIP_WARNINGS === "true";
    
        var results = results || [];
        var summary = results.reduce(
            function(seq, current) {
                current.messages.forEach(function(msg) {
                    var logMessage = {
                        filePath: current.filePath,
                        ruleId: msg.ruleId,
                        message: msg.message,
                        line: msg.line,
                        column: msg.column
                    };
    
                    if (msg.severity === 1) {
                        logMessage.type = "warning";
                        seq.warnings.push(logMessage);
                    }
                    if (msg.severity === 2) {
                        logMessage.type = "error";
                        seq.errors.push(logMessage);
                    }
                });
                return seq;
            },
            {
                errors: [],
                warnings: []
            }
        );
    
        if (summary.errors.length > 0 || summary.warnings.length > 0) {
            var warnings = !skipWarnings ? summary.warnings : []; // skip the warnings in that case
    
            var lines = summary.errors
                .concat(warnings)
                .map(function(msg) {
                    return (
                        "\n" +
                        msg.type +
                        " " +
                        msg.ruleId +
                        "\n  " +
                        msg.filePath +
                        ":" +
                        msg.line +
                        ":" +
                        msg.column
                    );
                })
                .join("\n");
    
            return lines + "\n";
        }
    };

           This PMDA extracts performance data from BIND (Berkeley Internet
           Name Domain).  It enables collection of most of the statistics
           metrics from the Bind server version 9 or later, which includes:
    
           â¢ overall memory statistics
    
           â¢ overall per-query statistics (general queries, EDNS/truncated
             responses, Update/Notify/AXFR/IXFR messages)
    
           â¢ overall error statistics (Rejected, SERVFAIL, Update/XFR

             protcol and IP version including errors

           (2% CPU usage on Intel i7-4700MQ @2.4 GHz, cca 30 MB RAM).

# Optimizing SQL Query Performance with Compound Indexes and Structured WHERE Clauses

When working with large datasets in SQL databases, query performance can quickly become a bottleneck if the underlying queries are not carefully planned. The difference between a query that completes in milliseconds and one that drags on for seconds—or even minutes—often comes down to how indexes are utilized and how the `WHERE` clause is constructed. This article explores strategies for leveraging compound indexes and structuring conditions to avoid costly full table scans.

## Understanding Indexes and Their Role

Indexes act like a roadmap for the database engine, allowing it to locate rows matching certain criteria without scanning every record. A single-column index is straightforward: it accelerates lookups or range queries on that one field. However, real-world applications often require filtering or sorting on multiple fields simultaneously. This is where compound indexes—indexes built on two or more columns—become critical.

A compound index stores combined values from the indexed columns in a sorted structure. The order in which columns are defined in the index matters; the database can only efficiently use the index for queries that filter or sort based on the leftmost prefix of indexed columns. For example, an index on `(last_name, first_name)` can speed up queries filtering by `last_name` alone or by both `last_name` and `first_name`, but not by `first_name` alone.

## Structuring WHERE Clauses for Efficiency

The `WHERE` clause is the heart of query filtering, but its structure directly impacts whether the database can use an index. A common mistake is mixing different types of conditions across multiple columns without considering the index design. When conditions on multiple fields are combined, the database engine will only use indexes effectively if those fields are part of a compound index that matches the query structure.

For instance, consider a table of `orders` with columns `order_date`, `customer_id`, and `total_amount`. Suppose you have a compound index on `(customer_id, order_date)`. A query like:

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 123 AND order_date > '2023-01-01';
```

will make full use of the compound index. However, if you write:

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE total_amount > 100 AND order_date > '2023-01-01';
```

and there’s no index covering both `total_amount` and `order_date`, the database may fall back to scanning the entire table.

## Avoiding Full Table Scans

Full table scans are the enemy of performance in large datasets. They occur when the database engine has no suitable index to narrow down the search, forcing it to read every row to find matches. To avoid them:

1. **Design indexes based on query patterns** – Analyze common queries and identify which columns are frequently filtered together. Create compound indexes that match these combinations.
2. **Use selective conditions** – Highly selective conditions (those that match a small fraction of the table) benefit most from indexing and drastically reduce the number of rows scanned.
3. **Leverage index coverage** – An index that includes all columns needed for the query can allow the database to satisfy the query directly from the index without touching the base table.

## Balancing Indexes and Write Performance

While indexes improve read performance, they come at a cost: every insert or update must also update the index structures. Too many indexes can slow down write operations and increase storage overhead. The key is to balance read optimization with acceptable write performance. This often means prioritizing indexes for the most critical queries and consolidating multiple single-column indexes into fewer compound indexes.

## Testing and Monitoring

Optimization is an iterative process. Use database tools to examine query execution plans and verify whether indexes are being used. Monitor performance metrics over time to ensure that changes to the schema or query patterns do not degrade performance. In some cases, rewriting the `WHERE` clause or adjusting the order of conditions can make a query more index-friendly without altering its logic.

---

By thoughtfully designing compound indexes and structuring `WHERE` clauses to align with those indexes, developers can dramatically improve query performance in SQL databases. This approach minimizes full table scans, reduces latency, and ensures that applications remain responsive even as datasets grow. The investment in careful planning and testing pays dividends in scalability and user satisfaction.

# Understanding Python’s Garbage Collector and Reference Cycles in Class Instances

One of Python’s greatest strengths is its built-in memory management system, which frees developers from manually allocating and deallocating memory. At the heart of this system is the garbage collector (GC), a mechanism that not only tracks object references but also detects and resolves reference cycles. This post will walk through how the garbage collector operates, especially in scenarios involving class instances and their attributes, and will provide concrete code examples to illustrate the cleanup process.

---

## Reference Counting and Its Limits

The primary memory management technique in CPython is **reference counting**. Every object maintains a counter that tracks how many references point to it. When the count drops to zero, the object’s memory is immediately reclaimed. This works flawlessly for straightforward reference graphs but has a limitation: it cannot automatically break **reference cycles**.

A reference cycle occurs when objects reference each other in a way that prevents their reference counts from ever reaching zero. For instance:

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.next = None

# Create two nodes referring to each other
a = Node('A')
b = Node('B')
a.next = b
b.next = a
```

Here, even if `a` and `b` go out of scope, they still hold references to each other, keeping their counts above zero. Without additional mechanisms, these objects would remain in memory indefinitely.

---

## Detecting Cycles with the Garbage Collector

Python’s `gc` module supplements reference counting with a **cycle detector**. This detector periodically scans objects in memory, looking for cycles of references that are no longer reachable from any program variables.

You can inspect and trigger the garbage collector manually:

```python
import gc

print(gc.get_count())  # Shows the current collection counts for generations

gc.collect()           # Forces a garbage collection cycle
```

When the GC finds a cycle, it determines if the objects in the cycle are unreachable from the program’s active scope. If so, it breaks the cycle and reclaims the memory.

---

## Class Instances and Attribute Cycles

Class instances can easily participate in cycles, especially when attributes store references to other instances. Consider:

```python
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.friend = None

alice = Person("Alice")
bob = Person("Bob")

alice.friend = bob
bob.friend = alice
```

This is a classic cycle: `alice` references `bob` and vice versa. If we delete both variables:

```python
del alice
del bob
```

The reference counts for these objects will not drop to zero because each still references the other. The garbage collector must intervene to free them.

---

## Demonstrating Cleanup in Practice

To see this in action, we can use `__del__` methods to log when objects are finalized:

```python
import gc

class Person:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.friend = None
    def __del__(self):
        print(f"{self.name} is being garbage collected")

gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_UNCOLLECTABLE | gc.DEBUG_COLLECTABLE)

alice = Person("Alice")
bob = Person("Bob")
alice.friend = bob
bob.friend = alice

del alice
del bob

print("Collecting...")
gc.collect()
```

When `gc.collect()` runs, the cycle detector finds the two `Person` instances no longer reachable from active variables and reclaims them, triggering their `__del__` messages.

---

## Special Considerations with `__del__`

One subtlety is that objects with `__del__` methods in a cycle are treated with caution. The GC may mark them as **uncollectable** in certain versions of Python, because calling `__del__` on objects in cycles can lead to unpredictable behavior. This is why it’s often recommended to avoid `__del__` for complex objects and instead use context managers or explicit cleanup methods.

---

## Best Practices to Avoid Unnecessary Cycles

While the garbage collector can handle cycles, reducing their occurrence can improve performance:

- Use weak references (`weakref` module) when appropriate to avoid strong reference loops.
- Break cycles manually by setting attributes to `None` before deleting objects.
- Limit the use of `__del__` in objects that may participate in cycles.

---

## Conclusion

Python’s garbage collector plays a crucial role in managing memory beyond simple reference counting. By detecting and cleaning up reference cycles, it ensures that even complex networks of objects, such as interlinked class instances, do not linger in memory unnecessarily. Understanding how the GC operates—and being mindful of cycles—can help you write more efficient and memory-safe Python code. With the right practices, you can trust Python’s GC to keep your applications running smoothly without leaking memory due to cyclical references.

` 'nonce-*' `

    

A cryptographic nonce (only used once) to allow scripts. The server must
generate a unique nonce value each time it transmits a policy. It is critical
to provide a nonce that cannot be guessed as bypassing a resource's policy is
otherwise trivial. This is used in conjunction with the [ script tag nonce
attribute ](/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/script#nonce) . For example, ` nonce-
DhcnhD3khTMePgXwdayK9BsMqXjhguVV ` .

` 'sha*-*' `

    

sha256, sha384, or sha512. Followed by a dash and then the sha* value. For
example, ` sha256-jzgBGA4UWFFmpOBq0JpdsySukE1FrEN5bUpoK8Z29fY= ` .

##  CSP in workers

[ Workers ](/en-US/docs/Web/API/Worker) are in general _not_ governed by the
content security policy of the document (or parent worker) that created them.
To specify a content security policy for the worker, set a ` Content-Security-
Policy ` response header for the request which requested the worker script
itself.

The exception to this is if the worker script's origin is a globally unique
identifier (for example, if its URL has a scheme of data or blob). In this
case, the worker does inherit the content security policy of the document or
worker that created it.

##  Multiple content security policies

The CSP mechanism allows multiple policies being specified for a resource,
including via the ` Content-Security-Policy ` header, the [ ` Content-
Security-Policy-Report-Only ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-
Policy-Report-Only) header and a [ ` <meta> ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/meta) element.

You can use the ` Content-Security-Policy ` header more than once, as in the
example below. Pay special attention to the [ ` connect-src ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/connect-src) directive here.
Even though the second policy would allow the connection, the first policy
contains ` connect-src 'none' ` . Adding additional policies _can only further
restrict_ the capabilities of the protected resource, which means that there
will be no connection allowed and, as the strictest policy, ` connect-src
'none' ` is enforced.

http

    
    
    Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self' http://example.com;
                              connect-src 'none';
    Content-Security-Policy: connect-src http://example.com/;
                              script-src http://example.com/
    

##  Examples

Example: Disable unsafe inline/eval, only allow loading of resources (images,
fonts, scripts, etc.) over http:

###  Using the HTTP header

http

    
    
    Content-Security-Policy: default-src https:
    

###  Using the HTML meta element

html

    
    
    <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src https:" />
    

Example: Pre-existing site that uses too much inline code to fix but wants to
ensure resources are loaded only over HTTPS and to disable plugins:

http

    
    
    Content-Security-Policy: default-src https: 'unsafe-eval' 'unsafe-inline'; object-src 'none'
    

Example: Do not implement the above policy yet; instead just report violations
that would have occurred:

http

    
    
    Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only: default-src https:; report-uri /csp-violation-report-endpoint/
    

See [ Mozilla Web Security Guidelines
](https://infosec.mozilla.org/guidelines/web_security#Examples_5) for more
examples.

##  Other models  ¶

You can now get the current user directly in the _path operation functions_
and deal with the security mechanisms at the **Dependency Injection** level,
using ` Depends ` .

And you can use any model or data for the security requirements (in this case,
a Pydantic model ` User ` ).

But you are not restricted to using some specific data model, class or type.

Do you want to have an ` id ` and ` email ` and not have any ` username ` in
your model? Sure. You can use these same tools.

Do you want to just have a ` str ` ? Or just a ` dict ` ? Or a database class
model instance directly? It all works the same way.

You actually don't have users that log in to your application but robots,
bots, or other systems, that have just an access token? Again, it all works
the same.

Just use any kind of model, any kind of class, any kind of database that you
need for your application. **FastAPI** has you covered with the dependency
injection system.

##  Timestamps vs. time spans  #

Timestamped data is the most basic type of time series data that associates
values with points in time. For pandas objects it means using the points in
time.

    
    
    In [28]: import datetime
    
    In [29]: pd.Timestamp(datetime.datetime(2012, 5, 1))
    Out[29]: Timestamp('2012-05-01 00:00:00')
    
    In [30]: pd.Timestamp("2012-05-01")
    Out[30]: Timestamp('2012-05-01 00:00:00')
    
    In [31]: pd.Timestamp(2012, 5, 1)
    Out[31]: Timestamp('2012-05-01 00:00:00')
    

However, in many cases it is more natural to associate things like change
variables with a time span instead. The span represented by ` Period  ` can be
specified explicitly, or inferred from datetime string format.

    Out[32]: Period('2011-01', 'M')
    
    In [33]: pd.Period("2012-05", freq="D")

ESLint has a very lightweight development environment that makes updating code
fast and easy. This is a step-by-step guide to setting up a local development
environment that will let you contribute back to the project.

##  Step 1: Install Node.js

Go to [ https://nodejs.org/ ](https://nodejs.org/) to download and install the
latest stable version for your operating system.

Most of the installers already come with [ npm ](https://www.npmjs.com/) but
if for some reason npm doesn’t work on your system, you can install it
manually using the instructions on the site.

##  Step 2: Fork and Checkout Your Own ESLint Repository

Go to [ https://github.com/eslint/eslint ](https://github.com/eslint/eslint)
and click the “Fork” button. Follow the [ GitHub documentation
](https://help.github.com/articles/fork-a-repo) for forking and cloning.

Clone your fork:

    
    
    git clone https://github.com/<Your Github Username>/eslint
    
    
    1  
    

Once you’ve cloned the repository, run ` npm install ` to get all the
necessary dependencies:

    
    
    cd eslint
    npm install
    
    
    1  
    2  
    

You must be connected to the Internet for this step to work. You’ll see a lot
of utilities being downloaded.

**Note:** It’s a good idea to re-run ` npm install ` whenever you pull from
the main repository to ensure you have the latest development dependencies.

##  Step 3: Add the Upstream Source

The _upstream source_ is the main ESLint repository where active development
happens. While you won’t have push access to upstream, you will have pull
access, allowing you to pull in the latest code whenever you want.

To add the upstream source for ESLint, run the following in your repository:

    
    
    git remote add upstream git@github.com:eslint/eslint.git
    
    
    1  
    

Now, the remote ` upstream ` points to the upstream source.

##  Step 4: Install the Yeoman Generator

[ Yeoman ](https://yeoman.io) is a scaffold generator that ESLint uses to help
streamline development of new rules. If you don’t already have Yeoman
installed, you can install it via npm:

    
    
    npm install -g yo
    
    
    1  
    

Then, you can install the ESLint Yeoman generator:

    
    
    npm install -g generator-eslint
    
    
    1  
    

Please see the [ generator documentation
](https://github.com/eslint/generator-eslint) for instructions on how to use
it.

##  Step 5: Run the Tests

Running the tests is the best way to ensure you have correctly set up your
development environment. Make sure you’re in the ` eslint ` directory and run:

    
    
    npm test
    
    
    1  
    

The testing takes a few minutes to complete. If any tests fail, that likely
means one or more parts of the environment setup didn’t complete correctly.
The upstream tests always pass.

# Mapping Months to Zodiac Signs for Personalized Horoscope Rankings

Horoscopes have long fascinated people across cultures, offering a blend of tradition, symbolism, and storytelling. One of the most common starting points for creating a horoscope is to identify an individual’s astrological zodiac sign based on their birth month and day. This blog post explores a systematic approach for converting month names into zodiac signs using a mapping table, and then demonstrates how these mappings can be used to create personalized horoscopes sorted by a predicted luck score.

---

## Understanding Zodiac Sign Boundaries

The twelve zodiac signs are defined by specific date ranges in the Gregorian calendar:

- **Capricorn**: December 22 – January 19  
- **Aquarius**: January 20 – February 18  
- **Pisces**: February 19 – March 20  
- **Aries**: March 21 – April 19  
- **Taurus**: April 20 – May 20  
- **Gemini**: May 21 – June 20  
- **Cancer**: June 21 – July 22  
- **Leo**: July 23 – August 22  
- **Virgo**: August 23 – September 22  
- **Libra**: September 23 – October 22  
- **Scorpio**: October 23 – November 21  
- **Sagittarius**: November 22 – December 21  

Because zodiac boundaries often fall mid-month rather than at the start, a mapping from month name alone to sign will be approximate unless day information is included. For purposes of certain horoscope applications, however, month-level granularity can be sufficient.

---

## Creating a Month-to-Zodiac Mapping Table

A mapping table acts as a lookup that associates each month with one or two possible zodiac signs. For example:

| Month       | Primary Sign | Secondary Sign |
|-------------|--------------|----------------|
| January     | Capricorn    | Aquarius       |
| February    | Aquarius     | Pisces         |
| March       | Pisces       | Aries          |
| April       | Aries        | Taurus         |
| May         | Taurus       | Gemini         |
| June        | Gemini       | Cancer         |
| July        | Cancer       | Leo            |
| August      | Leo          | Virgo          |
| September   | Virgo        | Libra          |
| October     | Libra        | Scorpio        |
| November    | Scorpio      | Sagittarius    |
| December    | Sagittarius  | Capricorn      |

If exact birth dates are unknown, the primary sign can be assigned as a default. This allows quick categorization of individuals by zodiac based solely on month names.

---

## Integrating the Mapping into Horoscope Generation

Once the month-to-zodiac mapping is established, it can be applied to a dataset containing month names. Each record’s month is matched to the mapping table to yield the corresponding zodiac sign. This step standardizes the data and enables further processing such as merging with a table of zodiac attributes.

For personalized horoscope generation, you can enrich the zodiac sign data with additional variables:

- **Element**: Fire, Earth, Air, Water  
- **Modality**: Cardinal, Fixed, Mutable  
- **Ruling Planet**: e.g., Mars for Aries, Venus for Taurus  
- **Typical Traits**: strengths, weaknesses, preferences  

By linking these attributes to each zodiac sign, the resulting dataset forms a rich profile that can be used to tailor content.

---

## Calculating and Sorting by Predicted Luck Score

A “predicted luck score” can be derived from various inputs: planetary transits, numerology, or even historical patterns tied to each sign. For example, suppose you have a table that assigns a daily luck score between 0 and 100 for each zodiac sign based on current astrological conditions. After mapping months to signs, you can join this luck score to each record and then sort the dataset in descending order to identify the most “fortunate” profiles for a given period.

This sorted list can be used for:

- Publishing daily or monthly “Top 5 luckiest signs” posts  
- Sending personalized horoscope emails to subscribers  
- Creating targeted recommendations in lifestyle apps  

Sorting by luck score transforms static zodiac data into actionable insights, making horoscopes more engaging and interactive.

---

## Practical Example

Imagine you have a list of customers with their birth months recorded as text entries like “March”, “July”, “October”. By applying the month-to-zodiac mapping, you assign each customer a zodiac sign. You then pull in a luck score table for the current month and merge it with your customer data. The merged dataset is sorted so that customers with the highest luck scores appear first, allowing you to prioritize outreach or craft special offers aligned with their forecast.

---

## Conclusion

Converting month names into zodiac signs is a straightforward process when guided by a mapping table. This approach provides the foundation for building personalized horoscopes enriched with sign-specific attributes and ranked by dynamic metrics such as predicted luck score. By combining traditional astrological knowledge with structured data handling, you can create compelling, customized content that resonates with audiences seeking both entertainment and a touch of cosmic insight.

Gets tags for inline scripts registered for a specific handle.

##  Parameters

` $handle ` string  required

    

Name of the script to get associated inline script tag for.  
Must be lowercase.

` $position ` string  optional

    

Whether to get tag for inline scripts in the before or after position. Default
` 'after' ` .

Default: ` 'after' `

##  Return

string  Inline script, which may be empty string.

##  Source

    
    
    public function get_inline_script_tag( $handle, $position = 'after' ) {
    	$js = $this->get_inline_script_data( $handle, $position );
    	if ( empty( $js ) ) {
    		return '';
    	}
    
    	$id = "{$handle}-js-{$position}";
    
    	return wp_get_inline_script_tag( $js, compact( 'id' ) );
    }

While adding an ordering on ` experience ` to the query will yield the same
set of documents and obviate re-ordering the results on the clients, the query
may read many more extraneous index entries than the earlier query. This is
because Cloud Firestore always prefers an index whose index fields prefix
match the order by clause of the query. If ` experience ` were added to the
order by clause, then Cloud Firestore will select the ` (experience [...],
salary [...]) ` index for computing query results. Since there are no other
constraints on ` experience ` , Cloud Firestore will read  all  index entries
of the ` employees ` collection before applying the ` salary ` filter to find
the final result set. This means that index entries which don't satisfy the `
salary ` filter are still read, thus increasing the latency and cost of the
query.

DataFrame.  rank  (  _ axis  =  0  _ , _ method  =  'average'  _ , _
numeric_only  =  False  _ , _ na_option  =  'keep'  _ , _ ascending  =  True
_ , _ pct  =  False  _ )  [ [source]  ](https://github.com/pandas-
dev/pandas/blob/v2.2.2/pandas/core/generic.py#L9949-L10104) #

    

Compute numerical data ranks (1 through n) along axis.

By default, equal values are assigned a rank that is the average of the ranks
of those values.

Parameters  :

    

**axis** {0 or âindexâ, 1 or âcolumnsâ}, default 0

    

Index to direct ranking. For  Series  this parameter is unused and defaults to
0.

**method** {âaverageâ, âminâ, âmaxâ, âfirstâ, âdenseâ},
default âaverageâ

    

How to rank the group of records that have the same value (i.e. ties):

  * average: average rank of the group 

  * min: lowest rank in the group 

  * max: highest rank in the group 

  * first: ranks assigned in order they appear in the array 

  * dense: like âminâ, but rank always increases by 1 between groups. 

**numeric_only** bool, default False

    

For DataFrame objects, rank only numeric columns if set to True.

Changed in version 2.0.0:  The default value of ` numeric_only  ` is now `
False  ` .

**na_option** {âkeepâ, âtopâ, âbottomâ}, default âkeepâ

    

How to rank NaN values:

  * keep: assign NaN rank to NaN values 

  * top: assign lowest rank to NaN values 

  * bottom: assign highest rank to NaN values 

**ascending** bool, default True

    

Whether or not the elements should be ranked in ascending order.

**pct** bool, default False

    

Whether or not to display the returned rankings in percentile form.

Returns  :

    

same type as caller

    

Return a Series or DataFrame with data ranks as values.

See also

[ ` core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.rank  `
](pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.rank.html#pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.rank
"pandas.core.groupby.DataFrameGroupBy.rank")

    

Rank of values within each group.

Rank of values within each group.

Examples

    
    
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame(data={'Animal': ['cat', 'penguin', 'dog',
    ...                                    'spider', 'snake'],
    ...                         'Number_legs': [4, 2, 4, 8, np.nan]})
    >>> df
        Animal  Number_legs
    0      cat          4.0
    1  penguin          2.0

    4    snake          NaN
    

Ties are assigned the mean of the ranks (by default) for the group.

    
    
    >>> s = pd.Series(range(5), index=list("abcde"))
    >>> s["d"] = s["b"]
    >>> s.rank()
    a    1.0
    b    2.5
    c    4.0
    d    2.5
    e    5.0
    dtype: float64
    

The following example shows how the method behaves with the above parameters:

  * default_rank: this is the default behaviour obtained without using any parameter. 

  * max_rank: setting ` method  =  'max'  ` the records that have the same values are ranked using the highest rank (e.g.: since âcatâ and âdogâ are both in the 2nd and 3rd position, rank 3 is assigned.) 

  * NA_bottom: choosing ` na_option  =  'bottom'  ` , if there are records with NaN values they are placed at the bottom of the ranking. 

  * pct_rank: when setting ` pct  =  True  ` , the ranking is expressed as percentile rank.

#  String

The **` String ` ** object is used to represent and manipulate a sequence of
characters.

##  Description

Strings are useful for holding data that can be represented in text form. Some
of the most-used operations on strings are to check their [ ` length ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/length) , to build and
concatenate them using the [ ` + ` and ` += ` string operators ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Expressions_and_operators#string_operators) ,
checking for the existence or location of substrings with the [ ` indexOf() `
](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/indexOf) method,
or extracting substrings with the [ ` substring() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/substring) method.

###  Creating strings

Strings can be created as primitives, from string literals, or as objects,
using the [ ` String() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/String) constructor:

js

    
    
    const string1 = "A string primitive";
    const string2 = 'Also a string primitive';
    const string3 = `Yet another string primitive`;
    

js

    
    
    const string4 = new String("A String object");
    

String primitives and string objects share many behaviors, but have other
important differences and caveats. See "  String primitives and String objects
" below.

String literals can be specified using single or double quotes, which are
treated identically, or using the backtick character ` ` ` . This last form
specifies a [ template literal ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Template_literals) : with this form you can
interpolate expressions. For more information on the syntax of string
literals, see [ lexical grammar ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Lexical_grammar#string_literals) .

###  Character access

There are two ways to access an individual character in a string. The first is
the [ ` charAt() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/charAt) method:

js

    
    
    "cat".charAt(1); // gives value "a"
    

The other way is to treat the string as an array-like object, where individual
characters correspond to a numerical index:

js

    
    
    "cat"[1]; // gives value "a"
    

When using bracket notation for character access, attempting to delete or
assign a value to these properties will not succeed. The properties involved
are neither writable nor configurable. (See [ ` Object.defineProperty() `
](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/defineProperty)
for more information.)

###  Comparing strings

Use the [ less-than and greater-than operators ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators) to compare strings:

js

    
    
    const a = "a";
    const b = "b";
    if (a < b) {
      // true
      console.log(`${a} is less than ${b}`);
    } else if (a > b) {
      console.log(`${a} is greater than ${b}`);
    } else {
      console.log(`${a} and ${b} are equal.`);
    }
    

Note that all comparison operators, including [ ` === ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Strict_equality) and [ ` == `
](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Equality) , compare strings
case-sensitively. A common way to compare strings case-insensitively is to
convert both to the same case (upper or lower) before comparing them.

# Modularizing Node.js Backends for Multiple Microservices: Strategies for Performance and API Route Structuring

As applications scale, the backend often evolves into a network of cooperating microservices. While microservices offer benefits in scalability, maintainability, and fault isolation, they also introduce complexity in code organization, API management, and performance optimization. In a Node.js environment, where asynchronous I/O and event-driven architecture are core strengths, effective modularization becomes essential for keeping development productive and systems performant.

## The Case for Modularization

Modularization in a microservices-based Node.js backend means structuring code so that each service is self-contained, yet able to interact with others through well-defined interfaces. This approach:

- Reduces coupling between services, making it easier to update or replace components.
- Improves testability by isolating functionality.
- Enhances scalability by enabling independent deployment and scaling of services.

The goal is to design services that expose clear APIs and keep internal logic encapsulated, while maintaining a central orchestration layer when necessary.

## Organizing Code by Domain

A common strategy is to organize the backend codebase into domain-driven modules. Each microservice should have a directory structure reflecting its responsibilities:

```
/services
  /auth
    /controllers
    /models
    /routes
    /utils
  /billing
    /controllers
    /models
    /routes
    /utils
  /notifications
    /controllers
    /models
    /routes
    /utils
```

Within each service, **controllers** handle request logic, **models** interact with databases, **routes** define HTTP endpoints, and **utils** house helper functions. This separation allows individual services to be developed and maintained independently, while still following consistent patterns.

## API Gateway and Route Structuring

When multiple microservices are exposed to clients, an API gateway can unify routing and enforce cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, rate limiting, and logging. In Node.js, this gateway is often implemented with frameworks like Express or Fastify.

**Best practices for route structuring:**

- **Prefix routes by service**: e.g., `/auth/login`, `/billing/invoice`, `/notifications/send`.
- Use **versioning** in route paths to manage changes without breaking clients: `/v1/auth/login`.
- Implement **central middleware** at the gateway level for tasks applicable to all services.
- Delegate service-specific logic to the respective microservice module, avoiding duplicated logic in the gateway.

This separation ensures that route changes in one service do not ripple through unrelated parts of the system.

## Performance Optimization Across Services

Performance in a microservice architecture depends on both internal efficiency and inter-service communication. Key strategies include:

1. **Connection pooling** for databases in each service to reduce overhead from frequent connection creation.
2. **Caching responses** at the gateway or service level using in-memory stores like Redis, especially for frequently accessed data.
3. **Batching requests** when communicating between services to minimize network overhead.
4. Employing **asynchronous message queues** (e.g., RabbitMQ, Kafka) for non-blocking inter-service tasks, reducing synchronous API calls.

Node.js excels at handling concurrent requests, but excessive synchronous dependencies between services can lead to bottlenecks. Where possible, design services to operate independently and reconcile state asynchronously.

## Shared Libraries and Utilities

While each microservice should be self-contained, some functionality may be common across services (e.g., logging, configuration parsing, error handling). These should be abstracted into shared libraries:

```
/lib
  logger.js
  config.js
  errorHandler.js
```

These libraries can be imported by individual services, ensuring consistency without duplicating code. Care must be taken to avoid introducing tight coupling or dependencies that hinder independent deployment.

## Deployment Considerations

Modularized services can be deployed in containers, with orchestration handled by Kubernetes or Docker Compose. Each service should have its own deployment pipeline, enabling independent scaling based on load. Monitoring and observability tools (Prometheus, Grafana) should be integrated to track performance metrics and detect issues across the service network.

## Conclusion

Integrating multiple microservices in a Node.js backend requires deliberate modularization strategies. By organizing code by domain, structuring API routes via a gateway, optimizing performance through asynchronous patterns, and maintaining shared utilities, teams can build scalable and maintainable systems. These practices not only improve developer productivity but also ensure that the backend can evolve gracefully as business requirements grow. The result is a robust architecture that leverages Node.js’s strengths while managing the complexity inherent in microservice ecosystems.

# Optimizing Large-Scale JavaScript Builds with Webpack Code-Splitting and Lazy Loading

In modern web development, performance is a critical factor influencing user experience and engagement. As applications grow in complexity, their JavaScript bundles can become massive, leading to slow initial load times and degraded responsiveness. Webpack, as one of the most popular module bundlers, offers advanced code-splitting features and lazy loading techniques that can dramatically reduce bundle sizes and improve page load performance for large-scale projects.

## Understanding Code-Splitting

Code-splitting is the practice of breaking your application’s code into smaller “chunks” that can be loaded on demand rather than in a single monolithic bundle. This approach ensures that users only download the code they need at any given moment. Webpack supports several forms of code-splitting:

1. **Entry Points Splitting** – Configuring multiple entry points in your Webpack configuration to produce separate bundles for distinct sections of the application.
2. **Dynamic Imports** – Leveraging the `import()` syntax to load modules asynchronously when they are needed.
3. **Vendor Splitting** – Separating third-party dependencies from application logic, often using the `SplitChunksPlugin` to create a dedicated vendor bundle.

By splitting code intelligently, you reduce the amount of JavaScript the browser must parse and execute during the initial page load.

## Lazy Loading for Performance Gains

Lazy loading complements code-splitting by deferring the loading of non-critical resources until they are required. This technique is particularly effective for components or features that are not immediately visible or necessary when the user first accesses the application.

For example, a dashboard application might lazy load charts, reports, or advanced settings panels only when the user navigates to those sections. In practice, this can be implemented using dynamic imports:

```javascript
const ChartComponent = () => import(/* webpackChunkName: "chart" */ './ChartComponent');
```

When the user triggers the view containing `ChartComponent`, Webpack fetches the corresponding chunk from the server, reducing the initial payload.

## Configuring Webpack for Effective Code-Splitting

A well-tuned Webpack configuration is essential for reaping the full benefits of code-splitting and lazy loading. Key strategies include:

- **Using `optimization.splitChunks`**: This option allows fine-grained control over how chunks are created. You can set cache groups to separate vendor code, common modules, or specific feature sets.
- **Enabling async chunk loading**: Ensure that your server is configured to serve chunk files correctly and that your application handles asynchronous loading gracefully.
- **Naming chunks**: Use `webpackChunkName` comments in dynamic imports to give meaningful names to generated files. This aids in debugging and cache management.

An example configuration snippet:

```javascript
optimization: {
  splitChunks: {
    chunks: 'all',
    cacheGroups: {
      vendor: {
        test: /[\\/]node_modules[\\/]/,
        name: 'vendors',
        chunks: 'all',
      },
    },
  },
},
```

## Balancing Performance and Complexity

While code-splitting and lazy loading offer clear performance advantages, they introduce added complexity to the build process and runtime behavior. Developers must account for:

- **Chunk management**: Ensuring correct loading order and avoiding redundant downloads.
- **Error handling**: Managing network failures when loading chunks dynamically.
- **Caching strategies**: Leveraging long-term caching for vendor bundles while enabling cache busting for frequently updated application chunks.

Testing is crucial to ensure that lazy-loaded components behave as expected across different devices and network conditions.

## Monitoring and Iterating

Optimization is an iterative process. Tools such as Webpack Bundle Analyzer can visualize the composition of your bundles, highlighting opportunities for further splitting or dependency reduction. Monitoring real-world performance metrics using services like Google Lighthouse or WebPageTest provides concrete feedback on the impact of changes.

By continuously refining your code-splitting strategy and lazy loading logic, you can keep large-scale JavaScript applications performant even as they evolve and grow.

---

**Conclusion**  
Webpack’s advanced code-splitting capabilities, when paired with thoughtful lazy loading, can transform the performance profile of large-scale web applications. By delivering only the code that users need, when they need it, developers can minimize initial load times, reduce bandwidth consumption, and create a more responsive user experience. The key lies in balancing the technical complexity of these optimizations with the tangible performance benefits they bring, ensuring that the application remains maintainable and scalable over time.

the handler for this signal is expected to process the received data and then
call gtk_drag_finish(), setting the ` success ` parameter depending on whether
the data was processed successfully.

######  [ GtkWidget::drag-drop ](signal.Widget.drag-drop.html)

The ::drag-drop signal is emitted on the drop site when the user drops the
data onto the widget. The signal handler must determine whether the cursor
position is in a drop zone or not. If it is not in a drop zone, it returns `
FALSE ` and no further processing is necessary. Otherwise, the handler returns
` TRUE ` . In this case, the handler must ensure that ` gtk_drag_finish() ` is
called to let the source know that the drop is done. The call to `
gtk_drag_finish() ` can be done either directly or in a ` GtkWidget::drag-
data-received ` handler which gets triggered by calling ` gtk_drag_get_data()
` to receive the data for one or more of the supported targets.

typical reason to connect to this signal is to undo things done in `

The ::drag-failed signal is emitted on the drag source when a drag has failed.
The signal handler may hook custom code to handle a failed DnD operation based
on the type of error, it returns ` TRUE ` is the failure has been already
handled (not showing the default “drag operation failed” animation), otherwise
it returns ` FALSE ` .

The ::drag-leave signal is emitted on the drop site when the cursor leaves the

#  userhooks: Functions to Get and Set Hooks for Load, Attach, Detach and
Unload

##  Description

These functions allow users to set actions to be taken before packages are
attached/detached and namespaces are (un)loaded.

##  Usage

    
    
    getHook(hookName)
    setHook(hookName, value,
            action = c("append", "prepend", "replace"))
    
    packageEvent(pkgname,
                 event = c("onLoad", "attach", "detach", "onUnload"))

##  Arguments

hookName

character string: the hook name

pkgname

character string: the package/namespace name

event

character string: an event for the package. Can be abbreviated.

value

A function or a list of functions, or for ` action = "replace" ` , ` NULL `

action

The action to be taken. Can be abbreviated.

##  Value

For ` getHook ` function, a list of functions (possibly empty). For ` setHook
` function, no return value. For ` packageEvent ` , the derived hook name (a
character string).

##  Details

` setHook ` provides a general mechanism for users to register hooks, a list
of functions to be called from system (or user) functions. The initial set of
hooks was associated with events on packages/namespaces: these hooks are named
via calls to ` packageEvent ` .

To remove a hook completely, call ` setHook(hookName, NULL, "replace") ` .

When an  R  package is attached by ` [ library
](/link/library?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` or loaded by other means, it can
call initialization code. See ` [ .onLoad
](/link/.onLoad?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` for a description of the package
hook functions called during initialization. Users can add their own
initialization code via the hooks provided by ` setHook() ` , functions which
will be called as ` funname(pkgname, pkgpath) ` inside a ` [ try
](/link/try?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` call.

The sequence of events depends on which hooks are defined, and whether a
package is attached or just loaded. In the case where all hooks are defined
and a package is attached, the order of initialization events is as follows:

  1. The package namespace is loaded. 

  2. The package's ` [ .onLoad ](/link/.onLoad?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` function is run. 

  3. If S4 methods dispatch is on, any actions set by ` [ setLoadAction ](/link/setLoadAction?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` are run. 

  4. The namespace is sealed. 

  5. The user's ` "onLoad" ` hook is run. 

  6. The package is added to the search path. 

  7. The package's ` [ .onAttach ](/link/.onAttach?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` function is run. 

  8. The package environment is sealed. 

  9. The user's ` "attach" ` hook is run. 

A similar sequence (but in reverse) is run when a package is detached and its
namespace unloaded:

  1. The user's ` "detach" ` hook is run. 

  2. The package's ` [ .Last.lib ](/link/.Last.lib?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` function is run. 

  3. The package is removed from the search path. 

  4. The user's ` "onUnload" ` hook is run. 

  5. The package's ` [ .onUnload ](/link/.onUnload?package=base&version=3.6.2) ` function is run. 

  6. The package namespace is unloaded. 

Note that when an  R  session is finished, packages are not detached and
namespaces are not unloaded, so the corresponding hooks will not be run.

Also note that some of the user hooks are run without the package being on the
search path, so in those hooks objects in the package need to be referred to
using the double (or triple) colon operator, as in the example.

If multiple hooks are added, they are normally run in the order shown by `
getHook ` , but the ` "detach" ` and ` "onUnload" ` hooks are run in reverse
order so the default for package events is to add hooks ‘inside’ existing
ones.

The hooks are stored in the environment ` .userHooksEnv `
