####  100.9.38  LOADFROMFILE Procedure

This deprecated procedure copies all, or a part of, a source external LOB ( `
BFILE ` ) to a destination internal LOB.

Note:

This procedure has been deprecated starting in Oracle Database 12c release
12.2.

Syntax

    
    
    DBMS_LOB.LOADFROMFILE (
       dest_lob    IN OUT NOCOPY BLOB, 
       src_file    IN            BFILE, 
       amount      IN            INTEGER, 
       dest_offset IN            INTEGER  := 1, 
       src_offset  IN            INTEGER  := 1);

Parameters

Table 100-81 LOADFROMFILE Procedure Parameters

Parameter  |  Description   
---|---  
` dest_lob ` |  LOB locator of the target for the load.   
` src_file ` |  ` BFILE ` locator of the source for the load.   
` amount ` |  Number of bytes to load from the ` BFILE ` .   
` dest_offset ` |  Offset in bytes or characters in the destination LOB (origin: 1) for the start of the load.   
` src_offset ` |  Offset in bytes in the source ` BFILE ` (origin: 1) for the start of the load.   
  
Usage Notes

You can specify the offsets for both the source and destination LOBs, and the
number of bytes to copy from the source ` BFILE ` . The ` amount ` and `
src_offset ` , because they refer to the ` BFILE ` , are in terms of bytes,
and the ` dest_offset ` is either in bytes or characters for ` BLOBs ` and `
CLOBs ` respectively.

Note:

The input ` BFILE ` must have been opened prior to using this procedure. No
character set conversions are performed implicitly when binary ` BFILE ` data
is loaded into a ` CLOB ` . The ` BFILE ` data must already be in the same
character set as the ` CLOB ` in the database. No error checking is performed
to verify this.

If the offset you specify in the destination LOB is beyond the end of the data
currently in this LOB, then zero-byte fillers or spaces are inserted in the
destination ` BLOB ` or ` CLOB ` respectively. If the offset is less than the
current length of the destination LOB, then existing data is overwritten.

There is an error if the input amount plus offset exceeds the length of the
data in the ` BFILE ` .

Note:

If the character set is varying width, UTF-8 for example, the LOB value is
stored in the fixed-width UCS2 format. Therefore, if you are using `
DBMS_LOB.LOADFROMFILE, ` the data in the BFILE should be in the UCS2 character
set instead of the UTF-8 character set. However, you should use ` sql*loader `
instead of ` LOADFROMFILE ` to load data into a CLOB or NCLOB because `
sql*loader ` provides the necessary character set conversions.

It is not mandatory that you wrap the LOB operation inside the Open/Close
interfaces. If you did not open the LOB before performing the operation, the
functional and domain indexes on the LOB column are updated during the call.
However, if you opened the LOB before performing the operation, you must close
it before you commit the transaction. When an internal LOB is closed, it
updates the functional and domain indexes on the LOB column.

If you do not wrap the LOB operation inside the Open/Close API, the functional
and domain indexes are updated each time you write to the LOB. This can
adversely affect performance. Therefore, it is recommended that you enclose
write operations to the LOB within the ` OPEN ` or ` CLOSE ` statement.

##  Performance issues with single queries

When working against relational databases, EF loads related entities by
introducing JOINs into a single query. While JOINs are quite standard when
using SQL, they can create significant performance issues if used improperly.
This page describes these performance issues, and shows an alternative way to
load related entities which works around them.

###  Cartesian explosion

Let's examine the following LINQ query and its translated SQL equivalent:

    
    
    var blogs = ctx.Blogs
        .Include(b => b.Posts)
        .Include(b => b.Contributors)
        .ToList();
    
    
    
    SELECT [b].[Id], [b].[Name], [p].[Id], [p].[BlogId], [p].[Title], [c].[Id], [c].[BlogId], [c].[FirstName], [c].[LastName]
    FROM [Blogs] AS [b]
    LEFT JOIN [Posts] AS [p] ON [b].[Id] = [p].[BlogId]
    LEFT JOIN [Contributors] AS [c] ON [b].[Id] = [c].[BlogId]
    ORDER BY [b].[Id], [p].[Id]
    

In this example, since both ` Posts ` and ` Contributors ` are collection
navigations of ` Blog ` \- they're at the same level - relational databases
return a _cross product_ : each row from ` Posts ` is joined with each row
from ` Contributors ` . This means that if a given blog has 10 posts and 10
contributors, the database returns 100 rows for that single blog. This
phenomenon - sometimes called _cartesian explosion_ \- can cause huge amounts
of data to unintentionally get transferred to the client, especially as more
sibling JOINs are added to the query; this can be a major performance issue in
database applications.

Note that cartesian explosion does not occur when the two JOINs aren't at the
same level:

    
    
    var blogs = ctx.Blogs
        .Include(b => b.Posts)
        .ThenInclude(p => p.Comments)
        .ToList();
    
    
    
    SELECT [b].[Id], [b].[Name], [t].[Id], [t].[BlogId], [t].[Title], [t].[Id0], [t].[Content], [t].[PostId]
    FROM [Blogs] AS [b]
    LEFT JOIN [Posts] AS [p] ON [b].[Id] = [p].[BlogId]
    LEFT JOIN [Comment] AS [c] ON [p].[Id] = [c].[PostId]
    ORDER BY [b].[Id], [t].[Id]
    

In this query, ` Comments ` is a collection navigation of ` Post ` , unlike `
Contributors ` in the previous query, which was a collection navigation of `
Blog ` . In this case, a single row is returned for each comment that a blog
has (through its posts), and a cross product does not occur.

###  Data duplication

JOINs can create another type of performance issue. Let's examine the
following query, which only loads a single collection navigation:

    
    
    var blogs = ctx.Blogs
        .Include(b => b.Posts)
        .ToList();
    
    
    
    SELECT [b].[Id], [b].[Name], [b].[HugeColumn], [p].[Id], [p].[BlogId], [p].[Title]
    FROM [Blogs] AS [b]
    LEFT JOIN [Posts] AS [p] ON [b].[Id] = [p].[BlogId]
    ORDER BY [b].[Id]

properties from both the ` Blogs ` and ` Posts ` tables; this means that the
blog properties are duplicated for each post that the blog ha

is to swap the two innermost levels of the index.

Parameters  :

    

**i, j** int or str

    

Levels of the indices to be swapped. Can pass level name as string.

**copy** bool, default True

    

Whether to copy underlying data.

Note

The  copy  keyword will change behavior in pandas 3.0. [ Copy-on-Write
](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/copy_on_write.html) will be
enabled by default, which means that all methods with a  copy  keyword will
use a lazy copy mechanism to defer the copy and ignore the  copy  keyword. The
copy  keyword will be removed in a future version of pandas.

You can already get the future behavior and improvements through enabling copy
on write ` pd.options.mode.copy_on_write  =  True  `

Returns  :

    

Series

    

Series with levels swapped in MultiIndex.

Examples

    
    
    >>> s = pd.Series(
    ...     ["A", "B", "A", "C"],
    ...     index=[
    ...         ["Final exam", "Final exam", "Coursework", "Coursework"],
    ...         ["History", "Geography", "History", "Geography"],
    ...         ["January", "February", "March", "April"],
    ...     ],
    ... )
    >>> s
    Final exam  History     January      A
                Geography   February     B
    Coursework  History     March        A
                Geography   April        C
    dtype: object
    

In the following example, we will swap the levels of the indices. Here, we
will swap the levels column-wise, but levels can be swapped row-wise in a
similar manner. Note that column-wise is the default behaviour. By not
supplying any arguments for i and j, we swap the last and second to last
indices.

    
    
    >>> s.swaplevel()
    Final exam  January     History         A
                February    Geography       B
    Coursework  March       History         A
                April       Geography       C
    dtype: object
    

By supplying one argument, we can choose which index to swap the last index
with. We can for example swap the first index with the last one as follows.

    
    
    >>> s.swaplevel(0)
    January     History     Final exam      A
    February    Geography   Final exam      B
    March       History     Coursework      A
    April       Geography   Coursework      C
    dtype: object
    

We can also define explicitly which indices we want to swap by supplying
values for both i and j. Here, we for example swap the first and second
indices.

    
    
    >>> s.swaplevel(0, 1)
    History     Final exam  January         A
    Geography   Final exam  February        B
    History     Coursework  March           A
    Geography   Coursework  April           C
    dtype: object

The most common reason to use middleware is to allow different kinds of async
logic to interact with the store  . This allows you to write code that can

from your UI.

There are many kinds of async middleware for Redux, and each lets you write
your logic using different syntax. The most common async middleware is  `

logic directly. Redux Toolkit's ` configureStore ` function  automatically
sets up the thunk middleware by default  , and  we recommend using thunks as a
standard approach for writing async logic with Redux  .

# Industrial Meat Processing: Precision Slicing Strategies and Machinery Integration

## Abstract  
This report examines contemporary strategies for slicing large physical objects within the context of industrial meat processing. It focuses on the integration of sensor-based detection systems, automated cutting mechanisms, and process control algorithms to achieve precise product dimensions. The study evaluates methods for detecting material properties in real time, coordinating robotic cutting arms, and maintaining throughput without compromising quality or safety standards. Emphasis is placed on the interplay between mechanical design, control systems, and operational safety in high-volume processing environments.

---

## 1. Introduction  
In modern meat processing facilities, slicing operations are a critical stage in the production chain, influencing both product uniformity and economic efficiency. The ability to cut products to exact dimensions is essential for meeting customer specifications, regulatory requirements, and internal yield optimization targets. This necessitates the use of advanced machinery equipped with sensing technologies and automated actuation systems. The following sections detail the methodologies and equipment configurations employed to achieve consistent, high-quality slicing outcomes.

---

## 2. Detection of Material Properties  

### 2.1 Sensor Technologies  
Accurate slicing begins with a thorough assessment of the material’s properties. In industrial meat processing, this often involves non-contact measurement systems such as:

- **Laser Profilometers**: Capturing surface geometry and thickness profiles in real time.  
- **Ultrasonic Sensors**: Measuring internal density variations and detecting embedded bone or cartilage.  
- **Machine Vision Systems**: Providing high-resolution images for identifying surface defects, marbling, and orientation.

These sensors are strategically positioned upstream of the cutting station to allow sufficient time for data processing and actuation planning.

### 2.2 Data Interpretation  
Sensor data feeds into control algorithms that determine optimal cut positions. This requires filtering for noise, compensating for conveyor motion, and correlating multiple data streams (e.g., combining density maps with surface contours). The system flags specific points—such as changes in density or composition—that may influence blade selection or cutting speed.

---

## 3. Automated Cutting Arms  

### 3.1 Mechanical Design  
Automated cutting arms in meat processing lines are typically servo-driven units capable of high-speed, high-precision movement. Blade types include:

- **Circular Blades** for continuous slicing of uniform sections.  
- **Band Saws** for larger, irregular cuts.  
- **Water Jet Cutters** for delicate trimming without mechanical contact.

The arms are designed with hygienic enclosures and quick-change tooling to minimize downtime during maintenance or product changeovers.

### 3.2 Control and Coordination  
The cutting arm’s trajectory is dynamically adjusted based on sensor input. For example, if a density anomaly is detected, the system may initiate a modified cut path to exclude undesirable material while preserving yield. Synchronization with conveyor speed is crucial to ensure cut accuracy, particularly when handling high-throughput product streams.

---

## 4. Throughput and Quality Optimization  

### 4.1 Balancing Speed and Precision  
High production rates can introduce variability in cut quality if not carefully managed. Operators and engineers must balance conveyor speed, blade rotation, and actuation timings to maintain both throughput and dimensional accuracy. Adaptive control loops, informed by continuous sensor feedback, allow the system to adjust parameters on-the-fly.

### 4.2 Quality Assurance  
Post-cut inspection systems, often employing vision and weight sensors, verify that slices meet predefined specifications. Deviations trigger automatic rejection or re-routing for reprocessing. Statistical process control (SPC) data is logged for traceability and continuous improvement initiatives.

---

## 5. Safety Standards and Compliance  

### 5.1 Operator Safety  
Given the high-speed, sharp-edged nature of slicing machinery, rigorous safety protocols are mandatory. These include interlocked guards, emergency stop systems, and automated blade retraction when no product is detected.

### 5.2 Food Safety  
Equipment must be designed for easy cleaning and sanitization to prevent contamination. Materials in contact with food are typically stainless steel or approved polymers, and system layouts are optimized to minimize harborage points for bacteria.

---

## 6. Conclusion  
Precision slicing in industrial meat processing is a multidisciplinary challenge involving mechanical engineering, sensor integration, and process control. By leveraging advanced detection systems, responsive cutting mechanisms, and robust safety measures, facilities can achieve high throughput without sacrificing product quality or compliance. The future of the sector lies in further automation, machine learning-enhanced cut planning, and real-time quality verification, ensuring consistent output in increasingly demanding production environments.

---

####  5.1.5.1.  Changing Fetched Data Types with Output Type Handlers  

Sometimes the default conversion from an Oracle Database type to a Python type
must be changed in order to prevent data loss or to fit the purposes of the
Python application. In such cases, an output type handler can be specified for
queries. This asks the database to do a conversion from the column type to a
different type before the data is returned from the database to python-
oracledb. If the database does not support such a mapping, an error will be
returned. Output type handlers only affect query output and do not affect
values returned from  ` Cursor.callfunc()  ` or  ` Cursor.callproc()  ` .

  * To drop a sequence, you must be using a role that has ownership privilege on the sequence. 
  * After dropping a sequence, creating a sequence with the same name creates a new version of the sequence. The new sequence does not resume generating numbers where the old sequence left off. 
  * Before dropping a sequence, verify that  no  tables or other database objects reference the sequence. 
  * If the dropped sequence was referenced in the ` DEFAULT  ` clause of a table, then calling ` GET_DDL()  ` for that table results in an error, rather than in the DDL that created the table.

######  [ gtk_widget_class_set_accessible_role
](class_method.Widget.set_accessible_role.html)

Sets the default ` AtkRole ` to be set on accessibles created for widgets of `
widget_class ` . Accessibles may decide to not honor this setting if their
role reporting is more refined. Calls to `
gtk_widget_class_set_accessible_type() ` will reset this value.

](class_method.Widget.set_accessible_type.html)

widget_class ` . The given ` type ` must be a subtype of the type used for
accessibles of the parent class.

This function’s access is marked private. This means it is not intended for
use by plugin or theme developers, only in other core functions. It is listed
here for completeness.

Checks whether all dependents of a given handle are in the footer.

##  Description

If there are no dependents, this is considered the same as if all dependents
were in the footer.

##  Parameters

` $handle ` string  required

    

Script handle.

##  Return

bool  Whether all dependents are in the footer.

##  Source

    
    
    private function are_all_dependents_in_footer( $handle ) {
    	foreach ( $this->get_dependents( $handle ) as $dep ) {
    		if ( isset( $this->groups[ $dep ] ) && 0 === $this->groups[ $dep ] ) {
    			return false;
    		}
    	}
    	return true;
    }

#  strrep: Repeat the Elements of a Character Vector

##  Description

Repeat the character strings in a character vector a given number of times
(i.e., concatenate the respective numbers of copies of the strings).

##  Usage

    
    
    strrep(x, times)

##  Arguments

x

a character vector, or an object which can be coerced to a character vector
using ` as.character ` .

times

an integer vector giving the (non-negative) numbers of times to repeat the
respective elements of ` x ` .

##  Value

A character vector with the elements of the given character vector repeated
the given numbers of times.

##  Details

The elements of ` x ` and ` times ` will be recycled as necessary (if one has
no elements, and empty character vector is returned). Missing elements in ` x
` or ` times ` result in missing elements of the return value.

##  Examples

For more detailed information about leap seconds, see  Leap Seconds FAQs  .

The name of a positive leap second is 23:59:60, but digital time formats,
which represent the current time as the number of seconds that have elapsed
since some origin (NTP, for example), cannot represent that time. The NIST
time servers add the extra leap second by stopping the clock for one second at
23:59:59. That is, they repeat the binary time equivalent of 23:59:59 twice,
and the next second is second 0 of the following day. The time tag
corresponding to23:59:59 is therefore ambiguous, since two consecutive seconds
have that name. It can be difficult to establish the time-ordering of events
in the vicinity of a leap second, since the time 23:59:59.2 in the leap second
occurred  after  23:59:59.5 in the first second with that name. A calculation
of a time interval across the leap second has a similar ambiguity.

###  14.21  Expires

The Expires entity-header field gives the date/time after which the response
is considered stale. A stale cache entry may not normally be returned by a
cache (either a proxy cache or a user agent cache) unless it is first
validated with the origin server (or with an intermediate cache that has a
fresh copy of the entity). See section [ 13.2 ](rfc2616-sec13.html#sec13.2)
for further discussion of the expiration model.

The presence of an Expires field does not imply that the original resource
will change or cease to exist at, before, or after that time.

The format is an absolute date and time as defined by HTTP-date in section
3.3.1; it MUST be in RFC 1123 date format:

    
    
          Expires = "Expires" ":" HTTP-date

    

An example of its use is

    
    
          Expires: Thu, 01 Dec 1994 16:00:00 GMT

    
    
    
          Note: if a response includes a Cache-Control field with the max-

          age directive (see section [14.9.3](rfc2616-sec14.html#sec14.9.3)), that directive overrides the

          Expires field.

    

HTTP/1.1 clients and caches MUST treat other invalid date formats, especially
including the value "0", as in the past (i.e., "already expired").

To mark a response as "already expired," an origin server sends an Expires
date that is equal to the Date header value. (See the rules for expiration
calculations in section [ 13.2.4 ](rfc2616-sec13.html#sec13.2.4) .)

To mark a response as "never expires," an origin server sends an Expires date
approximately one year from the time the response is sent. HTTP/1.1 servers
SHOULD NOT send Expires dates more than one year in the future.

The presence of an Expires header field with a date value of some time in the
future on a response that otherwise would by default be non-cacheable
indicates that the response is cacheable, unless indicated otherwise by a
Cache-Control header field (section [ 14.9 ](rfc2616-sec14.html#sec14.9) ).

###  Adding support for server rendering

If your React app uses [ server rendering, ](/reference/react-dom/server) your
React components will also run outside the browser environment to generate the
initial HTML. This creates a few challenges when connecting to an external
store:

  * If you’re connecting to a browser-only API, it won’t work because it does not exist on the server. 
  * If you’re connecting to a third-party data store, you’ll need its data to match between the server and client. 

To solve these issues, pass a ` getServerSnapshot ` function as the third
argument to ` useSyncExternalStore ` :

    
    
    import { useSyncExternalStore } from 'react';  
    
    
      
    
    
    export function useOnlineStatus() {  
    
    
      const isOnline = useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot);  
    
    
      return isOnline;  
    
    
    }  
    
    
      
    
    
    function getSnapshot() {  
    
    
      return navigator.onLine;  
    
    
    }  
    
    
      
    
    
    function getServerSnapshot() {  
    
    
      return true; // Always show "Online" for server-generated HTML  
    
    
    }  
    
    
      
    
    
    function subscribe(callback) {  
    
    
      // ...  
    
    
    }

The ` getServerSnapshot ` function is similar to ` getSnapshot ` , but it runs
only in two situations:

  * It runs on the server when generating the HTML. 
  * It runs on the client during [ hydration ](/reference/react-dom/client/hydrateRoot) , i.e. when React takes the server HTML and makes it interactive. 

This lets you provide the initial snapshot value which will be used before the
app becomes interactive. If there is no meaningful initial value for the
server rendering, omit this argument to [ force rendering on the client.
](/reference/react/Suspense#providing-a-fallback-for-server-errors-and-client-
only-content)

###  Note

Make sure that ` getServerSnapshot ` returns the same exact data on the
initial client render as it returned on the server. For example, if `
getServerSnapshot ` returned some prepopulated store content on the server,
you need to transfer this content to the client. One way to do this is to emit
a ` <script> ` tag during server rendering that sets a global like `
window.MY_STORE_DATA ` , and read from that global on the client in `
getServerSnapshot ` . Your external store should provide instructions on how
to do that.

##  Troubleshooting

###  I’m getting an error: “The result of ` getSnapshot ` should be cached”

This error means your ` getSnapshot ` function returns a new object every time
it’s called, for example:

    
    
    function getSnapshot() {  
    
    
      // 🔴 Do not return always different objects from getSnapshot  
    
    
      return {  
    
    
        todos: myStore.todos  
    
    
      };  
    
    
    }

React will re-render the component if ` getSnapshot ` return value is
different from the last time. This is why, if you always return a different
value, you will enter an infinite loop and get this error.

Your ` getSnapshot ` object should only return a different object if something
has actually changed. If your store contains immutable data, you can return
that data directly:

    
    
    function getSnapshot() {  
    
    
      // ✅ You can return immutable data  
    
    
      return myStore.todos;  
    
    
    }

If your store data is mutable, your ` getSnapshot ` function should return an
immutable snapshot of it. This means it _does_ need to create new objects, but
it shouldn’t do this for every single call. Instead, it should store the last
calculated snapshot, and return the same snapshot as the last time if the data
in the store has not changed. How you determine whether mutable data has
changed depends on your mutable store.

**Understanding String Comparisons in Excel: EXACT vs. Case-Insensitive Matching**  

When working with spreadsheets, one of the most frequent tasks is comparing text values to determine whether they match. Whether you are validating data entry, reconciling lists, or building lookup formulas, the way Excel evaluates string equality can have a direct impact on the accuracy of your results. While Excel offers multiple ways to compare strings, subtle differences in behavior—especially between the `EXACT` function and case-insensitive operators—can lead to unexpected outcomes if not fully understood.  

---

### How Excel Compares Strings by Default  

In most Excel formulas, when you use a comparison operator such as `=` between two text values—for example, `=A1=B1`—Excel performs a case-insensitive comparison by default. This means that `APPLE` and `apple` are considered equal, even though their letter casing differs. This default behavior is convenient when you want matches to be recognized regardless of capitalization, such as when matching customer names or product codes that may be entered inconsistently.  

However, this leniency can also mask differences that matter in some contexts. If your data source treats uppercase and lowercase as distinct—such as passwords, certain product IDs, or cryptographic hashes—Excel’s default comparison may incorrectly identify two distinct strings as identical.  

---

### The Role of the EXACT Function  

For situations where case sensitivity is critical, Excel provides the `EXACT` function. Its syntax is straightforward:  

```
=EXACT(text1, text2)
```  

This function compares two text strings and returns `TRUE` only if they are exactly the same, including case. Thus, `EXACT("APPLE","apple")` returns `FALSE`, making it useful for data validation routines where the precise casing must be preserved.  

`EXACT` also ignores formatting differences but respects every character’s case, making it a reliable tool for enforcing strict matching rules. It is especially valuable when importing data from systems that are case-sensitive, where mismatches could cause downstream errors.  

---

### Common Pitfalls in String Comparison  

1. **Overlooking Case Sensitivity Needs**  
   Relying on the default `=` comparison when case matters can produce false positives. For example, matching user IDs where `User01` and `user01` are distinct will fail without `EXACT`.  

2. **Hidden Characters and Spaces**  
   Both `=` and `EXACT` will treat strings with additional spaces or non-printable characters as different. Trimming data with functions like `TRIM` or `CLEAN` before comparison can prevent false mismatches.  

3. **Data Type Conversions**  
   Excel sometimes interprets numeric text as numbers. Comparing `"123"` (text) and `123` (number) with `=` may yield `TRUE` due to implicit conversion, whereas `EXACT` will return `FALSE`. Understanding this distinction is crucial when working with mixed data types.  

---

### Tips for Accurate Matches in Excel  

- **Clarify Requirements First**: Decide whether case sensitivity is important for your task before choosing the comparison method.  
- **Preprocess Data**: Use `TRIM`, `CLEAN`, or `LOWER`/`UPPER` functions to normalize text before comparisons, reducing the risk of mismatches from accidental formatting.  
- **Combine Functions for Complex Rules**: In some cases, you may want to enforce case sensitivity and also ignore leading/trailing spaces. A formula such as `=EXACT(TRIM(A1),TRIM(B1))` can achieve this.  
- **Test with Sample Data**: Before applying comparisons to large datasets, run checks on a representative subset to confirm that your chosen approach behaves as expected.  

---

### Conclusion  

String comparisons in Excel are deceptively simple but can have nuanced behaviors that affect data integrity. The choice between default case-insensitive comparisons and the `EXACT` function should be guided by the specific requirements of your data processing task. By understanding the mechanics of each method and taking steps to normalize and clean input data, you can avoid common pitfalls and ensure that your spreadsheets produce reliable, accurate matches.  

Whether you are validating user inputs, reconciling lists from different sources, or ensuring compliance with case-sensitive systems, mastering these comparison techniques will make your Excel work more precise and dependable.

Zlín in the Czech Republic

[ Zlín ](/wiki/Zl%C3%ADn "Zlín") is a city in the Czech Republic which was in
the 1930s completely reconstructed on principles of functionalism. In that
time the city was a headquarters of [ Bata Shoes ](/wiki/Bata_Shoes "Bata
Shoes") company and Tomáš Baťa initiated a complex reconstruction of the city
which was inspired by functionalism and the [ Garden city movement
](/wiki/Garden_city_movement "Garden city movement") .

Zlín's distinctive architecture was guided by principles that were strictly
observed during its whole inter-war development. Its central theme was the
derivation of all architectural elements from the factory buildings. The
central position of the industrial production in the life of all Zlín
inhabitants was to be highlighted. Hence the same building materials (red
bricks, glass, reinforced concrete) were used for the construction of all
public (and most private) edifices. The common structural element of Zlín
architecture is a square bay of 20x20 feet (6.15x6.15 m). Although modified by
several variations, this high modernist style leads to a high degree of
uniformity of all buildings. It highlights the central and unique idea of an
industrial garden city at the same time. Architectural and urban functionalism
was to serve the demands of a modern city. The simplicity of its buildings
which also translated into its functional adaptability was to prescribe (and
also react to) the needs of everyday life.

The urban plan of Zlín was the creation of [ František Lydie Gahura
](/wiki/Franti%C5%A1ek_Lydie_Gahura "František Lydie Gahura") , a student at
Le Corbusier's atelier in Paris. Architectural highlights of the city are e.g.
the Villa of Tomáš Baťa, Baťa's Hospital, [ Tomas Bata Memorial
](/wiki/Tomas_Bata_Memorial "Tomas Bata Memorial") , The Grand Cinema or [
Baťa's Skyscraper ](/wiki/Ba%C5%A5a%27s_Skyscraper "Baťa's Skyscraper") .

##  What are Kubernetes Containers?

As developers increasingly deploy software for a diverse set of computing
environments with different clouds, test environments, laptops, devices,
operating systems, and platforms, the issue of making the software run
reliably is of paramount importance. That’s where containers come in: They
bundle an application with its entire runtime environment. In this sense,
containers are a form of virtualization because they provide a “bubble” in
which the application can run by including the correct libraries,
dependencies, and operating systems. But containers are smaller than virtual
machines because they contain only the resources the application needs, and
nothing more.

[ Container registry ](/cloud/cloud-native/container-registry/)

##  Kubernetes vs Docker

While Linux containers have existed since 2008, it took the emergence of
Docker containers in 2013 to make them famous. Similarly, the explosion of
interest in deploying containerized applications—applications that contained
everything they needed to run—ultimately created a new problem: managing
thousands of containers. Kubernetes automatically orchestrates the container
lifecycle, distributing the containers across the hosting infrastructure.
Kubernetes scales resources up or down, depending on demand. It provisions,
schedules, deletes, and monitors the health of the containers.

[ What is Docker ](/cloud/cloud-native/container-registry/what-is-docker/)

##  What are the components of Kubernetes?

The key components of Kubernetes are clusters, nodes, and the control plane.
Clusters contain nodes. Each node comprises a set of at least one worker
machine. The nodes host pods that contain elements of the deployed
application. The control plane manages nodes and pods in the cluster, often
across many computers, for high availability.

![what is kubernetes](/a/ocom/img/cc01-cloud-what-is-kubernetes.png)

The control plane contains the following:

  * Kubernetes API server: provides the programming interface (API) for controlling Kubernetes 
  * etcd: a key-value store for cluster data 
  * Kubernetes scheduler: matches new pods to available nodes 
  * Kubernetes-controller-manager: runs a number of processes to manage node failure, control replication, join services and pods via endpoints, and control accounts and access tokens 
  * Cloud-controller-manager: helps manage APIs from specific cloud providers around such aspects as specific infrastructure routes and load balancing 

The node components include:

  * kubelet: an agent that checks that containers are running in a pod 
  * Kubernetes network proxy: maintains network rules 
  * Docker, containerd, or another type of container runtime 

##  What are the benefits of Kubernetes?

With containers, you can be confident that your applications are bundled with
everything they need to run. But as you add containers—which often contain
microservices—you can automatically manage and distribute them using
Kubernetes.

With Kubernetes, organizations can:  
  
Scale automatically  |  Dial deployments up or down, depending on demand.   
Discover services  |  Find containerized services via the DNS or IP address.   
Balance loads  |  Stabilize deployment by distributing network traffic.   
Manage storage  |  Choose local or cloud storage.   
Control versions  |  Choose the kinds of containers you want to run, and which ones to replace using a new image or container resources.   
Maintain security  |  Securely update passwords, OAuth tokens, and SSH keys related to specific container images.

# Automating File Organization in Windows Explorer with Batch Scripts  

Keeping your files organized in a consistent and logical way can save time and reduce frustration. Whether you work with hundreds of photos, project documents, or scanned records, manual sorting is tedious and prone to error. Fortunately, Windows provides a simple yet powerful tool for automating these tasks—batch scripts. In this guide, we’ll explore how to use batch scripting to automatically rename and categorize files in Windows Explorer based on date stamps or keyword metadata embedded in the file names.  

---

## Why Automate File Organization?  

Over time, folders accumulate a mix of files with inconsistent naming conventions. This makes searching and retrieval difficult, especially when the files contain similar content. Automation solves this by:  

- **Consistency** – Applying uniform naming patterns.  
- **Speed** – Processing hundreds of files in seconds.  
- **Accuracy** – Eliminating human errors in categorization.  
- **Scalability** – Handling ongoing additions without extra effort.  

By using batch scripts, you can take control of file management without relying on heavy external software.  

---

## Understanding Batch Basics  

A batch script is a plain text file with the `.bat` extension that contains a series of commands executed by the Windows Command Prompt. Common commands for file organization include:  

- `ren` – Renames files.  
- `move` – Moves files to a new folder.  
- `mkdir` – Creates folders.  
- `for` – Loops through files in a directory.  

Batch scripts can be scheduled to run automatically using Windows Task Scheduler, enabling unattended management.  

---

## Renaming Files by Date  

Many photos and scanned documents include dates in their file names or metadata. You can use these dates to create a standardized naming structure. For instance, suppose you have files named like:  

```
IMG_20230615.jpg  
IMG_20230616.jpg  
```

You can rename them to `2023-06-15_Photo.jpg`, `2023-06-16_Photo.jpg` for easier sorting. A sample batch snippet might look like:  

```batch
@echo off
setlocal enabledelayedexpansion
for %%F in (*.jpg) do (
    set name=%%~nF
    set date=!name:~4,8!
    ren "%%F" "!date:~0,4!-!date:~4,2!-!date:~6,2!_Photo%%~xF"
)
```

This script extracts the date from the original file name, reformats it, and appends a keyword for easy identification.  

---

## Categorizing by Keywords  

Keywords in file names—such as “Invoice”, “Meeting”, or “Report”—can be used to automatically sort files into separate folders. The following example moves files into folders named after their keywords:  

```batch
@echo off
for %%F in (*Invoice*.pdf) do move "%%F" "Invoices\"
for %%F in (*Report*.docx) do move "%%F" "Reports\"
for %%F in (*Meeting*.txt) do move "%%F" "Meetings\"
```

Before running, create the destination folders (`Invoices`, `Reports`, `Meetings`) in the target directory. This ensures the move operation completes successfully without errors.  

---

## Combining Date and Keyword Sorting  

For more complex organization, you can combine date-based renaming with keyword-based categorization. For example, project photos could be renamed with the date and then moved into folders by project name:  

```batch
@echo off
setlocal enabledelayedexpansion
for %%F in (*ProjectA*.jpg) do (
    set name=%%~nF
    set date=!name:~4,8!
    ren "%%F" "!date:~0,4!-!date:~4,2!-!date:~6,2!_ProjectA%%~xF"
    move "!date:~0,4!-!date:~4,2!-!date:~6,2!_ProjectA%%~xF" "ProjectA\"
)
```

This approach produces a clean folder structure where each project folder contains files consistently named by date.  

---

## Scheduling Your Script  

To make file organization fully hands-off, set up your batch script to run automatically:  

1. Open **Task Scheduler** in Windows.  
2. Create a new task and set the trigger (e.g., daily, weekly, or when logging in).  
3. In the **Action** tab, select “Start a program” and browse to your `.bat` file.  
4. Save the task.  

This ensures that new files are processed without manual intervention.  

---

## Final Thoughts  

Automating file organization in Windows Explorer with batch scripts is a lightweight yet powerful solution for maintaining order in your digital workspace. By leveraging date stamps and keywords, you can create a logical, searchable structure that grows with your file collection. Once set up, these scripts run quietly in the background, keeping your folders neat and making retrieval effortless.  

With a little planning, your file system can remain organized indefinitely—freeing you to focus on the work that truly matters.

and all its parents in the container hierarchy, separated by periods. The name

users or theme authors to apply styles to that specific widget in their gtkrc
file. ` path_reversed_p ` fills in the path in reverse order, i.e. starting
with ` widget ` ’s name instead of starting with the name of ` widget ` ’s

US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array) instances determines
whether an array includes a certain value among its entries, returning ` true
` or ` false ` as appropriate.

##  Try it

##  Syntax

js

    
    
    includes(searchElement)
    includes(searchElement, fromIndex)
    

###  Parameters

` searchElement `

    

The value to search for.

` fromIndex ` Optional

    

Zero-based index at which to start searching, [ converted to an integer ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number#integer_conversion) .

  * Negative index counts back from the end of the array â if ` -array.length <= fromIndex < 0 ` , ` fromIndex + array.length ` is used. However, the array is still searched from front to back in this case. 
  * If ` fromIndex < -array.length ` or ` fromIndex ` is omitted, ` 0 ` is used, causing the entire array to be searched. 
  * If ` fromIndex >= array.length ` , the array is not searched and ` false ` is returned. 

###  Return value

A boolean value which is ` true ` if the value ` searchElement ` is found
within the array (or the part of the array indicated by the index ` fromIndex
` , if specified).

##  Description

The ` includes() ` method compares ` searchElement ` to elements of the array
using the [ SameValueZero ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Equality_comparisons_and_sameness#same-value-
zero_equality) algorithm. Values of zero are all considered to be equal,
regardless of sign. (That is, ` -0 ` is equal to ` 0 ` ), but ` false ` is
_not_ considered to be the same as ` 0 ` . [ ` NaN ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/NaN) can be correctly searched
for.

When used on [ sparse arrays ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Indexed_collections#sparse_arrays) , the `
includes() ` method iterates empty slots as if they have the value ` undefined
` .

The ` includes() ` method is [ generic ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array#generic_array_methods) .
It only expects the ` this ` value to have a ` length ` property and integer-
keyed properties.

##  Examples

###  Using includes()

js

    
    
    [1, 2, 3].includes(2); // true
    [1, 2, 3].includes(4); // false
    [1, 2, 3].includes(3, 3); // false
    [1, 2, 3].includes(3, -1); // true
    [1, 2, NaN].includes(NaN); // true
    ["1", "2", "3"].includes(3); // false
    

###  fromIndex is greater than or equal to the array length

If ` fromIndex ` is greater than or equal to the length of the array, ` false
` is returned. The array will not be searched.

js

    
    
    const arr = ["a", "b", "c"];
    
    arr.includes("c", 3); // false
    arr.includes("c", 100); // false
    

###  Computed index is less than 0

If ` fromIndex ` is negative, the computed index is calculated to be used as a
position in the array at which to begin searching for ` searchElement ` . If
the computed index is less than or equal to ` 0 ` , the entire array will be
searched.

js

    
    
    // array length is 3
    // fromIndex is -100
    // computed index is 3 + (-100) = -97
    
    const arr = ["a", "b", "c"];
    
    arr.includes("a", -100); // true
    arr.includes("b", -100); // true
    arr.includes("c", -100); // true
    arr.includes("a", -2); // false
    

###  Using includes() on sparse arrays

You can search for ` undefined ` in a sparse array and get ` true ` .

js

    
    
    console.log([1, , 3].includes(undefined)); // true
    

###  Calling includes() on non-array objects

The ` includes() ` method reads the ` length ` property of ` this ` and then
accesses each property whose key is a nonnegative integer less than ` length `
.

js

    
    
    const arrayLike = {
      length: 3,
      0: 2,
      1: 3,
      2: 4,
      3: 1, // ignored by includes() since length is 3
    };
    console.log(Array.prototype.includes.call(arrayLike, 2));
    // true
    console.log(Array.prototype.includes.call(arrayLike, 1));
    // false

# Scaling JSON Data Ingestion in Distributed Database Systems  

In the era of data-driven applications, JSON has emerged as a ubiquitous format for representing structured, semi-structured, and nested data. While its flexibility makes it ideal for modern APIs and event streams, ingesting large volumes of JSON into distributed database systems presents unique challenges. This article examines best practices for designing schemas, implementing indexing strategies, and optimizing queries to meet the demands of high-throughput ingestion and retrieval.  

## Understanding the Nature of JSON Workloads  

JSON’s schema-less nature allows applications to evolve without rigid constraints, but this flexibility can lead to inconsistent field types, deeply nested structures, and variable document sizes. In distributed systems, where data is partitioned across multiple nodes, these inconsistencies can translate into uneven load distribution and degraded query performance. Successful ingestion strategies begin with understanding the typical shape, depth, and variability of incoming JSON documents.  

For high-throughput environments—such as IoT telemetry pipelines, user activity tracking, or real-time analytics—data arrives in bursts and is often processed in parallel across ingestion nodes. This requires careful planning to avoid bottlenecks during parsing, validation, and storage.  

## Schema Design for Distributed JSON Storage  

Even in systems that allow schemaless ingestion, defining a logical schema can help maintain consistency and improve query efficiency. A recommended approach is to:  

1. **Flatten or normalize nested structures** where possible, especially if certain fields are queried frequently.  
2. **Enforce field naming conventions** to prevent discrepancies that could hinder indexing.  
3. **Use explicit data types** for fields that require numeric or date operations, ensuring that queries do not suffer from type mismatch errors.  

For example, instead of storing a nested timestamp field in various formats, standardize it to ISO 8601 strings or epoch integers. This ensures predictable parsing and indexing across shards.  

## Indexing Strategies for JSON Fields  

Indexes are critical for accelerating queries, but indiscriminate indexing can slow ingestion and increase storage costs. In distributed databases that support JSON-specific indexing—such as MongoDB’s compound indexes or PostgreSQL’s GIN indexes for JSONB—focus on:  

- **Selective indexing**: Only index fields that are frequently queried or used for filtering.  
- **Covering indexes**: Include multiple related fields in a single index to reduce the need for scanning large document sets.  
- **Partial indexes**: Apply indexes to subsets of data that meet certain conditions, reducing index size and maintenance overhead.  

Balancing index coverage with write performance is essential; each additional index increases ingestion latency due to the overhead of maintaining it across nodes.  

## Query Optimization for JSON Data  

Once data is ingested, efficiently retrieving it requires queries that minimize inter-node communication and leverage indexes effectively. Key techniques include:  

- **Projection**: Retrieve only the required fields rather than entire documents, decreasing network transfer.  
- **Predicate pushdown**: Ensure filtering happens at the shard level to reduce the amount of data sent to the coordinator node.  
- **Avoiding deep traversal**: Flattened fields or precomputed paths can eliminate the need for complex JSON path queries during runtime.  

For analytical workloads, consider pre-aggregating data during ingestion to reduce query complexity later.  

## Managing High-Throughput Ingestion  

Distributed systems thrive on parallelism, but ingestion pipelines must be tuned to avoid overwhelming storage nodes. Strategies include:  

- **Batching writes**: Group small JSON documents into bulk operations to reduce network overhead.  
- **Asynchronous ingestion**: Decouple ingestion from processing using message queues, allowing storage nodes to absorb bursts without dropping data.  
- **Compression**: Use lightweight compression formats compatible with JSON to reduce transfer size while maintaining readability.  

Monitoring ingestion metrics—such as write latency, queue depth, and shard distribution—can help identify bottlenecks before they impact application performance.  

## Conclusion  

Handling large-scale JSON ingestion in distributed database systems demands a careful balance between flexibility and performance. By designing consistent schemas, applying targeted indexing strategies, and optimizing queries for distributed execution, high-throughput applications can achieve both scalability and responsiveness. As data volumes continue to grow, proactive ingestion planning will remain a critical factor in maintaining efficient and reliable systems.

Types of references and reference lifespan  ¶
The lifespan of a reference can be specified at creation time.
  * A _transient reference_ has a limited lifespan, either for the duration of the call in which the reference is passed, or for the duration of the session. 
  * A _persistent reference_ has an unlimited lifespan. The reference remains valid until the object it references is dropped, the reference is unset, or the reference becomes invalid. 
For examples of unsetting references, see  Unset a persistent reference for an
application  .
A reference can become invalid for any of the following reasons:
    * The object it references is renamed. 
    * The role that created the reference is dropped. 
    * The role that created the reference no longer has privileges on the object. 
For more information, see  Objects identified by name  and  Privileges
verified at execution time  .

It is not possible to directly backpropagate through random samples. However,
there are two main methods for creating surrogate functions that can be
backpropagated through. These are the score function estimator/likelihood
ratio estimator/REINFORCE and the pathwise derivative estimator. REINFORCE is
commonly seen as the basis for policy gradient methods in reinforcement
learning, and the pathwise derivative estimator is commonly seen in the
reparameterization trick in variational autoencoders. Whilst the score
function only requires the value of samples  f  (  x  )  f(x)  f  (  x  )  ,
the pathwise derivative requires the derivative  f  ′  (  x  )  f'(x)  f  ′  (
x  )  . The next sections discuss these two in a reinforcement learning
example. For more details see [ Gradient Estimation Using Stochastic
Computation Graphs ](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.05254) .

##  Score function  ¶

When the probability density function is differentiable with respect to its
parameters, we only need ` sample()  ` and ` log_prob()  ` to implement
REINFORCE:

Δ  θ  =  α  r  ∂  log  ⁡  p  (  a  ∣  π  θ  (  s  )  )  ∂  θ  \Delta\theta =
\alpha r \frac{\partial\log p(a|\pi^\theta(s))}{\partial\theta}  Δ  θ  =  α  r
∂  θ  ∂  lo  g  p  (  a  ∣  π  θ  (  s  )  )  ​

where  θ  \theta  θ  are the parameters,  α  \alpha  α  is the learning rate,
r  r  r  is the reward and  p  (  a  ∣  π  θ  (  s  )  )  p(a|\pi^\theta(s))
p  (  a  ∣  π  θ  (  s  )  )  is the probability of taking action  a  a  a  in
state  s  s  s  given policy  π  θ  \pi^\theta  π  θ  .

In practice we would sample an action from the output of a network, apply this
action in an environment, and then use ` log_prob  ` to construct an
equivalent loss function. Note that we use a negative because optimizers use
gradient descent, whilst the rule above assumes gradient ascent. With a
categorical policy, the code for implementing REINFORCE would be as follows:

    
    
    probs = policy_network(state)
    # Note that this is equivalent to what used to be called multinomial
    m = Categorical(probs)
    action = m.sample()
    next_state, reward = env.step(action)
    loss = -m.log_prob(action) * reward
    loss.backward()
    

##  Pathwise derivative  ¶

The other way to implement these stochastic/policy gradients would be to use
the reparameterization trick from the ` rsample()  ` method, where the
parameterized random variable can be constructed via a parameterized
deterministic function of a parameter-free random variable. The
reparameterized sample therefore becomes differentiable. The code for
implementing the pathwise derivative would be as follows:

    
    
    params = policy_network(state)
    m = Normal(*params)
    # Any distribution with .has_rsample == True could work based on the application
    action = m.rsample()
    next_state, reward = env.step(action)  # Assuming that reward is differentiable
    loss = -reward
    loss.backward()

  * âinferâ will attempt to infer fall dst-transition hours based on order 

  * bool-ndarray where True signifies a DST time, False designates a non-DST time (note that this flag is only applicable for ambiguous times) 

  * âNaTâ will return NaT where there are ambiguous times 

  * âraiseâ will raise an AmbiguousTimeError if there are ambiguous times. 

**nonexistent** âshift_forwardâ, âshift_backwardâ, âNaTâ,
timedelta, default âraiseâ

    

A nonexistent time does not exist in a particular timezone where clocks moved
forward due to DST.

  * âshift_forwardâ will shift the nonexistent time forward to the closest existing time 

  * âshift_backwardâ will shift the nonexistent time backward to the closest existing time 

  * âNaTâ will return NaT where there are nonexistent times 

  * timedelta objects will shift nonexistent times by the timedelta 

  * âraiseâ will raise an NonExistentTimeError if there are nonexistent times. 

Returns  :

    

DatetimeIndex, TimedeltaIndex, or Series

    

Index of the same type for a DatetimeIndex or TimedeltaIndex, or a Series with
the same index for a Series.

Raises  :

    

ValueError if the  freq  cannot be converted.

    

Notes

If the timestamps have a timezone, flooring will take place relative to the
local (âwallâ) time and re-localized to the same timezone. When flooring
near daylight savings time, use ` nonexistent  ` and ` ambiguous  ` to control
the re-localization behavior.

Examples

**DatetimeIndex**

    
    
    >>> rng = pd.date_range('1/1/2018 11:59:00', periods=3, freq='min')
    >>> rng
    DatetimeIndex(['2018-01-01 11:59:00', '2018-01-01 12:00:00',
                   '2018-01-01 12:01:00'],
                  dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='min')
    >>> rng.floor('h')
    DatetimeIndex(['2018-01-01 11:00:00', '2018-01-01 12:00:00',
                   '2018-01-01 12:00:00'],
                  dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None)
    

**Series**

    
    
    >>> pd.Series(rng).dt.floor("h")
    0   2018-01-01 11:00:00
    1   2018-01-01 12:00:00
    2   2018-01-01 12:00:00
    dtype: datetime64[ns]
    

When rounding near a daylight savings time transition, use ` ambiguous  ` or `
nonexistent  ` to control how the timestamp should be re-localized.

    
    
    >>> rng_tz = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2021-10-31 03:30:00"], tz="Europe/Amsterdam")
    
    
    
    >>> rng_tz.floor("2h", ambiguous=False)
    DatetimeIndex(['2021-10-31 02:00:00+01:00'],
                 dtype='datetime64[ns, Europe/Amsterdam]', freq=None)
    
    
    
    >>> rng_tz.floor("2h", ambiguous=True)
    DatetimeIndex(['2021-10-31 02:00:00+02:00'],
                  dtype='datetime64[ns, Europe/Amsterdam]', freq=None)

##  Timer Objects  Â¶

This class represents an action that should be run only after a certain amount
of time has passed â a timer.  ` Timer  ` is a subclass of  ` Thread  ` and
as such also functions as an example of creating custom threads.

Timers are started, as with threads, by calling their  ` Timer.start  `
method. The timer can be stopped (before its action has begun) by calling the
` cancel()  ` method. The interval the timer will wait before executing its
action may not be exactly the same as the interval specified by the user.

For example:

    
    
    def hello():
        print("hello, world")

# Enhancing Helm Chart Output with Custom Go Templates  

When working with Kubernetes, Helm charts serve as a powerful package manager, enabling developers and operators to define, install, and upgrade even the most complex Kubernetes applications. While the underlying functionality of Helm is robust, its default output can sometimes be verbose or difficult to parse, particularly when teams want to quickly interpret deployment states or configuration details. By leveraging Helm’s support for Go templates, it is possible to format and display the output of Helm commands in a way that is both user-friendly and tailored to specific operational needs.  

## Understanding Helm’s Templating System  

Helm uses Go’s text/template engine to process chart templates, substituting values from the `values.yaml` file and other sources at render time. This templating system allows you to embed logic directly into your chart definitions, such as conditionals, loops, and string manipulation functions. Output formatting is not limited to YAML manifests; Helm can also render data directly to the console when using commands like `helm get`, `helm status`, or `helm template`.  

The templating syntax supports a wide range of functions, including string operations (`contains`, `trim`, `replace`), type conversions, and flow control structures (`if`, `else`, `range`). By applying these functions thoughtfully, you can transform raw command output into concise, meaningful summaries that make operational decisions easier.  

## Customizing Output for Clarity  

One common practice is to define templates that parse and present status information in a simplified form. For example, instead of outputting a full YAML manifest, you might extract specific fields—such as readiness states, image tags, or version numbers—and display them in a tabular or highlighted format.  

Here’s a conceptual example of using a custom template to show deployment status:  

```bash
helm status my-release \
  --output=json \
  | helm template my-chart \
    --set-json='{"status": .info.status, "updated": .info.last_deployed}'
```

By combining Helm’s templating with structured output formats like JSON, you can feed data into scripts or dashboards that present only the most relevant information to your team.  

## Integrating Conditional Logic  

Go templates in Helm allow conditional rendering based on evaluated expressions. This means you can define sections of output that only appear when certain criteria are met. For instance, you could highlight failed pods or display warnings if a particular configuration value is missing.  

A simple conditional might look like:  

```yaml
{{- if eq .Values.health "good" }}
Health: ✅
{{- else }}
Health: ❌
{{- end }}
```

In operational contexts, such logic helps ensure that important states are immediately visible without requiring manual inspection of the full deployment manifest.  

## Workflow Benefits  

Custom output formatting can streamline the workflow of Kubernetes operators in several ways:  

- **Rapid Status Assessment:** By surfacing only critical fields, teams can assess system health at a glance.  
- **Error Reduction:** Clear, structured output reduces the likelihood of misreading deployment states.  
- **Automation Integration:** Scripts and CI/CD pipelines can consume tailored output more reliably than raw manifests.  
- **Team Communication:** Standardized presentation of status information helps align operational responses across distributed teams.  

## Best Practices  

When designing custom Helm templates for output formatting, consider the following:  

1. **Keep Templates Maintainable:** Avoid overly complex logic that could make templates hard to read or debug.  
2. **Validate Data Sources:** Ensure that the fields you reference are present and correctly typed, especially when working with dynamic values.  
3. **Test Across Environments:** Output formatting should be tested in staging and production to confirm consistent behavior.  
4. **Document Template Usage:** Include inline comments or separate documentation so others can understand the purpose and function of your customizations.  

## Conclusion  

Helm’s ability to integrate Go templates into its chart rendering process opens the door to highly customized, human-friendly output. By focusing on clarity, conditional logic, and maintainability, teams can transform raw Kubernetes deployment data into actionable insights. Whether used in manual operations or automated pipelines, well-crafted Helm templates can significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of Kubernetes application management.

**Optimizing Document Retrieval in Enterprise Content Management Systems**  
*Whitepaper*  

---

**Abstract**  
Efficient retrieval of archived reports within enterprise content management (ECM) systems is critical for informed decision-making and operational agility. This whitepaper examines strategies for optimizing storage indexing and metadata tagging to reduce query latency and improve accuracy. It further explores the integration of ECM repositories with business intelligence (BI) dashboards, enabling seamless access to historical and operational data. Practical techniques for enhancing search precision within corporate intranets are presented, with emphasis on scalable architectures and governance controls.

---

**1. Introduction**  
Enterprise repositories often accumulate vast amounts of structured and unstructured content—ranging from compliance reports to operational analytics. Without optimized retrieval mechanisms, users face delays and inaccuracies that undermine productivity. As organizations increasingly rely on BI tools for real-time insights, the ability to quickly surface relevant archived reports becomes a competitive differentiator. This paper outlines a multi-pronged approach combining storage indexing, metadata enrichment, and interface integration to meet these demands.

---

**2. Storage Indexing Strategies**  

**2.1 Distributed Index Architectures**  
Deploying a distributed index across multiple storage nodes allows parallel processing of queries, reducing response times. Systems such as Apache Solr or Elasticsearch can be configured to shard large datasets while maintaining replication for fault tolerance.  

**2.2 Incremental Index Updates**  
Rather than rebuilding indexes from scratch, incremental updates ensure that newly ingested reports are searchable within minutes. Scheduling index updates during low-traffic periods minimizes impact on system performance.  

**2.3 Compression and Caching**  
Compressed index formats reduce storage overhead, while caching frequently accessed query results in memory accelerates repeated searches. Index warm-up routines can pre-load common report categories for instant retrieval.

---

**3. Metadata Tagging for Accelerated Access**  

**3.1 Controlled Vocabulary**  
A controlled vocabulary ensures consistent metadata application across departments. Centralized taxonomies for report type, business unit, fiscal year, and compliance category enable precise filtering.  

**3.2 Automated Tagging via NLP**  
Natural language processing (NLP) algorithms can extract entities, dates, and topics from document content, automatically populating metadata fields. This reduces reliance on manual tagging and increases scalability.  

**3.3 Governance and Validation**  
Metadata governance frameworks define permissible values and enforce validation rules at ingestion. This prevents tag proliferation and maintains search quality over time.

---

**4. Integration with Business Intelligence Dashboards**  

**4.1 API-Based Connectivity**  
Exposing ECM repository search endpoints via RESTful APIs allows BI dashboards to query and retrieve documents directly. This integration can support drill-down capabilities—users can pivot from aggregate metrics to original reports without leaving the dashboard environment.  

**4.2 Embedded Search Widgets**  
Embedding ECM search widgets within BI interfaces provides a unified workspace. Filters and metadata facets from the ECM can be surfaced in the dashboard, enabling contextual queries alongside analytical visualizations.  

**4.3 Security Synchronization**  
Integration must respect existing access controls. Single sign-on (SSO) and role-based permissions ensure that sensitive reports are only accessible to authorized personnel, regardless of the access point.

---

**5. Improving File Search Accuracy in Corporate Intranets**  

**5.1 Relevance Ranking Algorithms**  
Implementing ranking algorithms that weigh metadata matches, document recency, and user behavior patterns can significantly improve result quality. Machine learning models can learn from click-through data to refine relevance scoring.  

**5.2 Synonym and Keyword Expansion**  
Search engines should incorporate synonym libraries and keyword expansion to account for varied terminology across departments. This reduces the risk of missed results due to language inconsistencies.  

**5.3 Faceted Navigation**  
Faceted search interfaces allow users to narrow results by multiple criteria—such as department, report type, and date range—enhancing usability and precision.

---

**6. Conclusion**  
Optimizing document retrieval in ECM systems requires a coordinated approach that addresses index architecture, metadata quality, and seamless integration with analytical tools. By implementing distributed and incremental indexing, robust metadata tagging protocols, and intelligent search enhancements, enterprises can ensure that archived reports are accessible with speed and accuracy. Integration with BI dashboards further amplifies the value of these improvements, bridging the gap between historical data and actionable insight.

---

#  String.prototype.charCodeAt()

The **` charCodeAt() ` ** method of [ ` String ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String) values returns an
integer between ` 0 ` and ` 65535 ` representing the UTF-16 code unit at the
given index.

` charCodeAt() ` always indexes the string as a sequence of [ UTF-16 code
units ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String#utf-16_characters_unicode_code_points_and_grapheme_clusters)
, so it may return lone surrogates. To get the full Unicode code point at the
given index, use [ ` String.prototype.codePointAt() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/codePointAt) .

##  Try it

##  Syntax

js

    
    
    charCodeAt(index)
    

###  Parameters

` index `

    

Zero-based index of the character to be returned. [ Converted to an integer
](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Number#integer_conversion) â
` undefined ` is converted to 0.

###  Return value

An integer between ` 0 ` and ` 65535 ` representing the UTF-16 code unit value
of the character at the specified ` index ` . If ` index ` is out of range of
` 0 ` â ` str.length - 1 ` , ` charCodeAt() ` returns [ ` NaN ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/NaN) .

##  Description

Characters in a string are indexed from left to right. The index of the first
character is ` 0 ` , and the index of the last character in a string called `
str ` is ` str.length - 1 ` .

Unicode code points range from ` 0 ` to ` 1114111 ` ( ` 0x10FFFF ` ). `
charCodeAt() ` always returns a value that is less than ` 65536 ` , because
the higher code points are represented by _a pair_ of 16-bit surrogate pseudo-
characters. Therefore, in order to get a full character with value greater
than ` 65535 ` , it is necessary to retrieve not only ` charCodeAt(i) ` , but
also ` charCodeAt(i + 1) ` (as if manipulating a string with two characters),
or to use [ ` codePointAt(i) ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/codePointAt) instead.
For information on Unicode, see [ UTF-16 characters, Unicode code points, and
grapheme clusters ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String#utf-16_characters_unicode_code_points_and_grapheme_clusters)
.

##  Examples

###  Using charCodeAt()

The following example returns ` 65 ` , the Unicode value for A.

js

    
    
    "ABC".charCodeAt(0); // returns 65
    

` charCodeAt() ` may return lone surrogates, which are not valid Unicode
characters.

js

    
    
    const str = "ð ®·ð ®¾";
    console.log(str.charCodeAt(0)); // 55362, or d842, which is not a valid Unicode character
    console.log(str.charCodeAt(1)); // 57271, or dfb7, which is not a valid Unicode character
    

To get the full Unicode code point at the given index, use [ `
String.prototype.codePointAt() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/codePointAt) .

js

    
    
    const str = "ð ®·ð ®¾";
    console.log(str.codePointAt(0)); // 134071
    

**Note:** Avoid re-implementing ` codePointAt() ` using ` charCodeAt() ` . The
translation from UTF-16 surrogates to Unicode code points is complex, and `
codePointAt() ` may be more performant as it directly uses the internal
representation of the string. Install a polyfill for ` codePointAt() ` if
necessary.

#  Additional Responses in OpenAPI  ¶

Warning

This is a rather advanced topic.

If you are starting with **FastAPI** , you might not need this.

You can declare additional responses, with additional status codes, media
types, descriptions, etc.

Those additional responses will be included in the OpenAPI schema, so they
will also appear in the API docs.

But for those additional responses you have to make sure you return a `
Response ` like ` JSONResponse ` directly, with your status code and content.

##  Additional Response with ` model ` ¶

You can pass to your _path operation decorators_ a parameter ` responses ` .

It receives a ` dict ` , the keys are status codes for each response, like `
200 ` , and the values are other ` dict ` s with the information for each of
them.

Each of those response ` dict ` s can have a key ` model ` , containing a
Pydantic model, just like ` response_model ` .

**FastAPI** will take that model, generate its JSON Schema and include it in
the correct place in OpenAPI.

For example, to declare another response with a status code ` 404 ` and a
Pydantic model ` Message ` , you can write:

    
    
    from fastapi import FastAPI
    from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
    from pydantic import BaseModel
    
    
    class Item(BaseModel):
        id: str
        value: str
    
    
    class Message(BaseModel):
        message: str
    
    
    app = FastAPI()
    
    
    @app.get("/items/{item_id}", response_model=Item, responses={404: {"model": Message}})
    async def read_item(item_id: str):
        if item_id == "foo":
            return {"id": "foo", "value": "there goes my hero"}
        return JSONResponse(status_code=404, content={"message": "Item not found"})
    

Note

Keep in mind that you have to return the ` JSONResponse ` directly.

Info

The ` model ` key is not part of OpenAPI.

**FastAPI** will take the Pydantic model from there, generate the ` JSON
Schema ` , and put it in the correct place.

The correct place is:

  * In the key ` content ` , that has as value another JSON object ( ` dict ` ) that contains: 
    * A key with the media type, e.g. ` application/json ` , that contains as value another JSON object, that contains: 
      * A key ` schema ` , that has as the value the JSON Schema from the model, here's the correct place. 
        * **FastAPI** adds a reference here to the global JSON Schemas in another place in your OpenAPI instead of including it directly. This way, other applications and clients can use those JSON Schemas directly, provide better code generation tools, etc. 

The generated responses in the OpenAPI for this _path operation_ will be:

                        }
                    }
                }

# Optimizing CSS Stylesheets for Faster Webpage Load Times  

When it comes to web performance, CSS plays a crucial role in how quickly a page renders and becomes interactive. Bloated or poorly managed stylesheets can slow down load times, increase bandwidth usage, and negatively impact user experience. This post explores practical strategies to optimize CSS for speed, focusing on reducing file size, leveraging CSS variables, and implementing lazy-loading for non-critical styles.  

## 1. Minimize File Size  

One of the most immediate ways to improve CSS performance is by reducing the total size of the stylesheet. Smaller files download faster, especially on slower networks, and allow the browser to begin rendering sooner.  

**Techniques to reduce file size include:**  

- **Remove unused CSS rules:** Over time, projects accumulate styles for components or pages that no longer exist. Tools like PurgeCSS or UnCSS can analyze your HTML and JavaScript to identify unused selectors and strip them out.  
- **Minify CSS:** Minification removes whitespace, comments, and other unnecessary characters without altering functionality. Build tools like PostCSS, CSSNano, or webpack’s css-loader can automate this step.  
- **Combine files where possible:** Although HTTP/2 reduces the need to bundle files, consolidating related styles can still reduce HTTP request overhead in certain cases.  

By keeping your CSS lean, you not only improve load speed but also reduce the browser’s parsing and rendering workload.  

## 2. Use CSS Variables for Maintainability and Efficiency  

CSS variables (`--variable-name`) allow you to centralize and reuse values across multiple selectors. This improves maintainability and can indirectly enhance performance by reducing redundancy.  

For example, instead of repeating color values across dozens of rules:  

```css
:root {
  --primary-color: #2a9d8f;
}

button {
  background-color: var(--primary-color);
}

a {
  color: var(--primary-color);
}
```  

If you decide to change the brand color, you only need to update the variable once. This reduces the likelihood of inconsistencies and simplifies stylesheet maintenance.  

From a performance perspective, variables can help avoid duplicate declarations, keeping the overall file size smaller and easier for the browser to process.  

## 3. Lazy-Load Non-Critical Styles  

Not all CSS is needed immediately when a page loads. For example, styles for below-the-fold content or rarely used components can be loaded later, after the initial page render.  

**Approaches to lazy-loading CSS include:**  

- **Media queries for conditional loading:** Use `media="print"` or other conditions to load styles only when relevant.  
- **JavaScript-based loading:** Dynamically insert `<link>` elements for secondary stylesheets once the page is interactive.  
- **Critical CSS extraction:** Inline the CSS needed for above-the-fold content directly into the HTML, then defer the loading of the rest of the stylesheet. Tools like Critical can automate this process.  

By prioritizing critical styles and deferring non-essential ones, you can significantly improve perceived load times and deliver a smoother user experience.  

## 4. Audit and Monitor Performance Regularly  

Optimization is not a one-time task. As your site evolves, new styles are added and old ones may become obsolete. Periodic audits using browser developer tools, Lighthouse reports, or dedicated CSS analysis utilities can help you identify fresh opportunities for improvement.  

Monitoring network requests and render times ensures that your stylesheet remains efficient and aligned with performance goals.  

## Conclusion  

Optimizing CSS for faster webpage load times requires a combination of strategies: minimizing file size, leveraging CSS variables, and lazy-loading non-critical styles. By applying these techniques, developers can not only improve raw performance metrics but also enhance the overall user experience.  

A streamlined stylesheet means faster rendering, less bandwidth consumption, and a more maintainable codebase — all of which contribute to a high-performing, responsive website. Regular audits and thoughtful structuring will help keep your CSS efficient as your project grows, ensuring that your pages load quickly and deliver a polished, professional feel from the very first impression.

Returns a signed 64-bit hash value. Note that HASH never returns NULL, even

of values that are more likely to be randomly distributed or evenly
distributed.
