##  [ Handling application settings hierarchy more easily with Python’s
ChainMap ](https://blog.peterlamut.com/2017/11/27/handling-application-
settings-hierarchy-more-easily-with-pythons-chainmap/)

Say you have an application that, as almost every more complex application,
exposes some settings that affect how that application behaves. These settings
can be configured in several ways, such as specifying them in a configuration
file, or by using the system’s environment variables. They can also be
provided as command line arguments when starting the application.

If the same setting is provided at more than a single configuration layer, the
value from the layer with the highest precedence is taken. This could mean
that, for example, configuration file settings override those from environment
variables, but command line arguments have precedence over both. If a
particular setting is not specified in any of these three layers, its default
value is used.

Ordered by priority (highest first), our hierarchy of settings layers looks as
follows:

  * command line arguments 
  * configuration file 
  * environment variables 
  * application defaults 

A natural way of representing settings is by using a dictionary, one for each
layer. An application might thus contain the following:

    
    
    defaults = {
        'items_per_page': 100,
        'log_level': 'WARNING',
        'max_retries': 5,
    }
    
    env_vars = {
        'max_retries': 10
    }
    
    config_file = {
        'log_level': 'INFO'
    }
    
    cmd_args = {
        'max_retries': 2
    }
    

Putting them all together while taking the precedence levels into account,
here’s how the application settings would look like:

    
    
    >>> settings  # all settings put together
    {
        'items_per_page': 100,  # a default value
        'log_level': 'INFO',  # from the config file
        'max_retries': 2,  # from a command line argument
    }
    

There is a point in the code where a decision needs to be made on what setting
value to consider. One way of of determining that is by examining the
dictionaries one by one until the setting is found:  1

    
    
    setting_name = 'log_level'
    
    for settings in (cmd_args, config_file, env_vars, defaults):
        if setting_name in settings:
            value = settings[setting_name]
            break
    else:
        raise ValueError('Setting not found: {}'.format(setting_name))
    
    # do something with value...
    

A somewhat verbose approach, but at least better than a series of if-elif
statements.

An alternative approach is to merge all settings into a single dictionary
before using any of their values:

    
    
    settings = defaults.copy()
    for d in (env_vars, config_file, cmd_args):
        settings.update(d)
    

Mind that here the order of applying the settings layers must be reversed,
i.e. the highest priority layers get applied last, so that no lower-level
layers can override them. This works quite well, with a possibly only downside
that if any of the underlying settings dictionaries get updated, the “main”
settings dictionary must be rebuilt, because the changes are not reflected in
it automatically:

    
    
    >>> config_file['items_per_page'] = 25
    >>> settings['items_per_page']
    100  # change not propagated

##  Plotting directly with Matplotlib  #

In some situations it may still be preferable or necessary to prepare plots
directly with matplotlib, for instance when a certain type of plot or
customization is not (yet) supported by pandas. ` Series  ` and ` DataFrame  `
objects behave like arrays and can therefore be passed directly to matplotlib
functions without explicit casts.

pandas also automatically registers formatters and locators that recognize
date indices, thereby extending date and time support to practically all plot
types available in matplotlib. Although this formatting does not provide the
same level of refinement you would get when plotting via pandas, it can be
faster when plotting a large number of points.

       .....:     np.random.randn(150).cumsum(),
       .....:     index=pd.date_range("2000-1-1", periods=150, freq="B"),
       .....: )
       .....: 
    
    In [215]: ma = price.rolling(20).mean()
    
    In [216]: mstd = price.rolling(20).std()
    
    In [217]: plt.figure();
    
    In [218]: plt.plot(price.index, price, "k");
    
    In [219]: plt.plot(ma.index, ma, "b");
    
    In [220]: plt.fill_between(mstd.index, ma - 2 * mstd, ma + 2 * mstd, color="b", alpha=0.2);

##  Plotting backends  #

pandas can be extended with third-party plotting backends. The main idea is
letting users select a plotting backend different than the provided one based
on Matplotlib.

This can be done by passing âbackend.moduleâ as the argument ` backend  `
in ` plot  ` function. For example:

    
    
    >>> Series([1, 2, 3]).plot(backend="backend.module")
    

Alternatively, you can also set this option globally, do you donât need to
specify the keyword in each ` plot  ` call. For example:

    
    
    >>> pd.set_option("plotting.backend", "backend.module")
    >>> pd.Series([1, 2, 3]).plot()
    

Or:

    
    
    >>> pd.options.plotting.backend = "backend.module"
    >>> pd.Series([1, 2, 3]).plot()
    

This would be more or less equivalent to:

    
    
    >>> import backend.module
    >>> backend.module.plot(pd.Series([1, 2, 3]))
    

The backend module can then use other visualization tools (Bokeh, Altair,
hvplot,â¦) to generate the plots. Some libraries implementing a backend for
pandas are listed on [ the ecosystem page
](https://pandas.pydata.org/community/ecosystem.html) .

Developers guide can be found at [
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/development/extending.html#plotting-
backends

Examples

**Getting values**

    
    
    >>> df = pd.DataFrame([[1, 2], [4, 5], [7, 8]],
    ...                   index=['cobra', 'viper', 'sidewinder'],
    ...                   columns=['max_speed', 'shield'])
    >>> df
                max_speed  shield
    cobra               1       2
    viper               4       5
    sidewinder          7       8
    

Single label. Note this returns the row as a Series.

    
    
    >>> df.loc['viper']
    max_speed    4
    shield       5
    Name: viper, dtype: int64
    

List of labels. Note using ` [[]]  ` returns a DataFrame.

    
    
    >>> df.loc[['viper', 'sidewinder']]
                max_speed  shield
    viper               4       5
    sidewinder          7       8
    

Single label for row and column

    
    
    >>> df.loc['cobra', 'shield']
    2
    

Slice with labels for row and single label for column. As mentioned above,
note that both the start and stop of the slice are included.

    
    
    >>> df.loc['cobra':'viper', 'max_speed']
    cobra    1
    viper    4
    Name: max_speed, dtype: int64
    

Boolean list with the same length as the row axis

    
    
    >>> df.loc[[False, False, True]]
                max_speed  shield
    sidewinder          7       8
    

Alignable boolean Series:

    
    
    >>> df.loc[pd.Series([False, True, False],
    ...                  index=['viper', 'sidewinder', 'cobra'])]
                         max_speed  shield
    sidewinder          7       8
    

Index (same behavior as ` df.reindex  ` )

    
    
    >>> df.loc[pd.Index(["cobra", "viper"], name="foo")]

    foo
    cobra          1       2
    viper          4       5

    sidewinder          7       8
    

Conditional that returns a boolean Series with column labels specified

    
    
    >>> df.loc[df['shield'] > 6, ['max_speed']]
                max_speed
    sidewinder          7
    

Multiple conditional using ` & ` that returns a boolean Series

    
    
    >>> df.loc[(df['max_speed'] > 1) & (df['shield'] < 8)]
                max_speed  shield
    viper          4       5

keeps apps in memory after they've been closed so the user can quickly switch
back to them. For this reason, Android devices often run with very little free
memory. Memory management is vital to properly allocate memory among important
system processes and many user applications.

This page discusses the basics of how Android allocates memory for the system
and for user applications. It also explains how the operating system reacts to
low memory situations.

##  Types of memory

Android devices contain three different types of memory: RAM, zRAM, and
storage. Note that both the CPU and GPU access the same RAM.

![Types of memory](/static/images/games/memory-types.svg)

**Figure 1.** Types of memory - RAM, zRAM, and storage

  * RAM is the fastest type of memory, but is usually limited in size. High-end devices typically have the largest amounts of RAM. 

  * zRAM is a partition of RAM used for swap space. Everything is compressed when placed into zRAM, and then decompressed when copied out of zRAM. This portion of RAM grows or shrinks in size as pages are moved into or taken out of zRAM. Device manufacturers can set the maximum size. 

  * Storage contains all of the persistent data such as the file system and the included object code for all apps, libraries, and the platform. Storage has much more capacity than the other two types of memory. On Android, storage isn’t used for swap space like it is on other Linux implementations since frequent writing can cause wear on this memory, and shorten the life of the storage medium. 

##  Memory pages

RAM is broken up into _pages_ . Typically each page is 4KB of memory.

Pages are considered either _free_ or _used_ . Free pages are unused RAM. Used
pages are RAM that the system is actively using, and are grouped into the
following categories:

  * Cached: Memory backed by a file on storage (for example, code or memory-mapped files). There are two types of cached memory: 
    * Private: Owned by one process and not shared 
      * Clean: Unmodified copy of a file on storage, can be deleted by  ` kswapd ` to increase free memory 
      * Dirty: Modified copy of the file on storage; can be moved to, or compressed in, zRAM by ` kswapd ` to increase free memory 
    * Shared: Used by multiple processes 
      * Clean: Unmodified copy of the file on storage, can be deleted by ` kswapd ` to increase free memory 
      * Dirty: Modified copy of the file on storage; allows changes to be written back to the file in storage to increase free memory by ` kswapd ` , or explicitly using [ ` msync() ` ](/reference/android/system/Os#msync\(long,%2520long,%2520int\)) or [ ` munmap() ` ](/reference/android/system/Os#munmap\(long,%2520long\))
  * Anonymous: Memory **not** backed by a file on storage (for example, allocated by [ ` mmap() ` ](/reference/android/system/Os#mmap\(long,%2520long,%2520int,%2520int,%2520java.io.FileDescriptor,%2520long\)) with the ` MAP_ANONYMOUS ` flag set) 
    * Dirty: Can be moved/compressed in zRAM by ` kswapd ` to increase free memory 

**Note:** Clean pages contain an exact copy of a file (or portion of a file)
that exists in storage. A clean page becomes a dirty page when it no longer
contains an exact copy of the file (for example, from the result of an
application operation). Clean pages can be deleted because they can always be
regenerated using the data from storage; dirty pages cannot be deleted or else
data would be lost.

The proportions of free and used pages vary over time as the system actively
manages RAM. The concepts introduced in this section are key to managing low-
memory situations. The next section of this document explains them in greater
detail.

##  Low memory management

Android has two main mechanisms to deal with low memory situations: the kernel
swap daemon and low-memory killer.

#  Right shift assignment (>>=)

The **right shift assignment (` >>= ` ) ** operator performs [ right shift
](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Right_shift) on the two
operands and assigns the result to the left operand.

##  Try it

##  Syntax

js

    
    
    x >>= y
    

##  Description

` x >>= y ` is equivalent to ` x = x >> y ` , except that the expression ` x `
is only evaluated once.

##  Examples

###  Using right shift assignment

js

    
    
    let a = 5; //   (00000000000000000000000000000101)
    a >>= 2; //   1 (00000000000000000000000000000001)
    
    let b = -5; //  (-00000000000000000000000000000101)
    b >>= 2; //  -2 (-00000000000000000000000000000010)
    
    let c = 5n;
    c >>= 2n; // 1n

# Managing Build-Time Options in Maven with Environment Variables

When working on Java projects, especially those built with Maven, developers often encounter scenarios where certain features or configurations should be toggled at build time. This is particularly useful when the same codebase must be compiled differently for various environments, such as development, staging, or production. A practical and maintainable way to achieve this is by leveraging environment variables in conjunction with Maven’s profile system.

## Understanding Maven Profiles

Maven profiles are a mechanism that allows you to customize the build process based on certain conditions. A profile can define different dependencies, plugins, properties, and build configurations. Profiles are particularly effective when you need to adjust compilation behavior without changing the core `pom.xml` structure for every environment.

Profiles can be activated in several ways: via command-line switches, system properties, or environment variables. This flexibility enables you to integrate build-time decisions into your deployment pipeline without hardcoding values.

## Using Environment Variables in pom.xml

Environment variables can be referenced directly in Maven’s `pom.xml` using the `${env.VAR_NAME}` syntax. For example, if you have an environment variable called `BUILD_FEATURE_X`, you can use it to control the activation of a profile:

```xml
<profiles>
    <profile>
        <id>feature-x-enabled</id>
        <activation>
            <property>
                <name>env.BUILD_FEATURE_X</name>
                <value>true</value>
            </property>
        </activation>
        <properties>
            <feature.x.enabled>true</feature.x.enabled>
        </properties>
    </profile>
</profiles>
```

In this configuration, the profile `feature-x-enabled` will only activate if the environment variable `BUILD_FEATURE_X` is set to `true`.

## Structuring pom.xml for Build-Time Flexibility

To keep your `pom.xml` maintainable, it’s advisable to centralize profile definitions and property usage. One approach is to define build options as properties within each profile, and then reference those properties in plugin configurations or resource filtering.

For example:

```xml
<properties>
    <feature.x.enabled>false</feature.x.enabled>
</properties>

<profiles>
    <profile>
        <id>feature-x-enabled</id>
        <activation>
            <property>
                <name>env.BUILD_FEATURE_X</name>
                <value>true</value>
            </property>
        </activation>
        <properties>
            <feature.x.enabled>true</feature.x.enabled>
        </properties>
    </profile>
</profiles>

<build>
    <plugins>
        <plugin>
            <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
            <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
            <configuration>
                <compilerArgs>
                    <arg>-DfeatureX=${feature.x.enabled}</arg>
                </compilerArgs>
            </configuration>
        </plugin>
    </plugins>
</build>
```

Here, the compiler receives a flag indicating whether `featureX` should be enabled, based on the active profile.

## Activating Profiles via Command Line

While environment variables can be set in your operating system or CI/CD pipeline, you can also activate profiles directly from the command line for ad hoc builds:

```bash
export BUILD_FEATURE_X=true
mvn clean install
```

This will trigger the profile activation logic defined in your `pom.xml`, ensuring the correct build-time options are applied.

## Resource Filtering and Environment-Specific Configuration

Beyond compiler flags, you can use environment variables with Maven’s resource filtering to inject values into configuration files during the build. By enabling resource filtering in your build section, Maven replaces placeholders in your resource files with actual property values, which can be derived from environment variables.

Example:

```xml
<build>
    <resources>
        <resource>
            <directory>src/main/resources</directory>
            <filtering>true</filtering>
        </resource>
    </resources>
</build>
```

Then, in a resource file:

```
feature.x.enabled=${feature.x.enabled}
```

When the build runs, this placeholder will be replaced according to the active profile and associated environment variable.

## Conclusion

By structuring your Maven `pom.xml` to reference environment variables and control profile activation, you can achieve a clean separation between build configurations and source code. This approach makes your builds more adaptable, reduces the need for manual changes, and integrates well with automated pipelines. With careful planning, environment-driven profiles can serve as a powerful tool for managing build-time options in Maven-based Java projects.

#  eval

##  eval(fileToExecute: String, fs: Dictionary<String>, readerInputs: Dictionary<ReaderInput> = {}, inputValues: Dictionary<Any> = {}, configuration: RuntimeExecutionConfiguration = {}): EvalSuccess | ExecutionFailure 

Evaluates a script with the specified context and returns the result of that
evaluation.

_Experimental:_ This function is an experimental feature that is subject to
change or removal from future versions of DataWeave.

###  Parameters

Name  |  Description   
---|---  
` fileToExecute ` |  Name of the file to execute.   
` fs ` |  An object that contains the file to evaluate.   
` readerInputs ` |  Reader inputs to bind.   
` inputValues ` |  Additional literal values to bind   
` configuration ` |  The runtime configuration.   
  
###  Example

This example shows how ` eval ` behaves with different inputs.

##  Interpreting Data

# Report on Best Practices for Organizing Laboratory Experiment Logs

## Abstract

This report presents a structured approach to organizing laboratory experiment logs for long-term archival and data retrieval. It outlines strategies for categorizing and timestamping entries from biological assays and chemical reactions, with an emphasis on preserving metadata integrity. The report further explores labeling conventions for experiments, linking results to sample batches, and integrating these practices into laboratory information management systems (LIMS). By implementing the recommended protocols, laboratories can enhance reproducibility, traceability, and compliance with regulatory requirements.

## 1. Introduction

Laboratory experiment logs serve as the primary record of experimental activities, capturing procedural details, observations, and results. In both biological and chemical research, the volume and complexity of data necessitate rigorous organizational methods. Without standardized practices, data fragmentation, inconsistent labeling, and metadata loss can occur, undermining the scientific value of archived records. This report addresses these challenges by detailing best practices for experiment log structuring and metadata management.

## 2. Categorization of Experimental Entries

Categorization is the foundation of an organized laboratory log. Entries should be classified based on experiment type, assay or reaction category, and associated sample batch. For biological assays, categories might include enzyme kinetics, cell culture assays, or immunoassays, whereas chemical reactions may be classified by reaction class, synthesis stage, or analytical method.

A hierarchical categorization system is recommended, wherein each entry is assigned both a broad category (e.g., “Protein Quantification”) and a specific subcategory (e.g., “Bradford Assay”). This dual-level classification aids in both high-level overviews and detailed searches.

## 3. Timestamping and Chronological Integrity

Each log entry must include a precise timestamp, ideally in ISO 8601 format, to ensure consistency across systems. In time-sensitive experiments, such as those involving unstable intermediates or live cultures, additional time markers (e.g., start, intermediate checkpoints, and end times) are critical.

Chronological integrity is maintained by ensuring that entries are logged in the order they occur, with no retroactive insertion without annotation. When corrections or additions are necessary, the original entry should be preserved, and a linked amendment should be created.

## 4. Metadata Integrity

Metadata encompasses all contextual information that describes an experiment, including sample identifiers, environmental conditions, instrument settings, and operator information. To preserve metadata integrity:

- **Standardized Fields:** Define mandatory fields for each entry, such as operator ID, instrument ID, reagent lot numbers, and calibration dates.
- **Controlled Vocabularies:** Use predefined terms for reagents, procedures, and conditions to avoid ambiguity.
- **Validation Rules:** Implement validation checks within the LIMS to prevent incomplete or inconsistent metadata entry.

## 5. Labeling Experiments

Clear and consistent labeling is essential for linking results to their originating samples and experimental conditions. Labels should be unique, descriptive, and machine-readable. A recommended format includes:

```
[ProjectCode]-[SampleBatchID]-[ExperimentType]-[Date]-[RunNumber]
```

For example: `BIO123-BT45-ELISA-20240610-R2` provides immediate insight into the project, sample batch, assay type, date, and replicate number.

Physical sample containers should bear labels that match digital log identifiers, enabling unambiguous cross-referencing between physical and digital records.

## 6. Linking Results to Sample Batches

Linking experimental results to specific sample batches ensures traceability from raw material through final analysis. This linkage should be maintained through:

- **Unique Batch IDs:** Assigned at the point of sample collection or preparation, carried through all subsequent analyses.
- **Relational Database Structure:** Within the LIMS, batch IDs should serve as primary keys linking to all related experiments, results, and metadata.
- **Audit Trails:** Every change to a batch-linked record should be logged, including the user making the change and the timestamp.

## 7. Integration with Laboratory Information Management Systems

A robust LIMS is central to modern laboratory data management. Integration of logging practices into the LIMS should include:

- **Automated Data Capture:** Direct instrument-to-LIMS data transfer to minimize transcription errors.
- **Template-Based Entry:** Pre-configured templates for common experiment types to enforce consistency.
- **Search and Retrieval Tools:** Advanced query capabilities to filter by category, date range, sample batch, or metadata field.
- **Archival Policies:** Defined schedules and formats for long-term storage, ensuring compatibility with future systems.

## 8. Conclusion

Organizing laboratory experiment logs requires a systematic approach that combines categorical classification, precise timestamping, metadata integrity, and robust linking of results to sample batches. By adhering to standardized labeling and leveraging LIMS capabilities, laboratories can safeguard the long-term usability of their data. These practices not only streamline current research workflows but also ensure that archived records remain accessible and interpretable for future investigations and regulatory audits.

---

This structured methodology facilitates reproducible science, supports compliance with data management standards, and strengthens the reliability of laboratory archives.

##  Examples

###  Property access

You can reference elements in the array using standard array index syntax
(that is, using bracket notation). However, getting or setting indexed
properties on typed arrays will not search in the prototype chain for this
property, even when the indices are out of bound. Indexed properties will
consult the [ ` ArrayBuffer ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/ArrayBuffer) and will never
look at object properties. You can still use named properties, just like with
all objects.

js

    
    
    // Setting and getting using standard array syntax
    const int16 = new Int16Array(2);
    int16[0] = 42;
    console.log(int16[0]); // 42
    
    // Indexed properties on prototypes are not consulted (Fx 25)
    Int8Array.prototype[20] = "foo";
    new Int8Array(32)[20]; // 0
    // even when out of bound
    Int8Array.prototype[20] = "foo";
    new Int8Array(8)[20]; // undefined
    // or with negative integers
    Int8Array.prototype[-1] = "foo";
    new Int8Array(8)[-1]; // undefined
    
    // Named properties are allowed, though (Fx 30)
    Int8Array.prototype.foo = "bar";
    new Int8Array(32).foo; // "bar"
    

###  Cannot be frozen

` TypedArray ` s that aren't empty cannot be frozen, as their underlying `
ArrayBuffer ` could be mutated through another ` TypedArray ` view of the
buffer. This would mean that the object would never genuinely be frozen.

js

    
    
    const i8 = Int8Array.of(1, 2, 3);
    Object.freeze(i8);
    // TypeError: Cannot freeze array buffer views with elements
    

###  ByteOffset must be aligned

When constructing a ` TypedArray ` as a view onto an ` ArrayBuffer ` , the `
byteOffset ` argument must be aligned to its element size; in other words, the
offset must be a multiple of ` BYTES_PER_ELEMENT ` .

js

    
    
    const i32 = new Int32Array(new ArrayBuffer(4), 1);
    // RangeError: start offset of Int32Array should be a multiple of 4
    

js

    
    
    const i32 = new Int32Array(new ArrayBuffer(4), 0);
    

###  ByteLength must be aligned

Like the ` byteOffset ` parameter, the ` byteLength ` property of an `
ArrayBuffer ` passed to a ` TypedArray ` 's constructor must be a multiple of
the constructor's ` BYTES_PER_ELEMENT ` .

js

    
    
    const i32 = new Int32Array(new ArrayBuffer(3));
    // RangeError: byte length of Int32Array should be a multiple of 4
    

js

    
    
    const i32 = new Int32Array(new ArrayBuffer(4));

#  Models  ¶

A model is the single, definitive source of information about your data. It
contains the essential fields and behaviors of the data you’re storing.
Generally, each model maps to a single database table.

The basics:

  * Each model is a Python class that subclasses [ ` django.db.models.Model  ` ](../../../ref/models/instances/#django.db.models.Model "django.db.models.Model") . 
  * Each attribute of the model represents a database field. 
  * With all of this, Django gives you an automatically-generated database-access API; see [ Making queries  ](../queries/) .

# Optimizing Broadcast Notification Delivery in Smart-Home IoT Ecosystems  

In the modern smart-home landscape, seamless communication between devices is not just a convenience—it’s the foundation of reliable automation. Whether it’s a thermostat sending temperature updates to a central hub or a security camera triggering alerts across multiple displays, the efficiency of broadcast notification delivery directly impacts user experience. Yet, in many IoT ecosystems, packet loss and unstable connectivity can undermine this process, especially when using proprietary communication protocols over Wi-Fi.  

This post explores strategies for optimizing broadcast delivery in smart-home networks, with a focus on improving Wi-Fi signal stability and minimizing packet loss.  

---

## Understanding Broadcast Delivery in IoT  

Broadcast notifications in IoT systems differ from unicast messages in that they are sent to multiple devices simultaneously. In smart-home environments, these broadcasts often carry time-sensitive data—motion detection alerts, environmental sensor readings, or automation triggers. Proprietary communication protocols, layered over standard Wi-Fi, enable device-specific features but can also introduce complexity in packet routing and acknowledgment handling.  

The challenge lies in ensuring that every intended recipient receives the broadcast reliably, without delays or dropped messages, even in conditions where network congestion or interference is present.  

---

## Wi-Fi Signal Stability: The First Line of Defense  

For most smart-home IoT deployments, Wi-Fi forms the backbone of communication. Improving signal stability requires a combination of environmental adjustments and network configuration changes:  

1. **Optimal Access Point Placement**  
   Position routers or mesh nodes to minimize physical obstructions and reduce dead zones. Dense materials such as concrete or metal can significantly weaken signals.  

2. **Channel Optimization**  
   Many Wi-Fi routers default to auto-select channels, but manual tuning can reduce interference from neighboring networks. Tools that scan local Wi-Fi environments help identify the least congested channels for both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands.  

3. **Mesh Networking**  
   Deploying a mesh network ensures consistent coverage across larger homes and allows IoT devices to maintain stronger connections as they move or interact with mobile hubs.  

4. **Dedicated SSIDs for IoT Devices**  
   Separating IoT traffic onto a dedicated SSID reduces competition with high-bandwidth activities like video streaming and gaming, lowering latency for broadcast messages.  

---

## Reducing Packet Loss in Proprietary Protocols  

While Wi-Fi stability is critical, many smart-home ecosystems rely on proprietary communication layers for device-to-device interaction. Packet loss here can occur even when Wi-Fi is strong, often due to protocol-specific inefficiencies.  

**Key optimization techniques include:**  

- **Adaptive Retransmission Strategies**  
  Implement dynamic retry mechanisms that adjust based on network conditions. For example, if packet acknowledgments are delayed, the system can temporarily increase retransmission frequency without overwhelming the network.  

- **Priority Queuing for Critical Broadcasts**  
  Not all broadcasts are equal—security alerts or safety-related notifications should bypass standard queues to ensure immediate delivery.  

- **Compression and Payload Optimization**  
  Minimizing the size of broadcast packets reduces the chance of fragmentation and lowers transmission time, which in turn decreases the opportunity for packet loss.  

- **Heartbeat and Health Checks**  
  Regular lightweight status messages between devices help detect connectivity issues early, allowing the system to reroute broadcasts or trigger recovery routines before a full failure occurs.  

---

## Network Monitoring and Predictive Maintenance  

Continuous monitoring of broadcast success rates, latency, and packet integrity can provide actionable insights. Machine learning models, trained on historical network performance data, can predict potential failures or congestion periods. This allows preemptive adjustments—such as temporarily rerouting broadcasts through alternate nodes or increasing signal strength during peak usage times.  

Integration of these monitoring tools into the smart-home management interface empowers users to take informed actions, such as relocating devices or updating firmware, before communication issues escalate.  

---

## Conclusion  

Optimizing broadcast notification delivery in smart-home IoT ecosystems requires a dual focus: maintaining robust Wi-Fi connectivity and fine-tuning proprietary protocol behavior to minimize packet loss. By strategically placing network hardware, reducing interference, and implementing intelligent retransmission and prioritization strategies, smart-home systems can achieve near-instantaneous, reliable broadcasts across all connected devices.  

In environments where automation depends on precise, timely communication, these optimizations not only enhance performance but also safeguard user trust—ensuring that when a device speaks, every intended listener hears the message loud and clear.

and App Standby. _Doze_ reduces battery consumption by deferring background
CPU and network activity for apps when the device is unused for long periods
of time. _App Standby_ defers background network activity for apps with no
recent user activity.

While the device is in Doze, apps' access to certain battery-intensive
resources is deferred until the maintenance window. The specific restrictions
are listed in [ Power management restrictions
](/topic/performance/power/power-details) .

Doze and App Standby manage the behavior of all apps running on Android 6.0 or
higher, regardless of whether they are specifically targeting API level 23. To
help ensure the best experience for users, test your app in Doze and App
Standby modes and make any necessary adjustments to your code. The following
sections provide details.

##  Understand Doze

If a user leaves a device unplugged and stationary for a period of time, with
the screen off, the device enters Doze mode. In Doze mode, the system attempts
to conserve battery by restricting apps' access to network and CPU-intensive
services. It also prevents apps from accessing the network and defers their
jobs, syncs, and standard alarms.

Periodically, the system exits Doze for a brief time to let apps complete
their deferred activities. During this _maintenance window_ , the system runs
all pending syncs, jobs, and alarms, and lets apps access the network.

![](/static/images/training/doze.png) **Figure 1.** Doze provides a recurring
maintenance window for apps to use the network and handle pending activities.

When the maintenance window concludes, the system again enters Doze,
suspending network access and deferring jobs, syncs, and alarms. Over time,
the system schedules maintenance windows less frequently, helping reduce
battery consumption in cases of longer inactivity when the device isn't
charging.

When the user wakes the device by moving it, turning on the screen, or
connecting a charger, the system exits Doze and all apps resume normal
activity.

###  Doze restrictions

The system applies the following restrictions to your apps while in Doze:

  * Suspends network access. 
  * Ignores [ wake locks ](/reference/android/os/PowerManager.WakeLock) . 
  * Defers standard ` [ AlarmManager ](/reference/android/app/AlarmManager) ` alarms, including ` [ setExact() ](/reference/android/app/AlarmManager#setExact\(int, long, android.app.PendingIntent\)) ` and ` [ setWindow() ](/reference/android/app/AlarmManager#setWindow\(int, long, long, android.app.PendingIntent\)) ` , to the next maintenance window. 
    * If you need to set alarms that fire while in Doze, use ` [ setAndAllowWhileIdle() ](/reference/android/app/AlarmManager#setAndAllowWhileIdle\(int, long, android.app.PendingIntent\)) ` or ` [ setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() ](/reference/android/app/AlarmManager#setExactAndAllowWhileIdle\(int, long, android.app.PendingIntent\)) ` . 
    * Alarms set with ` [ setAlarmClock() ](/reference/android/app/AlarmManager#setAlarmClock\(android.app.AlarmManager.AlarmClockInfo, android.app.PendingIntent\)) ` continue to fire normally. The system exits Doze shortly before those alarms fire. 
  * Doesn't perform Wi-Fi scans. 
  * Doesn't let [ sync adapters ](/training/monitoring-device-state/training/sync-adapters) run. 
  * Doesn't let ` [ JobScheduler ](/reference/android/app/job/JobScheduler) ` run.  ` [ WorkManager ](/reference/androidx/work/WorkManager) ` uses ` JobScheduler ` internally, so ` WorkManager ` tasks don't run.

# Streamlining Hotkey Workflows in Graphic Design: Python and AutoHotkey Integration

For digital artists and designers, speed and precision are paramount. In applications like Adobe Photoshop and Illustrator, repetitive sequences of actions—layer adjustments, export procedures, brush switching—can eat into valuable creative time. While these programs offer customizable shortcuts, their built-in systems can be inflexible or limited in scope. By leveraging custom Python scripts alongside AutoHotkey (AHK), designers can build a highly optimized hotkey workflow that transcends the constraints of default configurations.

## Identifying Bottlenecks in the Creative Process

Every designer has a unique workflow, but common pain points emerge across the industry:  
- Navigating deep menu structures for frequently used commands  
- Repeating multi-step procedures dozens of times per project  
- Switching between tools while maintaining focus on the canvas  

These micro-delays can add up, subtly reducing productivity and creative flow. The first step toward optimization is to observe your own habits and note which actions are repeated most often, and which ones interrupt your focus.

## Bridging the Gap with Python

Python’s versatility makes it an ideal companion for Adobe Creative Suite automation. Through libraries such as `photoshop-python-api` or scripting interfaces provided by Illustrator, designers can write concise scripts that perform complex tasks—batch renaming layers, exporting assets in multiple formats, or applying predefined effects.

For example, a Python script might take a selected layer group in Photoshop and automatically export each layer as a PNG, applying a naming convention based on the project code. Such a script could be invoked from the command line, but integrating it into a hotkey-driven workflow makes it instantly accessible without breaking concentration.

## AutoHotkey: The Glue Between Keys and Actions

AutoHotkey serves as the bridge between your keyboard (or other input devices) and these custom Python scripts. AHK can listen for global hotkeys—even when Photoshop or Illustrator is not the active window—and trigger the execution of your Python code. This allows you to design a consistent set of shortcuts that work across applications, making your workflow more fluid.

A simple AHK script might look like this:

```ahk
^!p:: ; Ctrl + Alt + P
Run, python "C:\Scripts\export_layers.py"
return
```

This binds `Ctrl + Alt + P` to run the `export_layers.py` script, instantly performing the export procedure you’ve automated.

## Layered Shortcuts for Complex Tasks

One powerful approach is to implement layered shortcut logic. Instead of binding a single hotkey to one action, use AHK to detect context—such as which application is active, or whether certain keys are held together—and execute different scripts accordingly. For instance:

- `Ctrl + Alt + B` in Photoshop might trigger a Python script to switch to a specific brush set.
- The same shortcut in Illustrator could swap to a custom color palette.

This ensures that shortcuts are meaningful in every context, without overwhelming your memory with dozens of unique key combinations.

## Fine-Tuning for Efficiency

When designing your hotkey system, consider ergonomics and cognitive load. Place frequently used shortcuts on keys that are easy to reach without shifting hand position dramatically. Use mnemonic associations—`E` for “export,” `B` for “brush”—to make them intuitive.

It’s also worth building in feedback mechanisms. AHK can display a small tooltip or play a sound when a script is triggered, confirming that the action has been registered. This reduces uncertainty and prevents accidental repetition.

## Sustaining and Expanding the System

Once your initial hotkey workflow is in place, it’s important to maintain and evolve it. As your projects change and your skills grow, some shortcuts will become obsolete while new ones will emerge. Keep your AHK scripts and Python utilities organized in a version-controlled repository, allowing you to roll back changes and experiment safely.

You might also explore integrating hardware solutions—such as MIDI controllers, programmable keypads, or touch-based interfaces—to further expand your input options. These can be mapped via AHK to trigger the same Python scripts, offering tactile variety and potentially improving speed for certain actions.

---

By combining Python’s scripting capabilities with AutoHotkey’s robust hotkey management, graphic designers can transform their workflows into finely tuned systems that respond instantly to their needs. The result is more time spent on creative exploration and less time lost to repetitive, mechanical tasks—a tangible boost to both productivity and artistic satisfaction.

#  RegExp.input ($_)

**Deprecated:** This feature is no longer recommended. Though some browsers
might still support it, it may have already been removed from the relevant web
standards, may be in the process of being dropped, or may only be kept for
compatibility purposes. Avoid using it, and update existing code if possible;
see the  compatibility table  at the bottom of this page to guide your
decision. Be aware that this feature may cease to work at any time.

**Note:** All ` RegExp ` static properties that expose the last match state
globally are deprecated. See [ deprecated RegExp features ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Deprecated_and_obsolete_features#regexp) for
more information.

The **` RegExp.input ` ** static accessor property returns the string against
which a regular expression is matched. ` RegExp.$_ ` is an alias for this
property.

##  Description

Because ` input ` is a static property of [ ` RegExp ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/RegExp) , you always use it as
` RegExp.input ` or ` RegExp.$_ ` , rather than as a property of a ` RegExp `
object you created.

The value of ` input ` updates whenever a ` RegExp ` (but not a ` RegExp `
subclass) instance makes a successful match. If no matches have been made, `
input ` is an empty string. You can set the value of ` input ` , but this does
not affect other behaviors of the regex, and the value will be overwritten
again when the next successful match is made.

##  Examples

###  Using input and $_

js

    
    
    const re = /hi/g;
    re.test("hi there!");
    RegExp.input; // "hi there!"
    re.test("foo"); // new test, non-matching
    RegExp.$_; // "hi there!"
    re.test("hi world!"); // new test, matching
    RegExp.$_; // "hi world!"

##  Examples

###  Using the Set object

js

    
    
    const mySet1 = new Set();
    
    mySet1.add(1); // Set(1) { 1 }
    mySet1.add(5); // Set(2) { 1, 5 }
    mySet1.add(5); // Set(2) { 1, 5 }
    mySet1.add("some text"); // Set(3) { 1, 5, 'some text' }
    const o = { a: 1, b: 2 };
    mySet1.add(o);
    
    mySet1.add({ a: 1, b: 2 }); // o is referencing a different object, so this is okay
    
    mySet1.has(1); // true
    mySet1.has(3); // false, since 3 has not been added to the set
    mySet1.has(5); // true
    mySet1.has(Math.sqrt(25)); // true
    mySet1.has("Some Text".toLowerCase()); // true
    mySet1.has(o); // true
    
    mySet1.size; // 5
    
    mySet1.delete(5); // removes 5 from the set
    mySet1.has(5); // false, 5 has been removed
    
    mySet1.size; // 4, since we just removed one value
    
    mySet1.add(5); // Set(5) { 1, 'some text', {...}, {...}, 5 } - a previously deleted item will be added as a new item, it will not retain its original position before deletion
    
    console.log(mySet1); // Set(5) { 1, "some text", {â¦}, {â¦}, 5 }

js

    
    
    for (const item of mySet1) {
      console.log(item);
    }
    // 1, "some text", { "a": 1, "b": 2 }, { "a": 1, "b": 2 }, 5

See Notes under [ ` torch.nn.Embedding  ` ](generated/torch.nn.Embedding.html#torch.nn.Embedding "torch.nn.Embedding") for more details regarding sparse gradients.

where V = maximum index + 1 and embedding_dim = the embedding size

#  String.prototype.toLocaleLowerCase()

The **` toLocaleLowerCase() ` ** method of [ ` String ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String) values returns this
string converted to lower case, according to any locale-specific case
mappings.

##  Try it

##  Syntax

js

    
    
    toLocaleLowerCase()
    toLocaleLowerCase(locales)
    

###  Parameters

` locales ` Optional

    

A string with a BCP 47 language tag, or an array of such strings. Indicates
the locale to be used to convert to lower case according to any locale-
specific case mappings. For the general form and interpretation of the `
locales ` argument, see [ the parameter description on the ` Intl ` main page
](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl#locales_argument) .

Unlike other methods that use the ` locales ` argument, ` toLocaleLowerCase()
` does not allow locale matching. Therefore, after checking the validity of
the ` locales ` argument, ` toLocaleLowerCase() ` always uses the first locale
in the list (or the default locale if the list is empty), even if this locale
is not supported by the implementation.

###  Return value

A new string representing the calling string converted to lower case,
according to any locale-specific case mappings.

##  Description

The ` toLocaleLowerCase() ` method returns the value of the string converted
to lower case according to any locale-specific case mappings. `
toLocaleLowerCase() ` does not affect the value of the string itself. In most
cases, this will produce the same result as [ ` toLowerCase() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/toLowerCase) , but for
some locales, such as Turkish, whose case mappings do not follow the default
case mappings in Unicode, there may be a different result.

##  Examples

###  Using toLocaleLowerCase()

js

    
    
    "ALPHABET".toLocaleLowerCase(); // 'alphabet'
    
    "\u0130".toLocaleLowerCase("tr") === "i"; // true
    "\u0130".toLocaleLowerCase("en-US") === "i"; // false
    
    const locales = ["tr", "TR", "tr-TR", "tr-u-co-search", "tr-x-turkish"];
    "\u0130".toLocaleLowerCase(locales) === "i"; // true

# Understanding Python’s `Any` Type and Dynamic Typing Nuances

Python’s dynamic typing has always been one of its defining features. Variables can hold values of any type at any time, and the interpreter does not enforce type constraints during runtime. This flexibility fosters rapid development and prototyping but can also lead to subtle bugs that only surface during execution. With the introduction of type hints in PEP 484, Python gained a layer of optional static type checking, allowing developers to annotate their code with expected types. Within this system, the `Any` type occupies a unique conceptual space.

## The Evolution of Type Hints in Python

Type hints were designed to aid static analysis tools such as MyPy, Pyright, and others. They do not alter the runtime behavior of Python code but provide a form of contract between the developer and tooling. Initially, type hints supported basic types like `int`, `str`, and `list`, along with more complex generics like `List[int]`. Over time, the type system expanded to include concepts such as `Union`, `Optional`, and `Literal` to represent richer constraints.

Among these additions, `Any` was introduced for situations where type information is either unknown, irrelevant, or intentionally unrestricted. It acts as a signal to type checkers that a value can be treated as compatible with any other type.

## The Role of `Any` in Static Type Checking

From a static type checker’s perspective, `Any` is both permissive and opaque. When a variable is annotated as `Any`, the checker allows assignments from values of any type without error. Likewise, values of type `Any` can be assigned to variables of any other type. This bidirectional compatibility effectively disables type enforcement for that variable, making `Any` a tool for bypassing strict type constraints.

For example:

```python
from typing import Any

def process(data: Any) -> None:
    # Static checker accepts any usage of 'data'
    print(data)
```

Here, `process` can be called with an integer, a string, a list, or even a custom class instance. The type checker will not complain about the argument type or how `data` is used inside the function.

This behavior contrasts with other flexible types like `object` in Python’s type hints. While `object` can accept any value, a type checker will restrict operations on it to those available to all objects. `Any`, on the other hand, allows unrestricted operations—calling methods, accessing attributes—without requiring proof they exist.

## Benefits and Risks of Using `Any`

The main advantage of `Any` lies in its ability to allow incremental typing. In large codebases, it is often impractical to annotate every function and variable immediately. By using `Any`, developers can skip over sections of code that are either too complex to type at the moment or rely on dynamic behavior that defies static analysis. This can make adoption of type checking tools smoother.

However, this same permissiveness can undermine the benefits of static typing. Overuse of `Any` can lead to situations where type errors slip through undetected until runtime. It can mask incompatibilities between different parts of the code, reducing the safety net that type hints are meant to provide.

## Practical Strategies for `Any`

Many teams adopt guidelines for `Any` usage. Common strategies include:

- **Temporary Use:** Limit `Any` to transitional code, replacing it with more specific types as understanding improves.
- **Boundary Annotation:** Use `Any` at system boundaries, such as when interfacing with untyped third-party libraries or dynamically loaded data.
- **Minimal Scope:** Annotate only the smallest necessary scope with `Any`—for example, a single parameter—rather than entire functions or modules.

Static type checkers often provide configuration options to warn about excessive use of `Any`, helping maintain discipline in its application.

## Conclusion

`Any` in Python’s type hint system is a powerful construct that enables developers to opt out of static type enforcement when needed. Its flexibility mirrors the dynamic nature of Python itself, but with careful usage, it can coexist with a robust type checking strategy. Understanding how `Any` interacts with the broader type system—and the trade-offs it presents—is essential for leveraging Python’s typing capabilities effectively without sacrificing code reliability.

# Designing JSON-Based REST API Endpoints for Maximum Client Compatibility

In the modern web ecosystem, REST APIs serve as the backbone for communication between diverse client applications—mobile apps, web frontends, IoT devices, and even other backend services. While JSON has become the de facto data exchange format for many APIs, the way endpoints are structured plays a critical role in ensuring compatibility, maintainability, and ease of integration. This article outlines best practices for structuring JSON-based REST endpoints, focusing on URI design, HTTP method usage, and response code conventions.

---

## 1. Crafting Intuitive and Consistent URI Patterns

A well-structured URI should clearly convey the resource it represents and follow a consistent pattern across the API. Consistency reduces cognitive load for developers consuming the API and minimizes integration errors.

**Key recommendations:**
- **Use nouns for resources, not verbs:** For example, `/users` rather than `/getUsers`.
- **Hierarchical relationships:** Express nesting where logical, such as `/users/{user_id}/orders` to indicate orders belonging to a specific user.
- **Pluralization:** Apply plural nouns for collections (`/products`) and singular for specific resources (`/products/{product_id}`).
- **Avoid exposing implementation details:** URIs should describe the resource, not how it is stored or processed.

Consistency in URI structure ensures that clients can predict endpoint patterns and reduces the need for extensive documentation browsing.

---

## 2. Aligning HTTP Methods with Operations

REST principles rely on standard HTTP methods to signal the intended action. Misalignment between method semantics and server behavior can cause confusion and break client compatibility.

**Best practices:**
- **GET:** Retrieve representations of resources without side effects.
- **POST:** Create new resources or trigger actions that result in state changes.
- **PUT:** Replace an existing resource entirely.
- **PATCH:** Apply partial modifications to a resource.
- **DELETE:** Remove a resource.

For example, creating a new order might involve sending a `POST` request to `/orders`, while updating just the shipping address could use `PATCH /orders/{order_id}` with a JSON payload containing the new address field.

---

## 3. Standardizing Response Codes

HTTP status codes provide a universal language for signaling success or failure conditions. Standardizing them across endpoints improves interoperability and makes client-side error handling more predictable.

**Guidelines:**
- **200 OK:** Successful retrieval or update.
- **201 Created:** Resource successfully created; include a `Location` header pointing to the new resource.
- **204 No Content:** Successful operation with no response body (often for DELETE).
- **400 Bad Request:** Invalid input from the client.
- **404 Not Found:** Requested resource does not exist.
- **500 Internal Server Error:** Unexpected server-side failure.

Including meaningful messages in the JSON response body alongside status codes can further aid client developers in diagnosing issues.

---

## 4. Designing for Versioning and Extensibility

As APIs evolve, maintaining backward compatibility is essential for clients that may not upgrade immediately. Versioning strategies help manage this evolution without breaking existing integrations.

**Approaches:**
- **URI-based versioning:** e.g., `/v1/users` and `/v2/users`.
- **Header-based versioning:** Specify desired version in a custom header.
- **Query parameter versioning:** Append `?version=2` to requests (less common in REST).

When introducing new fields in JSON responses, ensure they are optional so older clients can ignore them gracefully.

---

## 5. Consistent JSON Response Structure

Beyond the endpoint design, the structure of the JSON payload itself should follow predictable patterns. Consider wrapping data in a top-level object that may include metadata, links, and the resource collection or object.

Example:
```json
{
  "data": {
    "id": 123,
    "name": "Sample Product"
  },
  "meta": {
    "request_id": "abc-456"
  }
}
```
This approach allows for easy extension without disrupting existing fields, and supports hypermedia-driven designs where links to related resources can be embedded.

The result is a more predictable, developer-friendly API that fosters trust and adoption across diverse platforms.

yields batched samples instead of individual samples. ` batch_size  ` and `
drop_last  ` arguments are used to specify how the data loader obtains batches
of dataset keys. For map-style datasets, users can alternatively specify `
batch_sampler  ` , which yields a list of keys at a time.

Note

The ` batch_size  ` and ` drop_last  ` arguments essentially are used to
construct a ` batch_sampler  ` from ` sampler  ` . For map-style datasets, the
` sampler  ` is either provided by user or constructed based on the ` shuffle
` argument. For iterable-style datasets, the ` sampler  ` is a dummy infinite
one. See  this section  on more details on samplers.

Note

When fetching from  iterable-style datasets  with  multi-processing  , the `
drop_last  ` argument drops the last non-full batch of each worker’s dataset
replica.

After fetching a list of samples using the indices from sampler, the function
passed as the ` collate_fn  ` argument is used to collate lists of samples
into batches.

In this case, loading from a map-style dataset is roughly equivalent with:

    
    
    for indices in batch_sampler:
        yield collate_fn([dataset[i] for i in indices])
    

and loading from an iterable-style dataset is roughly equivalent with:

    
    
    dataset_iter = iter(dataset)
    for indices in batch_sampler:
        yield collate_fn([next(dataset_iter) for _ in indices])
    

A custom ` collate_fn  ` can be used to customize collation, e.g., padding
sequential data to max length of a batch. See  this section  on more about `
collate_fn  ` .

###  Disable automatic batching  ¶

In certain cases, users may want to handle batching manually in dataset code,
or simply load individual samples. For example, it could be cheaper to
directly load batched data (e.g., bulk reads from a database or reading
continuous chunks of memory), or the batch size is data dependent, or the
program is designed to work on individual samples. Under these scenarios, it’s
likely better to not use automatic batching (where ` collate_fn  ` is used to
collate the samples), but let the data loader directly return each member of
the ` dataset  ` object.

When both ` batch_size  ` and ` batch_sampler  ` are ` None  ` (default value
for ` batch_sampler  ` is already ` None  ` ), automatic batching is disabled.
Each sample obtained from the ` dataset  ` is processed with the function
passed as the ` collate_fn  ` argument.

**When automatic batching is disabled** , the default ` collate_fn  ` simply
converts NumPy arrays into PyTorch Tensors, and keeps everything else
untouched.

In this case, loading from a map-style dataset is roughly equivalent with:

    
    
    for index in sampler:
        yield collate_fn(dataset[index])
    

and loading from an iterable-style dataset is roughly equivalent with:

    
    
    for data in iter(dataset):
        yield collate_fn(data)
    

See  this section  on more about ` collate_fn  ` .

###  Working with ` collate_fn  ` ¶

The use of ` collate_fn  ` is slightly different when automatic batching is
enabled or disabled.

**When automatic batching is disabled** , ` collate_fn  ` is called with each
individual data sample, and the output is yielded from the data loader
iterator. In this case, the default ` collate_fn  ` simply converts NumPy
arrays in PyTorch tensors.

**When automatic batching is enabled** , ` collate_fn  ` is called with a list
of data samples at each time. It is expected to collate the input samples into
a batch for yielding from the data loader iterator. The rest of this section
describes behavior of the default ` collate_fn  ` in this case.

For instance, if each data sample consists of a 3-channel image and an

       **Return values from callouts**
    
           The default return from the callout function is zero, which
           allows matching to continue. The **callout_fail** modifier can be
           given one or two numbers. If there is only one number, 1 is

           similar, except that PCRE2_ERROR_CALLOUT is returned, causing the
           entire matching process to be aborted. If both these modifiers
           are set for the same callout number, **callout_error** takes
           precedence. Note that callouts with string arguments are always
           given the number zero.
    
           The **callout_data** modifier can be given an unsigned or a negative
           number.  This is set as the "user data" that is passed to the
           matching function, and passed back when the callout function is
           invoked. Any value other than zero is used as a return from

           Inserting callouts can be helpful when using **pcre2test** to check

The partitions and divisions are how Dask parallelizes computation. A **Dask**
DataFrame is made up of many pandas [ ` pandas.DataFrame  `
](../reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame "pandas.DataFrame")
. A single method call on a Dask DataFrame ends up making many pandas method
calls, and Dask knows how to coordinate everything to get the result.

    
    
    In [36]: ddf.columns
    Out[36]: Index(['id', 'name', 'x', 'y'], dtype='object')
    
    In [37]: ddf.dtypes
    Out[37]: 
    id                int64
    name    string[pyarrow]
    x               float64
    y               float64
    dtype: object
    
    In [38]: ddf.npartitions
    Out[38]: 12
    

One major difference: the ` dask.dataframe  ` API is _lazy_ . If you look at
the repr above, youâll notice that the values arenât actually printed out;
just the column names and dtypes. Thatâs because Dask hasnât actually read
the data yet. Rather than executing immediately, doing operations build up a
**task graph** .

    
    
    In [39]: ddf
    Out[39]: 
    Dask DataFrame Structure:
                       id    name        x        y
    npartitions=12                                 
                    int64  string  float64  float64
                      ...     ...      ...      ...
    ...               ...     ...      ...      ...
                      ...     ...      ...      ...
                      ...     ...      ...      ...
    Dask Name: read-parquet, 1 graph layer
    
    In [40]: ddf["name"]
    Out[40]: 
    Dask Series Structure:
    npartitions=12
        string
           ...
         ...  
           ...
           ...
    Name: name, dtype: string
    Dask Name: getitem, 2 graph layers
    
    In [41]: ddf["name"].value_counts()
    Out[41]: 
    Dask Series Structure:
    npartitions=1
        int64[pyarrow]
                   ...
    Name: count, dtype: int64[pyarrow]
    Dask Name: value-counts-agg, 4 graph layers
    

Each of these calls is instant because the result isnât being computed yet.
Weâre just building up a list of computation to do when someone needs the
result. Dask knows that the return type of a [ ` pandas.Series.value_counts  `
](../reference/api/pandas.Series.value_counts.html#pandas.Series.value_counts
"pandas.Series.value_counts") is a pandas [ ` pandas.Series  `
](../reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series "pandas.Series") with a
certain dtype and a certain name. So the Dask version returns a Dask Series
with the same dtype and the same name.

To get the actual result you can call ` .compute()  ` .

    
    
    In [42]: %time ddf["name"].value_counts().compute()
    CPU times: user 538 ms, sys: 45.8 ms, total: 584 ms
    Wall time: 165 ms
    Out[42]: 
    name
    Charlie    1994875
    Alice      1994645
    Bob        1993692
    Name: count, dtype: int64[pyarrow]
    

At that point, you get back the same thing youâd get with pandas, in this
case a concrete pandas [ ` pandas.Series  `
](../reference/api/pandas.Series.html#pandas.Series "pandas.Series") with the
count of each ` name  ` .

Calling ` .compute  ` causes the full task graph to be executed. This includes
reading the data, selecting the columns, and doing the ` value_counts  ` . The
execution is done _in parallel_ where possible, and Dask tries to keep the
overall memory footprint small. You can work with datasets that are much
larger than memory, as long as each partition (a regular pandas [ `
pandas.DataFrame  ` ](../reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.html#pandas.DataFrame
"pandas.DataFrame") ) fits in memory.

By default, ` dask.dataframe  ` operations use a threadpool to do operations
in parallel. We can also connect to a cluster to distribute the work on many
machines. In this case weâll connect to a local âclusterâ made up of
several processes on this single machine.

    
    
    >>> from dask.distributed import Client, LocalCluster
    
    >>> cluster = LocalCluster()
    >>> client = Clien

###  Remarks

The [ BeginExecuteReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.beginexecutereader?view=dotnet-plat-
ext-8.0) method starts the process of asynchronously executing a Transact-SQL
statement or stored procedure that returns rows, so that other tasks can run
concurrently while the statement is executing. When the statement has
completed, developers must call the [ EndExecuteReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.endexecutereader?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0)
method to finish the operation and retrieve the [ SqlDataReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqldatareader?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0) returned by
the command. The [ BeginExecuteReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.beginexecutereader?view=dotnet-plat-
ext-8.0) method returns immediately, but until the code executes the
corresponding [ EndExecuteReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.endexecutereader?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0)
method call, it must not execute any other calls that start a synchronous or
asynchronous execution against the same [ SqlCommand
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0) object. Calling
the [ EndExecuteReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.endexecutereader?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0)
before the command's execution is completed causes the [ SqlCommand
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0) object to block
until the execution is finished.

Note that the command text and parameters are sent to the server
synchronously. If a large command or many parameters are sent, this method may
block during writes. After the command is sent, the method returns immediately
without waiting for an answer from the server--that is, reads are
asynchronous. Although command execution is asynchronous, value fetching is
still synchronous. This means that calls to [ Read
](system.data.sqlclient.sqldatareader.read?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0) may block
if more data is required and the underlying network's read operation blocks.

Because this overload does not support a callback procedure, developers must
either poll to determine whether the command has completed, using the [
IsCompleted ](system.iasyncresult.iscompleted?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0)
property of the [ IAsyncResult ](system.iasyncresult?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0)
returned by the [ BeginExecuteReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.beginexecutereader?view=dotnet-plat-
ext-8.0) method; or wait for the completion of one or more commands using the
[ AsyncWaitHandle ](system.iasyncresult.asyncwaithandle?view=dotnet-plat-
ext-8.0) property of the returned [ IAsyncResult
](system.iasyncresult?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0) .

If you use [ ExecuteReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.executereader?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0) or
[ BeginExecuteReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.beginexecutereader?view=dotnet-plat-
ext-8.0) to access XML data, SQL Server will return any XML results greater
than 2,033 characters in length in multiple rows of 2,033 characters each. To
avoid this behavior, use [ ExecuteXmlReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.executexmlreader?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0)
or [ BeginExecuteXmlReader
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.beginexecutexmlreader?view=dotnet-plat-
ext-8.0) to read FOR XML queries.

This method ignores the [ CommandTimeout
](system.data.sqlclient.sqlcommand.commandtimeout?view=dotnet-plat-ext-8.0)
property.

To make them more generalizable, these methods don't just accept ` Set `
objects, but anything that's  set-like  .

###  Set-like objects

All  set composition methods  require [ ` this ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/this) to be an actual ` Set `
instance, but their arguments just need to be set-like. A _set-like object_ is
an object that provides the following:

  * A [ ` size ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set/size) property that contains a number. 
  * A [ ` has() ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set/has) method that takes an element and returns a boolean. 
  * A [ ` keys() ` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set/keys) method that returns an [ iterator ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Iteration_protocols) of the elements in the set. 

For example, [ ` Map ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map) objects are set-like
because they also have [ ` size ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map/size) , [ ` has() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map/has) , and [ ` keys() `
](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Map/keys) , so they
behave just like sets of keys when used in set methods:

js

    
    
    const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
    const b = new Map([
      [1, "one"],
      [2, "two"],
      [4, "four"],
    ]);
    console.log(a.union(b)); // Set(4) {1, 2, 3, 4}
    

**Note:** The set-like protocol invokes the ` keys() ` method instead of [ `
[@@iterator]() ` ](/en-
US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Set/@@iterator) to produce
elements. This is to make maps valid set-like objects, because for maps, the
iterator produces _entries_ but the ` has() ` method takes _keys_ .

[ Arrays ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Array) are not
set-like because they don't have a ` has() ` method or the ` size ` property,
and their ` keys() ` method produces indices instead of elements. [ ` WeakSet
` ](/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/WeakSet) objects are
also not set-like because they don't have a ` keys() ` method.

###  Set-like browser APIs

Browser **` Set ` -like objects ** (or "setlike objects") are [ Web API ](/en-
US/docs/Web/API) interfaces that behave in many ways like a ` Set ` .

##  Compliance  ¶

Requests is intended to be compliant with all relevant specifications and RFCs
where that compliance will not cause difficulties for users. This attention to
the specification can lead to some behaviour that may seem unusual to those
not familiar with the relevant specification.

###  Encodings  ¶

When you receive a response, Requests makes a guess at the encoding to use for
decoding the response when you access the [ ` Response.text  `
](../../api/#requests.Response.text "requests.Response.text") attribute.
Requests will first check for an encoding in the HTTP header, and if none is
present, will use [ charset_normalizer
](https://pypi.org/project/charset_normalizer/) or [ chardet
](https://github.com/chardet/chardet) to attempt to guess the encoding.

If ` chardet  ` is installed, ` requests  ` uses it, however for python3 `
chardet  ` is no longer a mandatory dependency. The ` chardet  ` library is an
LGPL-licenced dependency and some users of requests cannot depend on mandatory
LGPL-licensed dependencies.

When you install ` requests  ` without specifying ` [use_chardet_on_py3]  `
extra, and ` chardet  ` is not already installed, ` requests  ` uses `
charset-normalizer  ` (MIT-licensed) to guess the encoding.

The only time Requests will not guess the encoding is if no explicit charset
is present in the HTTP headers **and** the ` Content-Type  ` header contains `
text  ` . In this situation, [ RFC 2616
](https://www.w3.org/Protocols/rfc2616/rfc2616-sec3.html#sec3.7.1) specifies
that the default charset must be ` ISO-8859-1  ` . Requests follows the
specification in this case. If you require a different encoding, you can
manually set the [ ` Response.encoding  `
](../../api/#requests.Response.encoding "requests.Response.encoding")
property, or use the raw [ ` Response.content  `
](../../api/#requests.Response.content "requests.Response.content") .

##  3.12. Recording to a circular stream  ¶

This is similar to  Recording video to a stream  but uses a special kind of
in-memory stream provided by the picamera library. The [ ` PiCameraCircularIO
` ](api_streams.html#picamera.PiCameraCircularIO
"picamera.PiCameraCircularIO") class implements a [ ring buffer
](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circular_buffer) based stream, specifically
for video recording. This enables you to keep an in-memory stream containing
the last _n_ seconds of video recorded (where _n_ is determined by the bitrate
of the video recording and the size of the ring buffer underlying the stream).

A typical use-case for this sort of storage is security applications where one
wishes to detect motion and only record to disk the video where motion was
detected. This example keeps 20 seconds of video in memory until the `
write_now  ` function returns ` True  ` (in this implementation this is random
but one could, for example, replace this with some sort of motion detection
algorithm). Once ` write_now  ` returns ` True  ` , the script waits 10 more
seconds (so that the buffer contains 10 seconds of video from before the
event, and 10 seconds after) and writes the resulting video to disk before
going back to waiting:

    
    
    import io
    import random
    import picamera
    
    def motion_detected():
        # Randomly return True (like a fake motion detection routine)
        return random.randint(0, 10) == 0
    
    camera = picamera.PiCamera()
    stream = picamera.PiCameraCircularIO(camera, seconds=20)
    camera.start_recording(stream, format='h264')
    try:
        while True:
            camera.wait_recording(1)
            if motion_detected():
                # Keep recording for 10 seconds and only then write the
                # stream to disk
                camera.wait_recording(10)
                stream.copy_to('motion.h264')
    finally:
        camera.stop_recording()
    

In the above script we use the special [ ` copy_to()  `
](api_streams.html#picamera.PiCameraCircularIO.copy_to
"picamera.PiCameraCircularIO.copy_to") method to copy the stream to a disk
file. This automatically handles details like finding the start of the first
key-frame in the circular buffer, and also provides facilities like writing a
specific number of bytes or seconds.

Note

Note that _at least_ 20 seconds of video are in the stream. This is an
estimate only; if the H.264 encoder requires less than the specified bitrate
(17Mbps by default) for recording the video, then more than 20 seconds of
video will be available in the stream.

7.2.  Malicious Construction
    
       It is sometimes possible to construct a URI so that an attempt to
       perform a seemingly harmless, idempotent operation, such as the
       retrieval of a representation, will in fact cause a possibly damaging
       remote operation.  The unsafe URI is typically constructed by
       specifying a port number other than that reserved for the network
       protocol in question.  The client unwittingly contacts a site running
       a different protocol service, and data within the URI contains
       instructions that, when interpreted according to this other protocol,
       cause an unexpected operation.  A frequent example of such abuse has
       been the use of a protocol-based scheme with a port component of
       "25", thereby fooling user agent software into sending an unintended
       or impersonating message via an SMTP server.
    
       Applications should prevent dereference of a URI that specifies a TCP
       port number within the "well-known port" range (0 - 1023) unless the
       protocol being used to dereference that URI is compatible with the
       protocol expected on that well-known port.  Although IANA maintains a
       registry of well-known ports, applications should make such
       restrictions user-configurable to avoid preventing the deployment of
       new services.

       When a URI contains percent-encoded octets that match the delimiters

When a pull request is created, whether by a team member or an outside
contributor, it is placed in the “Needs Triage” column of the Triage board
automatically. The pull request should remain in that column until a team
member begins reviewing it.

If the pull request does not have a related issue, then it should be moved
through the normal [ triage process for issues ](./manage-issues) to be marked
as accepted. Once accepted, move the pull request to the “Implementing”
column.

If the pull request does have a related issue, then:

  * If the issue is accepted, move the pull request to the “Implementing” column. 
  * If the issue is not accepted, move the pull request to the “Evaluating” column until the issue is marked as accepted, at which point move the pull request to “Implementing”. 

Once the pull request has one approval, one of three things can happen:

  1. The pull request has the required approvals and the waiting period (see below) has passed so it can be merged. 
  2. The pull request has the required approvals and the waiting period has not passed, so it should be moved to the “Merge Candidates” column. 
  3. The pull request requires another approval before it can be merged, so it should be moved to the “Second Review Needed” column. 

When the pull request has a second approval, it should either be merged (if
100% ready) or moved to the “Merge Candidates” column if there are any
outstanding concerns that should be reviewed before the next release.

##  Who Can Merge a Pull Request

TSC members, reviewers, committers, and website team members may merge pull
requests, depending on the contents of the pull request, once it has received
the required approvals.

Website Team Members may merge a pull request in the ` eslint.org ` repository
if it is:

  1. A documentation change 
  2. A dependency upgrade 
  3. A chore 

##  When to Merge a Pull Request

We use the “Merge” button to merge requests into the repository. Before
merging a pull request, verify that:

  1. All comments have been addressed 
  2. Any team members who made comments have verified that their concerns were addressed 
  3. All automated tests are passing (never merge a pull request with failing tests) 

Be sure to say thank you to the submitter before merging, especially if they
put a lot of work into the pull request.

Team members may merge a pull request immediately if it:

  1. Makes a small documentation change 
  2. Is a chore 
  3. Fixes a block of other work on the repository (build-related, test-related, dependency-related, etc.) 
  4. Is an important fix to get into a patch release 

Otherwise, team members should observe a waiting period before merging a pull
request:

  * Wait **2 days** if the pull request was opened Monday through Friday. 
  * Wait **3 days** if the pull request was opened on Saturday or Sunday. 

The waiting period ensures that other team members have a chance to review the
pull request before it is merged.

**Note:** You should not merge your pull request unless you receive the
required approvals.

##  When to Close a Pull Request

There are several times when it’s appropriate to close a pull request without
merging:

  1. The pull request addresses an issue that is already fixed. 
  2. The pull request hasn’t been updated in 17 days. 
  3. The pull request submitter isn’t willing to follow project guidelines. 

In any of these cases, please be sure to leave a comment stating why the pull
request is being closed.

If a pull request hasn’t been updated in 17 days:
